Part II · Constructing the arithmetic inputs›Ch. 4 · From the global theta function to an integral jet›§4.1 The normalized function on a pair of lattices

To use a local coefficient estimate in a global height argument, the bound must hold for the theta function defining the actual map. Start with its Taylor series at a chosen algebraic embedding. The task is to express it as an integral series composed with an inverse logarithm and multiplied by an explicit exponential. In those coordinates the preceding chapter bounds each derivative. A determinant of derivatives then gives a matrix entry.

4.1The normalized function on a pair of lattices

Fix a nonzero ideal 𝔠 in the imaginary quadratic field K = ℚ(√−d), with d positive and squarefree as in the host construction. Require the absolute norm of 𝔠 to be coprime to 2d. Embed it in ℂ to obtain a period lattice Λ₀. Its discriminant is Δ(Λ₀) = g₂(Λ₀)³ − 27g₃(Λ₀)². Choose a nonzero δ with δ¹² = Δ(Λ₀) and use Λ = δΛ₀. Scaling each lattice point multiplies the Eisenstein sums defining g₂ and g₃ by δ⁻⁴ and δ⁻⁶. Consequently Δ(Λ) = δ⁻¹²Δ(Λ₀) = 1. This fixes the discriminant while allowing the twelfth-root choices in the construction.

In one variable, let F(z) be the Weierstrass sigma function multiplied by exp(−s₂z²/2). Choose a representative t of a nonzero two-torsion point. Translating F shifts its argument to z + t and multiplies it by exp(−πh(z,t) − πh(t,t)/2), where h(z,t) = z conj(t)/area(Λ). Divide the translated function by its value at z = 0. The constant exponential cancels, leaving exp(−πh(z,t)) F(z + t)/F(t). Its value at the origin is 1. The denominator is nonzero since the zeros of sigma are the lattice points. In the base datum a theta vector θM satisfies a fourth-tensor-power identity with the prescribed scalar κ and fourfold kernel. The existence and nonvanishing statements use the standard model hypotheses. Form the tensor product Θ₀(z) = ∏a,b θM(z·,a,b) on a pair of standard lattices of ranks N,N′.

Let L,L′ be self-dual lattices of even ranks N,N′. Write IA,B for the operator that changes a period lattice A to B. It sums the Hermitian translates over B/(A ∩ B), weights them by the semicharacter, and divides by √[B : A ∩ B]. First move the first lattice, then the second. Write dL and dL′ for their determinant ideals relative to the respective standard lattices. Here χ acts on determinant ideals. It is multiplicative on fractional ideals whose product with their conjugates is the unit ideal. On the principal ideal of a unitary element z it takes the product of the inverses of the chosen embeddings of z. The resulting family is

eχ(L,L′) = χ(dL)N′/2 χ(dL′)−N/2 I1,2I0,1Θ₀.

Here 0, 1 and 2 denote the period lattices for (standard, standard), (L, standard) and (L,L′). It enters the jet comparison with both character powers and the two square-root index normalizations.

4.2Which series represents the actual kernel?

Fix a stage i of the iterated construction and adjacent classes c,c′. Let H be the complex kernel between them. Fix a place of residue characteristic p satisfying the level-freeness condition and an embedding λ of the algebraic numbers into ℂp. The kernel comparison first proves that the two lattices are admitted. The parity comes from the even starting rank and the even rank increment. The tied data identify H with the prescribed kernel on those lattices. The kernel law expresses it as a finite sum H = ∑k akUtₖeχ. Here Ut is the Hermitian translate, including its exponential factor. Every tk has an annihilating positive integer prime to p modulo the period lattice. The coefficients ak are algebraic and |λ(ak)|p ≤ 1. The general combination condition permits lattices agreeing after localization at p. This kernel proof uses the same two lattices in every summand.

For a multi-index α, write Tα(H) = ∂αH(0)/∏jαj!. Algebraicity of the translated Taylor coefficients gives a coefficientwise identity of actual power series,

λ(Tα(H)) = ∑k λ(ak) λ(Tα(Utₖeχ)).

Differentiate the finite sum and divide each term by the same multi-factorial. Its summands are algebraic, so λ respects this finite sum and each product. Thus these coefficients lie in the domain of the chosen field embedding.

4.3Where the integral series comes from

Assume p ≥ 5 and the quadratic symbol (−d/p) equals −1. Use a Weierstrass change of variables giving integral coefficients and discriminant 1. Its formal parameter series must satisfy its Weierstrass equation. This fixes the invariant differential whose formal integral, with constant term zero, is the logarithm used in the substitution. Choose a basis b of the matrix lattice after localization at p, orthonormal for the trace Hermitian form. The local basis conditions permit denominators coprime to p in both changes of coordinates. If G is a Taylor series of the preceding form, the inert integrality theorem asserts that G, evaluated in the formal logarithm coordinates on this basis and multiplied by the correcting product, has all coefficients in the valuation ring. For odd p the product has one inverse sigma-derived factor for each coordinate.

The proof starts with a 2-by-2 block. Its four matrix entries each carry all the embedding coordinates. A translate of the tensor-product theta function factors into the four translates of the one-entry function at their projected torsion points. The logarithm substitution acts block by block, and the correcting product splits over the same four blocks. Relabelling each integral one-entry series and multiplying the four gives integral coefficients by the finite convolution formula for each monomial. The orthonormal basis can then be changed by the proved local invariance.

Tensoring the resulting translated functions and changing between integral orthonormal bases proves the assertion for even standard ranks. For lattices agreeing locally with the standard ones, the two index operators and character factors yield an integral finite linear combination of those translates. For an arbitrary admitted pair, weak approximation supplies unitary changes of basis taking it to such a locally standard pair. Covariance of the normalized family and compatibility of pullback with prime-to-p torsion transport the assertion back. Finally, for every monomial α, the ultrametric inequality gives |∑k rkuk,α|p ≤ maxk |rk|p|uk,α|p ≤ 1. The constructions supplying weak approximation, torsion pullback, the fourfold block and basis invariance are identified explicitly by the realization theorem.

The passage to the coordinates used for the valuation estimate assumes that the host classifies p as inert or signal. Each of these classes implies the quadratic-symbol condition used above. Given the genus-one model and the comparison between its curve coordinates and the theta coordinates, the proof supplies g₂, g₃, s₂ and a unit ε in the completed maximal unramified field. The construction matches the period lattice of that model to the lattice in the global theta datum. Weak approximation supplies an orthonormal local basis and the curve comparison translates the preceding product into the following exact form. Write ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 T(p²)ʲ/pj. Write φ for the model’s one-variable correcting series and Θb for the series in the scaled orthonormal coordinates. Then

V(X) = exp(∑j φ(Xj)) Θb(ℓ(X₁), …, ℓ(Xr)),   |[Xα]V|p ≤ 1.

The scaling of Θb is a unit. This identity fixes the plus sign when extracting the integral factor. Solving for the theta series restores an exponential with the opposite sign. The correcting series has constant term zero, so the factor at zero is 1.

4.4Passing to the frame used by the jet

The standard bases P,P′ at the embeddings of the coefficient field satisfy a local basis condition and a Frobenius-conjugate transpose identity. On the relevant inert and signal classes the standard scalar at each embedding is 1. Frame compatibility expresses the unit-scaled standard series as the orthonormal one evaluated at hyperbolic linear forms. Their Gram relations, together with a pair of trace-dual bases, allow passage to cyclic Frobenius-orbit coordinates. The all-orbits result requires a common even orbit length of at least 2, p ≥ 5, and either the inert class with nonzero hp or the signal class. A unit c and a standard correcting series are chosen before the ranks, lattice pairs, bases and Taylor combinations.

For a place label v and a fixed matrix entry, let v−2j denote the label reached by stepping back 2j times along its Frobenius cycle. The orbit logarithm has the form ℓv(X) = ∑j≥0 Xv−2j(p²)ʲ/pj. Let AR be the sum of the model’s standard orbit corrections over one representative from each orbit and all matrix entries, with the sign stripped off. In the all-places formula the realized sign is −1 at every representative. For the standard series Θstd of the actual entry one obtains

Θstd(c ℓ(X)) = U(X) exp(−AR(ℓ(X))),   |[Xα]U|p ≤ 1.

Here ℓ is the full vector of orbit logarithms. One factor in the proof is especially simple to check. Relabel the coordinate (r,s), consisting of an orbit representative and a position on its cycle, by the associated place. This map is bijective. Under an injective variable relabelling, a monomial has either its unique original coefficient or zero. Thus relabelling the integral factor preserves its bound. Composing the inverse logarithm with the logarithm removes that substitution on the integral factor. The exponential terms from each orbit assemble into the displayed sum. Applied to the actual kernel, the proof obtains P,P′ from the adapted bases, verifies both standard-basis conditions, rewrites the entry using the supplied frame equality and inserts the combination proved above.

4.5Recovering the differentiated coefficients

Set Y = ℓ(X) and write B for the inverse change of variables, so X = B(Y). The orbit identity now reads Θstd(cY) = U(B(Y)) exp(−AR(Y)). The inverse-logarithm bound controls the first factor, and the mixed-derivative bounds pay for the exponential. In derivative order κ, scaling every variable on the left by c multiplies the value at the origin by c|κ|. Since c is a local unit, its valuation contribution is zero.

A Young diagram at each orbit label prescribes a product P(X,Z) of determinants. The variables X record the frame and the variables Z specify the differential operator. Write this finite polynomial as ∑ aαβXαZβ. Applying it to a theta series at the origin is the concrete operation

[Xα]P(X,∂)Θ(0) = ∑β aαβ (∏j βj!) [Zβ]Θ.

For example, choosing one column of height 1 gives ∑a Xa∂a,bΘ(0). Two such columns in the same component produce second derivatives. A repeated derivative multiplies its degree-two Taylor coefficient by 2!. The coefficient estimate holds for every permitted choice of columns and every frame monomial. The proof recovers an integral orbit factor from the established expansion, checks that each column height fits the row dimension, passes through the unit-scaled frame, and invokes the weighted bound for its product of minors. For the inert branch used in the no-extra-operator estimate, it proves an integral bound and a shape-dependent gain separately and takes the stronger of the two after the numerical comparison.

A two-row entry. Take one column of height two at one label, two source rows, two target columns, and choose the two target columns in order. The factor in the defining polynomial is det(XZ) for two 2 × 2 matrices. Since det(XZ) = det(X)det(Z), its coefficient at X₁₁X₂₂ is Z₁₁Z₂₂ − Z₁₂Z₂₁. Replacing the Z’s by derivatives and evaluating gives ∂₁₁∂₂₂Θ(0) − ∂₁₂∂₂₁Θ(0). If the two derivative valuations are ≥ B, the ultrametric inequality gives the same lower bound for this entry, including when the two values cancel. This example explains why a bound on each differentiated monomial survives the alternating signs of a minor. Establishing that a global map has nonzero image is a separate rank calculation.

The pinned proof assembles this inert calculation with different results at conjugating Frobenius, at the distinguished discriminant prime, and away from it. The resulting kernel conditions join the twisted and untwisted admissibility argument. The family-size proof uses that admissibility together with further row, counting and comparison inputs to produce the uniform divisibility hypothesis. The prime classification supplies the other local bounds. The evaluation at the base tuple uses a separate positive-dimensional quotient. The global chapter follows the remaining uniform estimates.

4.6Which estimate belongs to which prime?

Fix a word, a twist μ, a step i and adjacent lattice classes. Let p be the residue characteristic of the chosen place. The entry estimates below require the place to be free of the level. Here p differs from the word’s level prime and its two designated type primes, and lies outside the twist set Q(μ). A different condition classifies p using the arithmetic data of the host. Keeping these two tests distinct lets us apply the result to a particular matrix entry.

First come the primes dividing the host integer QS, a set which includes 2. The distinguished primes q and d each form a separate class. Outside these three classes, the Jacobi symbol (−d/p) = 1 gives the split class. Otherwise there are two inert classes, distinguished by whether the host character takes value 1. Call the first the signal class. In the last two cases the symbol equals −1 because coprimality with the prime d rules out zero.

What the integral host supplies at an inert prime

For p ≥ 5 in either inert class the construction chooses a scalar c of norm one, a good CM curve model and a Frobenius lift on its unramified coefficient field. These choices work simultaneously for every admitted pair of lattices at this prime and embedding. For each pair it then chooses an orthonormal local matrix basis. Every allowed integral linear combination of prime-to-p torsion translates has an integral power series after the formal-logarithm substitution and multiplication by the curve’s correcting exponential. This order of choices ensures that the law and correcting series agree across the summands. The proof transfers the period lattice and embedding to the curve model, obtains its Frobenius and logarithm law, and uses weak approximation to choose the local bases.

The local formulas depend on the Frobenius coordinate h in the host’s finite additive group. Write a for its additive order. If p is in the signal class, the orbit length is 2·ord(2h). In the ordinary inert class it is a. The chain assumes its split-prime bound is at least three, which puts the two inert classes in the range p ≥ 5. On level-free places the same host feeds the following calculations.

  • Signal primes, and ordinary inert primes with even a, use the all-place expansion with one correction per orbit representative.
  • At an ordinary inert prime with h = 0, a = 1. At each place label the correction begins as a two-variable series. Its variables specialize to X and εX with |ε| = 1. After substitution, one half of the signed correction contributes to the exponential, alongside a coefficientwise integral factor.
  • If h ≠ 0 has odd order a, one instead obtains an orbit product using a correction on 2a variables, a unit scale and signs at representatives. Its auxiliary root of unity has order p2a − 1. This is the odd-degree lattice-pair theorem applied to the same integral host and adapted bases.

Building the curve at an inert prime

The local theta estimate needs an elliptic curve with good reduction and a coordinate over the same ring in which to compare its formal logarithm with the height-two logarithm. Fix a prime p ≥ 5 with (−d/p) = −1 and an embedding of the algebraic numbers into ℂp. Write U for the completed maximal unramified extension of ℚp inside ℂp and W for its ring of integers. The curve construction works for this embedding and every permitted curve ideal. The global theorem uses it at inert-class and signal primes. Level freeness is an additional condition when the resulting theta estimate is applied to matrix entries.

Let 𝔠 be the nonzero ideal in the imaginary quadratic field K = ℚ(√−d), with norm prime to 2d. In the chosen complex embedding write Λ = δ𝔠, where δ12 = Δ(𝔠) and Δ denotes the lattice discriminant. The local construction first needs the ideal norm prime to p. Inertness makes (p) a prime ideal, so we can factor 𝔠 = (p)k𝔠′ with p coprime to the norm of 𝔠′. Take δ′ = pkδ. Then δ′𝔠′ = Λ exactly, and Δ(𝔠) = p−12kΔ(𝔠′) gives (δ′)12 = Δ(𝔠′). The theta section will see the same lattice.

Obtaining a good equation. Let J be the embedded j-invariant of Λ. The CM integrality theorem gives v(J) ≥ 0, where v(p) = 1. To put J in U, the proof shows inertia fixes it. A finite set of primes is discarded so that distinct roots of a monic integral polynomial for J remain distinct after reduction. Chebotarev gives a degree-one Frobenius with the same action as a specified inertia element on these roots and the same Artin class. This class is trivial on inertia. The CM Frobenius congruence at the resulting principal prime identifies the reduction of the Frobenius image with that of J. Separation makes the two roots equal.

When J differs from 0 and 1728, two CM valuation theorems give integers a,b ≥ 0 with v(J) = 3a and v(J − 1728) = 2b. Set C = 27J/(J − 1728), t = pb−a, and put

G₂ = t²C,   G₃ = t³C,   G₂³ − 27G₃² = t⁶C²(C − 27).

Since 27 and 1728 are units, v(C) = 3a − 2b and v(C − 27) = −2b. The two invariants therefore have valuations a,b, while the discriminant has valuation 6(b − a) + 2(3a − 2b) − 2b = 0. This gives the equation y² = x³ − (G₂/4)x − G₃/4 over W, with nonsingular reduction. For J = 0 and 1728 the corresponding invariant pairs are (0,1) and (1,0). In each case a change of scale over ℂp identifies the equation with the original curve. The normalized lattice has discriminant one, so this scale has norm one. The same comparison proves the normalized period invariants algebraic, ensuring that extending the given embedding to the complex numbers respects their original images.

Obtaining a coordinate over the same ring. Let LE be the curve’s formal logarithm, eE its compositional inverse and σ the unramified Frobenius. Put ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 Tp2j/pj. Inertness exchanges the CM generator ω = (1 + √−d)/2 and 1 − ω under σ. Their difference is a unit and σ² fixes ω. Using the integral CM endomorphism and a unit coefficient of multiplication by p in degree at most p², the formal-group theorem gives a unit c such that LE(T) − (c/p) · (σ²LE)(Tp²) has integral coefficients. Here σ acts on the coefficients. Choose a unit ε with ε = cσ²(ε). Dividing the logarithm by ε now gives a functional equation with factor 1/p, the same factor seen in ℓ(T) − ℓ(Tp²)/p = T. The comparison theorem gives

Θ(T) = eE(εℓ(T)) ∈ W[[T]],   Θ(0) = 0,   Θ′(0) = ε.

This Θ is a formal change of coordinate. Because its linear coefficient is a unit, its inverse also has coefficients in W. Substitution gives ℓ(Θ−1(T)) = ε−1LE(T), the isomorphism required by the genus-one datum. The host next applies its separate curve-to-theta comparison, followed by the integral expansion in an orthonormal frame. The next two arguments explain the CM Frobenius congruence and the formal-group functional equation. The CM valuation divisibilities enter the construction of the good equation.

Check the ideal and the Frobenius for discriminant −23 at 5

Take K = ℚ(√−23) and ω = (1 + √−23)/2. Its integer ring is ℤ[ω], with ω² − ω + 6 = 0. Modulo 5, the discriminant −23 is 2, a nonsquare. Thus (5) is inert and has norm 25, coprime to 46. Start with 𝔠 = (5) and δ12 = Δ(5𝒪K). The replacement is 𝔠′ = 𝒪K, δ′ = 5δ. Both choices give exactly the lattice 5δ𝒪K. In the residue field ℤ[ω]/(5) one has ω² = ω − 1, hence ω³ = −1 and ω⁵ = 1 − ω. Arithmetic Frobenius really does exchange the roots, while (1 − 2ω)² ≡ 2 mod 5 verifies the unit difference. The first terms of the matching logarithm are T + T25/5 + T625/25. The calculation uses only these local data of the host construction.

Which Frobenius fixes the invariant, and which exchanges the CM roots?

The good model and its formal coordinate use Frobenius at two different primes. To place the singular modulus J in the unramified field at the target prime p, the proof must show that inertia at p fixes J. It tests an inertia element on the roots of an integral polynomial for J using an auxiliary prime ideal 𝔮 of the quadratic field. Chebotarev selects 𝔮 outside the finite set where two distinct roots can reduce to the same value, and its residue field has prime cardinality q. The chosen arithmetic Frobenius φ agrees with the inertia element on these roots and has the same ideal class under Artin reciprocity. That class is trivial, so 𝔮 is principal. The congruence needed is Jq ≡ J at this auxiliary place. The target inert ideal (p) has residue field of size p².

How a principal ideal gives the congruence for J

Write the complex period lattice as a nonzero scalar times ℤτ + ℤ. If 𝔮 has generator α = a + bω, multiplication by α preserves the lattice. Express ατ and α in the basis (τ,1) as Aτ + B and Cτ + D. The resulting integer matrix has determinant Norm(α) = q and fixes τ under the fractional linear action. Up to a determinant-one change of basis, the q + 1 matrices indexing the degree-q correspondence send τ to qτ or to (τ + b)/q for 0 ≤ b < q. Thus one of these points τ′ has j(τ′) = j(τ) = J.

Here is why a square occurs in the calculation. Put F = E₄³ and D = Δ, so j = F/D. Form the product G over these q + 1 points of F(τ)D(τ′) − F(τ′)D(τ). The equal j-values give G(τ) = 0. To compute the product modulo 1 − ζq, use the Fourier parameter y = exp(2πiτ/q) and write B = FDq − FqD for the corresponding series. Reduction sets ζq = 1 and takes place in characteristic q, where an integral series satisfies F(yq) = F(y)q. The factor for qτ becomes B(yq). Each of the other q factors becomes −B(y), so their product is −B(yq). The two groups together give the negative square.

The modular-form expansion theorem expresses G + B² as (1 − ζq)Δ2(q+1)Q(j), with Q a polynomial over ℤ[ζq]. At τ, divide by the nonzero power of Δ. This gives the first identity below with r = Q(J) an algebraic integer. The cyclotomic binomial identity gives (1 − ζq)q = qr₀ with r₀ integral, yielding the second.

(Jq − J)² = (1 − ζq)r,   (Jq − J)2q = qr₀rq.

At every extension of the valuation at 𝔮 the right side of the second identity reduces to zero. Hence Jq − J reduces to zero there too. Arithmetic Frobenius gives φ(J) ≡ Jq, so φ(J) and J are two roots with the same reduction. The choice of 𝔮 now gives equality in characteristic zero. The original inertia element has the same action on J, as required for the good model.

At the target prime p the calculation concerns the CM endomorphism ω = (1 + √−d)/2. Let δ = 1 − 2ω, so δ² = −d. Its reduction is a unit because p ∤ d. Inertness gives (−d)(p−1)/2 ≡ −1 modulo p. Multiplying by δ shows δp ≡ −δ. Lift δ into the completed unramified field by Hensel’s lemma. Its arithmetic Frobenius σ preserves δ², so σδ is one of ±δ. Reduction gives σδ ≡ δp ≡ −δ. The two signs remain distinct because 2δ is a unit. Thus σω = 1 − ω exactly, σ²ω = ω, and σω − ω is a unit. These last two properties enter the height-two formal-group comparison for the chosen coordinate.

Two primes for discriminant −23. At the target p = 5, δ² ≡ 2 and δ⁵ ≡ 4δ = −δ modulo 5. For an auxiliary example take τ = ω and α = 5 + 2ω. Since ω² = ω − 6, multiplication gives ατ = 7τ − 12 and α = 2τ + 5. The matrix has determinant 7·5 − (−12)·2 = 59. Thus (α) has prime norm 59 and the congruence at this ideal is J59 ≡ J. This example checks the congruence for a principal ideal. Applying it to a specified inertia element still requires the root-separation and Frobenius conditions in the first paragraph.

Why does the CM action have integral coefficients in the curve coordinate?

The Frobenius calculation distinguishes the linear multiplier α from its conjugate. The next argument uses a formal power series with this linear term. Let λ be the formal logarithm of the good elliptic curve and e its inverse. In characteristic zero, multiplication by α must act in the curve coordinate T as M(T) = e(αλ(T)). Even λ can have a denominator divisible by p. We need to know why every coefficient of this particular composition belongs to the valuation ring R = {x : |x|p ≤ 1}.

Take a CM lattice stable under ω = (1 + √−d)/2, with d ≡ 3 mod 4, and a good model at an inert prime p ≥ 5 with p ∤ d. The model supplies a rescaled lattice with the same CM action. Put n = (d + 1)/4 and let α be the image of ω. Its equation gives α(1 − α) = n. If p divided n, then −d ≡ 1 mod p, contradicting inertness. Both factors are integral roots of the monic quadratic, and their product is a unit. Thus α and 1 − α are units. Including the origin, the kernel of multiplication by ω on the complex torus has exactly n points.

What enters the coordinate formula? Choose representatives of its n − 1 nonzero points. For a representative P, ωP is a lattice point, and so is ω²P by stability. Their difference is nP. The prime-to-p torsion estimate therefore applies. In that estimate the product of max(1, |xQ|p) over the nonzero n-torsion representatives is at most 1. Every factor is at least 1, so each xQ is integral. Periodicity gives the same for xP. The good Weierstrass equation then bounds the other coordinate yP = ℘′(P)/2. For example, at d = 23 and p = 5, the five nonzero kernel points are all killed by 6. This distinction matters because the product bound uses the full 6-torsion, while the endomorphism formula sums over just those five points.

How does a squared coordinate determine every coefficient?

The curve’s x-coordinate has a double pole at the origin. Write A(T) = T²x(T) for the regularized coordinate, with constant term 1. The addition formula expresses the coordinate after applying the isogeny in terms of its translates by the kernel points. Clearing the pole gives an integral series V with V(0) = 1. In detail, the correction to A is T²(∑P(x+P(T) − xP) − r). Here x+P is the coordinate after translation on the curve, and r is the integral constant from the change of Weierstrass coordinates. Since M(0) = 0 and M′(0) = α ≠ 0, write M = αTg with g(0) = 1. Cancelling the common factor α²T² from the coordinate identity gives

g(T)² = A(αTg(T)) · V(T)−1.

Suppose the coefficients of g of degrees below k are integral, for k ≥ 1. The extra T in αTg means these coefficients already determine the right side through degree k. Inverting V costs no denominator because its constant term is 1. On the left the unknown gk occurs twice, each time multiplied by g₀ = 1. All remaining products have smaller indices. Thus

2gk = [Tk] A(αTg)V−1 − ∑1 ≤ i < k gigk−i.

Both terms on the right are integral, and 2 is a unit at p. This proves the next coefficient is integral and starts the induction at k = 1. Consequently M = αTg has integral coefficients.

See the cancellation on the good curve at 5

For d = 3 the good j = 0 model has equation y² = x³ − 1/4. Its logarithm has terms only in degrees 6j + 1. The multiplier satisfies α² − α + 1 = 0, hence α⁶ = 1. In every surviving degree α6j+1 = α, so λ(αT) = αλ(T). Applying the inverse series gives M(T) = αT exactly. For instance λ₂₅ = 99/1280 has a denominator divisible by 5, while the coefficient of degree 25 in M is zero. The explicit logarithm is calculated in the good-model example. For a general CM lattice the coefficient induction replaces this sixth-root symmetry.

The height-two proof uses two facts about this same series. Its coefficients are integral, so one can reduce it at p. Its derivative α is exchanged with 1 − α under Frobenius. The resulting difference is a unit, which is used in the two Frobenius steps.

Why the two logarithms give an integral change of coordinate

At the inert prime, the theta calculation uses the elliptic logarithm λ in one coordinate and the explicit series ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 T(p²)j/pj in another. Both have denominators. We want to match them by a substitution whose coefficients, and those of its inverse, are integral. Fix a squarefree d ≡ 3 mod 4, a complex period lattice stable under (1 + √−d)/2, and a prime p ≥ 5 at which −d is a nonzero nonsquare. Choose an embedding as in the good-model construction and any resulting good equation. Its invariants belong to the ring of integers W of the completed maximal unramified extension U of ℚp, with unit discriminant. Normalize the valuation by v(p) = 1. Write σ for the isometric arithmetic Frobenius on U, τ = σ² and q = p². On W, reduction of τ takes an element to its qth power.

Where the square in p² comes from. Let e(T) = [p](T) denote multiplication by p in the elliptic formal group. It has integral coefficients and λ(e(T)) = pλ(T), with λ′(0) = 1. The invariant differential λ′ has integral coefficients. Differentiation shows e′ ≡ 0 mod p, because λ′(e) has constant coefficient 1. Hence the reduction has the shape D(Tp). Let α be the image of (1 + √−d)/2. The integral CM endomorphism [α] commutes with [p]. After this first descent, D intertwines the Frobenius twist of [α] with [α] modulo p. Comparing linear terms gives (σα − α)D′(0) ≡ 0. The two roots are distinct modulo p, so D′(0) ≡ 0. For a formal group homomorphism, differentiating the addition identity transports its derivative at the origin to every coefficient of its derivative, using the unit invariant differentials. Thus D′ ≡ 0 and e(T) ≡ H(Tq) mod p. The torsion product calculation below gives a unit coefficient of e in some degree at most q. Its constant term is zero, so the first such degree must be exactly q. This degree is what height two means here.

The sigma product for an isogeny

Write F(z) = exp(−s₂z²/2) σ(z) for the normalized sigma function of the lattice Λ. Let α ≠ 0 satisfy αΛ ⊆ Λ, and let S contain one representative of each nonzero class of α−1Λ/Λ. The size of the full kernel is d = 1 + |S| = |α|². Indeed multiplication by α identifies this quotient with Λ/αΛ, and multiplies the area of a fundamental parallelogram by |α|². For z outside Λ the multiplication formula is

F(αz)² = α² F(z)2d ∏P∈S(℘(z) − ℘(P)).

To prove it, set BP(z) = −F(z + P)F(z − P)/F(P)². The sigma addition formula gives BP(z) = F(z)²(℘(z) − ℘(P)). The exponential factors match because (z + P)² + (z − P)² = 2z² + 2P². The entire function on the right is therefore represented by α²F(z)² ∏PBP(z). Weierstrass sigma addition formula[8].

The two entire functions vanish to order two on each kernel class. At zero this comes from the squared sigma factors. On a nonzero class Q, one zero comes from the unique choice P ≡ Q and one from P ≡ −Q. When Q = −Q in the quotient, both zeros occur in the same factor. There are no other zeros, since sigma has simple zeros precisely on Λ. Thus the quotient extends holomorphically through every kernel point. Zeros and quasi-periods of sigma[9].

Under a period shift ω, the exponential multiplier of F(z) is exp(πh(z,ω) + πh(ω,ω)/2), up to sign, with h(z,ω) = z conj(ω)/area(Λ). Each BP has the squared multiplier because the shifts by ±P cancel in the exponent. The same multiplier occurs a total of d times in the product, exactly the power on the left since h(αz,αω) = |α|²h(z,ω). The quotient is periodic, hence bounded on the plane by its maximum on a closed fundamental parallelogram. Liouville’s theorem makes it constant. Finally F(z)/z → 1 and each BP(0) = 1 by oddness. Both sides have leading term α²z², so the constant is one. Liouville’s theorem[10].

For α = p, the formula has p² − 1 factors. In the local curve parameter T, each ℘ difference contributes a denominator T², whereas the power of normalized sigma starts in degree 2p². Their difference leaves the initial degree two in the formal multiplication formula. The integral unit and the bound on the first surviving coefficient are established in the next argument.

How elliptic torsion puts a unit coefficient within degree p²

Why must the reduction of e(T) = [p](T) have a nonzero term by degree p²? Fix the good elliptic model above, with p ≥ 5. Its formal group law gives the integral series e by adding a point to itself p times. Its constant term is zero. To bound the degree, represent the curve by the corresponding complex torus ℂ/Λ. Its p-torsion is (p−1Λ)/Λ, with p choices in each of the two lattice directions. Take one representative P of each of its p² − 1 nonzero points. Write xP for its Weierstrass ℘-value transported into ℂp by the chosen field isomorphism. The representatives P and −P each contribute a factor.

In the local parameter T = −x/y, the series A(T) = T²x(T) is integral with constant term 1. The sigma multiplication formula in the integral curve model gives an integral series U with U(0) = 1 and the following factorization.

e(T)² = T²U(T)G(T),   G(T) = p² ∏P(A(T) − xPT²).
Why is the extra power series an integral unit?

Let R be the valuation ring and φ the correcting series of the good curve model, with φ(0) = 0. Write qₘ = φ([m](T)) for multiplication by an integer m in the formal group. For series with zero constant term write a ≡ b if exp(a − b) has all coefficients in R. Its constant term is one, so its inverse also has coefficients in R. Consequently these congruences can be added, subtracted and multiplied by integers.

The two curve identities used here say that the addition defect of φ is biadditive modulo this congruence and that q−1 ≡ φ. The second uses that 2 is a unit in R. Denote the defect on (T,T) by B = q₂ − 2φ. Applying biadditivity to (T,[m](T)) gives qm+1 ≡ φ + qₘ + mB. At m = −1 this reads 0 ≡ 2φ − B, because q₀ = 0. Thus successive differences satisfy qm+1 − qₘ ≡ (2m + 1)φ. Summation gives qₚ ≡ p²φ.

After the change to the formal parameter, the sigma identity reads e² exp(−2qₚ) T2(p²−1) = G T2p² exp(−2p²φ). Cancel the common power of T. The remaining factor is U = exp(2(qₚ − p²φ)), the square of the integral unit given by the congruence. In particular multiplying by U preserves the first nonzero degree after reduction.

For each factor, the maximum coefficient norm is max(1, |xP|p). It is first attained in degree 0 if |xP|p ≤ 1, and degree 2 otherwise. In a product the first degrees attaining the maxima add. At their sum the product of the first maximal coefficients is the unique summand of largest norm. Thus G attains its maximum coefficient norm M = |p²|p ∏P max(1, |xP|p) by degree 2(p² − 1). Also M ≤ 1 because G = U−1(e/T)² is integral.

What forces that maximum to equal one? Choose a nonzero half-period and let h be its transported ℘-value. It solves 4h³ − g₂h − g₃ = 0. Good reduction makes h integral and 3h² − g₂/4 a unit, since the reduced cubic has distinct roots. The torsion product identity at the half-period gives |p²|p ∏P|h − xP|p = 1. Each factor is bounded by max(1, |xP|p), so 1 ≤ M. Now reduce the squared multiplication formula modulo the maximal ideal. Multiplication by U preserves the first nonzero degree, and T² adds two. Hence the first nonzero degree of the reduced e² is at most 2(p² − 1) + 2 = 2p². Squaring doubles the first degree of a nonzero series over a field, giving the claimed bound. The two descents at an inert CM prime separately force that first degree to be a positive multiple of p². Together the arguments identify it exactly.

A good curve whose first unit occurs before degree 25

At p = 5 take y² = x³ − x. Its discriminant 64 is a unit. Write x = u−2 and y = −u−3√(1 − u⁴), taking the square root with constant term 1. Then T = u + u⁵/2 + O(u⁹) and the invariant differential gives dλ = dx/(2y) = (1 + u⁴/2 + O(u⁸)) du. Integration and substitution give λ(T) = T − 2T⁵/5 + O(T⁹). Write [5](T) = 5T + aT⁵ + O(T⁹). Comparing degree five in λ([5](T)) = 5λ(T) gives a = 2 · 5⁴ − 2 = 1248 ≡ 3 modulo 5. Here the first unit occurs at degree 5. The inert curve at the same prime reaches degree 25.

The correcting series φ and its congruence under formal negation

How does the correcting series φ(T) translate the analytic sigma product into a factorization in the local curve parameter T = −x/y? Let W be a Weierstrass equation over a characteristic-zero field K, with standard invariant b₂ = a₁² + 4a₂. In the formal uniformization variable z, the shifted coordinate series ℘reg,W(z) = xZ(z) + b₂/12 removes the constant Laurent term, leaving z−2 + P(z) with P(0) = 0. Write S(z) for the negative double formal integral of P(z) normalized by S(0) = S′(0) = 0, so that S″(z) = −P(z). For any scalar s₂ ∈ K, the normalized formal sigma series is σ*(z) = z exp(S(z) − ½s₂z²). If l(T) = T lU(T) with lU(0) = 1 denotes the formal logarithm of W in the parameter T, substituting z = l(T) factors out T times a unit exponential:

σ*(l(T)) = T exp(−φ(T)),   φ(T) = −S(l(T)) + ½s₂l(T)² − log lU(T).

Because S(0) = 0, l(0) = 0 and log lU(0) = 0, the correcting series satisfies φ(0) = 0. Fix a subring R ⊆ K. Two formal power series a, b over K with zero constant term are congruent modulo integral exponentials, written a ≡ b, when exp(a − b) has all coefficients in R. Since exp(a − b) then has constant term 1, its inverse exp(b − a) also has coefficients in R; Cauchy multiplication and formal composition make the zero-constant series congruent to 0 an additive subgroup preserved under substitution of zero-constant series with coefficients in R.

Assume now that the subring R ⊆ K contains all Weierstrass coefficients of W and ½ ∈ R, while s₂ ∈ K remains arbitrary. Write [−1]l(T) = l−1(−l(T)) for formal negation on W, and put q−1(T) = φ([−1]l(T)). Then q−1 ≡ φ. This congruence is proved as the instance α = ᾱ = −1, with empty nonzero kernel representative set, of the unified norm theorem for an integral endomorphism datum. Because W has coefficients in R, formal negation is an integral power series of the form [−1]l(T) = −T v(T) with v(T) ∈ 1 + TR[[T]]. Since P(z) is even, both S(z) and ½s₂z² are even, so σ*(−z) = −σ*(z). Evaluating at z = l(T), using l([−1]l(T)) = −l(T), and squaring both sides gives

([−1]l(T))² exp(−2q−1(T)) = T² exp(−2φ(T)).

Substituting [−1]l(T) = −T v(T) and cancelling T² in K[[T]] yields exp(−2(q−1 − φ)) = v(T)−2 ∈ 1 + TR[[T]], and hence exp(2(q−1 − φ)) = v(T)² ∈ 1 + TR[[T]]. For any series g with constant term 1, the identity g − 1 = ½(g² − 1 − (g − 1)²) expresses each positive-degree coefficient of g − 1 in terms of ½ ∈ R, the corresponding coefficient of g², and products of strictly lower positive-degree coefficients of g − 1; strong induction on degree therefore shows that g² ∈ 1 + TR[[T]] implies g ∈ 1 + TR[[T]]. Applying this square-root step to g = exp(q−1 − φ) places exp(q−1 − φ) in 1 + TR[[T]], proving q−1 ≡ φ; the same halving step handles simultaneously every integral endomorphism of unit norm once the squared sigma product supplies integrality of the doubled exponential.

The formal parallelogram and biadditivity of the addition defect

Taken individually, φ(T) acquires arbitrarily large rational denominators from both the double integration in S and the formal logarithm. Why does its addition defect βφ(X, Y) = φ(F(X, Y)) − φ(X) − φ(Y) under the formal group law F(X, Y) = l−1(l(X) + l(Y)) nevertheless become additive in each variable modulo integral exponentials? The formal sigma addition identity turns the two-variable parallelogram combination of φ into the logarithm of the integral one-unit governing chord intersection on the Weierstrass cubic, cancelling every polar and logarithmic denominator at once, and the invertibility of 2 then upgrades that two-variable parallelogram congruence into the three-variable cocycle of the cube.

Let K be a characteristic-zero ultrametric valued field whose closed unit ball R = {a ∈ K : |a| ≤ 1} satisfies |2| = 1, and let W be a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in R and arbitrary scalar s₂ ∈ K. For every indexing set of formal variables and all zero-constant power series x, x′, y with coefficients in R,

βφ(F(x, x′), y) ≡ βφ(x, y) + βφ(x′, y).

1. Formal sigma parallelogram via the wave equation. In two independent uniformization variables u, v, compare the parallelogram series S(u + v) + S(u − v) − 2S(u) − 2S(v) with log Q(u, v), where clearing the poles sets D(u, v) = −u²v²(℘reg,W(u) − ℘reg,W(v)) = u² − v² + u²v²(P(v) − P(u)), and evenness of P factors P(u) − P(v) = (u² − v²) RP(u, v) so that D(u, v) = (u² − v²) Q(u, v) with Q(u, v) = 1 − u²v² RP(u, v) ∈ 1 + (u, v)K[[u, v]]. The one-dimensional wave operator ∂u² − ∂v² annihilates every formal series in u + v or u − v, and since S″ = −P it sends the parallelogram of S to 2P(u) − 2P(v). On the other side, applying the cleared logarithmic wave operator L(H) = H(∂u² − ∂v²)H − ((∂uH)² − (∂vH)²) to D(u, v) and substituting the cleared reduced Weierstrass equations (℘reg,W′)² = 4℘reg,W³ − g₂℘reg,W − g₃ and ℘reg,W″ = 6℘reg,W² − ½g₂ yields L(D) = (2P(u) − 2P(v))D²; since L((u² − v²)Q) = (u² − v²)²L(Q), cancelling (u² − v²)² gives L(Q) = (2P(u) − 2P(v))Q², hence (∂u² − ∂v²) log Q(u, v) = 2P(u) − 2P(v) as well. Both series vanish together with their first v-derivatives along v = 0, so uniqueness for the formal Cauchy problem in characteristic zero makes them equal. Exponentiating and noting that ½s₂z² cancels in (u + v)² + (u − v)² − 2u² − 2v² = 0 gives

σ*(u + v) σ*(u − v) = −σ*(u)² σ*(v)² (℘reg,W(u) − ℘reg,W(v)).

2. Cancellation of poles by chord factorization on the cubic. In two formal curve parameters X₀, X₁, the shift b₂/12 cancels in ℘reg,W(l(X₀)) − ℘reg,W(l(X₁)) = x(X₀) − x(X₁). Writing A(T) = T²x(T) ∈ 1 + TR[[T]] for the integral coordinate series of constant term 1 (which agrees with T²℘reg,W(l(T)) up to b₂T²/12 and therefore gives the identical cross-difference), chord intersection on the integral Weierstrass cubic factors the two-variable series in R[[X₀, X₁]] as

X₁²A(X₀) − X₀²A(X₁) = c(X₀, X₁) F(X₀, X₁) F(X₀, [−1]l(X₁)),

where c ∈ R[[X₀, X₁]] has constant term c(0, 0) = −1 by comparing quadratic terms X₁² − X₀² = −(X₀² − X₁²). Substitute u = l(X₀) and v = l(X₁) into the sigma parallelogram, so that u + v = l(F(X₀, X₁)) and u − v = l(F(X₀, [−1]l(X₁))), and expand each factor via σ*(l(T)) = T exp(−φ(T)). The factors X₀², X₁², F(X₀, X₁) and F(X₀, [−1]l(X₁)) cancel identically in the integral domain K[[X₀, X₁]], leaving Πφ(X₀, X₁) = φ(F(X₀, X₁)) + φ(F(X₀, [−1]l(X₁))) − 2φ(X₀) − 2φ(X₁) = −log(−c(X₀, X₁)). Since −c has coefficients in R and constant term 1, both its inverse exponential −c = exp(−Πφ(X₀, X₁)) and (−c)−1 = exp(Πφ(X₀, X₁)) have all coefficients in R, hence Πφ(X₀, X₁) ≡ 0.

3. Three-variable cube combination. Because |2| = 1 in K, the doubling series [2]l(T) = F(T, T) = 2T + O(T²) ∈ R[[T]] has a unit linear coefficient, so its compositional inverse [½]l(T) = l−1(½l(T)) has zero constant term and coefficients in R. In R[[X₀, X₁, X₂]], set B = [½]l(F(X₁, X₂)), C = [½]l(F(X₁, [−1]l(X₂))) and A = F(X₀, B), so that F(B, C) = X₁ and F(B, [−1]l(C)) = X₂.

How four instances of the parallelogram give the three-variable defect

Adding and subtracting formal logarithms identifies the eight shifted arguments: F(A, B) = F(F(X₀, X₁), X₂) and F(A, [−1]l(B)) = X₀; F(A, C) = F(X₀, X₁) and F(A, [−1]l(C)) = F(X₀, X₂); F(B, B) = F(X₁, X₂) and F(B, [−1]l(B)) = 0; and finally F(B, C) = X₁ and F(B, [−1]l(C)) = X₂.

Using φ(0) = 0, the signed combination Πφ(A, B) − Πφ(A, C) − Πφ(B, B) + Πφ(B, C) eliminates φ(A), φ(B) and φ(C) with weights −2 + 2 = 0, −2 + 4 − 2 = 0 and +2 − 2 = 0, leaving φ(F(F(X₀, X₁), X₂)) − φ(F(X₀, X₁)) − φ(F(X₀, X₂)) − φ(F(X₁, X₂)) + φ(X₀) + φ(X₁) + φ(X₂) = βφ(F(X₀, X₁), X₂) − βφ(X₀, X₂) − βφ(X₁, X₂).

Because A, B and C are zero-constant series over R, substituting (A, B), (A, C), (B, B) and (B, C) into Πφ ≡ 0 produces four series congruent to 0, whose signed sum proves βφ(F(X₀, X₁), X₂) ≡ βφ(X₀, X₂) + βφ(X₁, X₂) universally. Substituting any zero-constant R-integral series (x, x′, y) for (X₀, X₁, X₂) preserves the congruence and completes the proof; combined with q−1 ≡ φ, this yields the quadratic recurrence qm ≡ m²φ used in extracting the integral unit above.

Which logarithm coefficients can have a denominator?

For a series F put (𝒮F)(T) = (τF)(Tq), where τ acts on coefficients. The proof first expands pλ by successively peeling off a₀𝒮λ, a₁𝒮²λ, and further terms, with errors in pW[[T]]. The remaining term after N steps is a zero-constant series in TqN+1, so it disappears in every fixed degree. The aᵢ are integral and a₀ is a unit because [p] has a unit in degree q. To combine the equations, one chooses integral multipliers t₀ = 1, t₁, … satisfying p tn = ∑0≤i<n tiτi(an−1−i) for n ≥ 2. The triangular systems used to construct them have unit diagonal τi(a₀) and successive corrections bounded by |p|k at iteration k. In the sum of the equations twisted by 𝒮i and weighted by ti, the displayed recurrence cancels every term with two or more twists. The coefficient of the first twist is the unit c = a₀ − p t₁.

λ − (c/p)𝒮λ ∈ W[[T]].

Write λn = [Tn]λ. If q does not divide n, this equation gives λn ∈ W. If q divides n, it gives λn = (c/p)τ(λn/q) + an integral coefficient. Each division of the index by q can therefore cost at most one factor of p in the denominator. In particular v(λn) ≥ −max{j : qj divides n} for n ≥ 1. At n = qm equality holds. Starting from λ₁ = 1, the twisted term has valuation −m and, for m ≥ 1, adding an integral coefficient preserves that valuation.

Choosing the unit and proving integrality in every degree

To turn c into 1 in the functional equation, choose a unit ε satisfying ε = cτ(ε). Modulo p the first step is to solve ε̄q−1 = c̄−1. If a unit u already has u − cτ(u) = pkρ, k ≥ 1, replace it by u + pkδ. Dividing the new error by pk leaves ρ + δ − cτ(δ). Its reduction vanishes if c̄δ̄q − δ̄ = ρ̄. Both residue equations are solvable in the algebraically closed residue field of W. Each correction improves the precision by a power of p and preserves the unit residue. Completeness gives ε.

Put f(T) = ε−1λ(εT). First dividing the output by ε converts the twisted coefficient into 1/p because ε = cτ(ε). Substituting the integral series εT preserves the condition f − 𝒮f/p ∈ W[[T]] and restores the linear coefficient 1. Meanwhile ℓ − 𝒮ℓ/p = T by shifting its sum by one index. Solve f(h) = ℓ over U using ordinary formal inversion. To prove h integral, suppose its coefficients below degree N are integral and let P be that truncation. The difference D = ℓ − f(P) has the same integral-error condition, by stability under integral substitution and subtraction. It vanishes below N. In degree N the term 𝒮D is therefore zero, since every coefficient it could use has smaller index. Thus [TN]D is integral. This is precisely [TN]h, because f has linear coefficient 1 and higher powers cannot detect the first difference between h and P in degree N.

Why does integral substitution preserve the logarithm’s functional equation?

The comparison uses two substitutions, first the linear series εT and then a polynomial consisting of the already known integral coefficients of the inverse coordinate. The input logarithm itself can have denominators. Work in the unramified coefficient field with integer ring W and vp(p) = 1. Set q = p² and τ = σ², so τ(a) ≡ aq mod p for every a ∈ W. For a series f with zero constant term put Δf = f(T) − (τf)(Tq)/p, with τ applied to the coefficients. Suppose Δf is integral. For every α ∈ TW[[T]] we need Δ(f ∘ α) to be integral as well.

Put A = α(T)q and B = (τα)(Tq). They agree modulo p because taking a qth power in characteristic p raises both the coefficients and the monomials to that power. Substituting in the two terms of the functional equation in their indicated order gives

Δ(f ∘ α) = (Δf) ∘ α + ((τf)(A) − (τf)(B))/p.

The first summand has integral coefficients. For the second, write fₙ = [Tn]f and gₙ = [Tn]Δf. If q ∤ n, then fₙ = gₙ. Otherwise fₙ = gₙ + τ(fn/q)/p. Thus for n = qkm > 0 with q ∤ m, both pkfₙ and pkτ(fₙ) are integral. Each division of the index by q costs at most one factor of p.

Now a pth power gains one power of p in a difference. If C − D ∈ prW[[T]] with C, D integral and r ≥ 1, expand (D + (C − D))p − Dp. Every intermediate binomial coefficient is divisible by p, and the last term gains enough because pr ≥ r + 1. Start with A ≡ B mod p and iterate 2k times. Raising the results to the remaining power m preserves their congruence by the difference-of-powers factorization. Hence An − Bn is divisible by p1+2k. Multiplying by τ(fₙ) and dividing by the outer p leaves a multiple of pk. Each coefficient receives only finitely many contributions since A and B have zero constant term. This proves stability.

Test the Frobenius and the denominators at 5

Take p = 5, q = 25 and the standard logarithm ℓ = T + T25/5 + T625/25 + ⋯. In the unramified cubic extension take u to be the Teichmüller lift of a residue element of order 31, which exists since 31 divides 125 − 1. This lift is the unique root of unity of that order with the given residue. For α = uT, the degree-25 coefficient of Δ(ℓ ∘ α) is (u25 − τ(u))/5 = 0. Applying the identity to coefficients instead would give (u25 − u)/5 of valuation −1, since 31 does not divide 24.

Over ℤ₅ choose α = T + T². At n = 25 the degree-630 coefficient of A25 − B25 is the binomial coefficient (625 choose 5). Indeed A25 = T625(1 + T)625, while all exponents of B25 are multiples of 25. Its valuation is 3 because (625 choose 5) = 125 · (624 choose 4) and (624 choose 4) ≡ 1 mod 5. The coefficient ℓ₂₅ and the outer division each cost one factor of 5. One factor remains, as the bound predicts.

It follows that the actual substitution Θ = εh = λ−1(εℓ) is integral, with Θ′(0) = ε. Its inverse is integral for the same reason a power series with unit linear coefficient is invertible over its coefficient ring. The host uses the resulting identity ℓ(Θ−1(T)) = ε−1λ(T). Passing from this one-variable coordinate to the translated theta section also uses the curve-to-theta comparison described above.

The first denominator on a good curve at 5

Take the j = 0 branch with d = 3 and p = 5. Here −3 ≡ 2 is a nonsquare. Take (G₂,G₃) = (0,1), giving y² = x³ − 1/4. Its standard parameter is T = −x/y. At the identity choose a formal variable u with x = u−2 and y = −u−3√(1 − u⁶/4), using the square root with constant term 1. Then T = u/√(1 − u⁶/4), and the normalized differential is dλ = dx/(2y) = du/√(1 − u⁶/4). By the formal Lagrange inversion formula, nλn is the coefficient of un−1 in (dλ/du)(u/T)n = (1 − u⁶/4)(n−1)/2. Thus λ6k+1 = (−1)kbinom(3k,k)/(4k(6k+1)), with all other positive-index coefficients zero.

In particular λ₇ = −3/28, λ₁₃ = 15/208 and λ₂₅ = 99/1280. The first two are 5-integral. The last gives 5λ₂₅ = 99/256 ≡ −1 mod 5. The functional equation at degree 25 says 5λ₂₅ ≡ c mod 5, so the residue of the normalizing unit has to satisfy ε̄²⁴ = −1. Every nonzero element of 𝔽₂₅ has 24th power 1. Even though this curve is defined over ℚ₅ and its CM roots reduce in 𝔽₂₅, the required unit must have residue in a larger unramified extension. The example determines the residue equation for this local curve. The lifting argument supplies a unit at all precisions, while the discriminant in the global counting theorem must meet its own size conditions.

An integral derivative at every level-free prime away from d

A single weaker estimate covers every p ≠ d, including split primes, primes dividing QS, q and both inert classes, whenever the level exclusions hold. For the translated theta series H in an allowed integral frame one has |α! [Xα]H|p ≤ 1. Here α! is the product of the factorials of the coordinate exponents. For example, at α = p in one variable this allows the coefficient 1/p!, whose norm is p. The corresponding derivative equals 1. This is precisely what the determinant differential operator needs. Each coefficient of its value at zero is a sum of integer multiples of these derivatives. The ultrametric triangle inequality gives norm at most one for every such coefficient.

The analytic input splits three ways. At 2 the proof uses a good model at the prescribed scale and the dyadic differential estimate. At 3 it uses a good model and the special three-adic theta-jet theorem. The extra hypothesis d ≡ 2 mod 3 follows from (−d/3) = 1, since 1 is the only nonzero square mod 3. At every other prime away from d one has p ≥ 5 and p ∤ d. The good model and the odd-prime differential estimate apply. The finite combination keeps the bound because its coefficients have norm at most one. The adapted frame changes the generators by units and then the identity defining the actual entry identifies the calculated series.

The calculations at 2 and 3 explain why this derivative bound survives the denominators in the small-prime curve models.

The half-valuation at the discriminant prime

At p = d the adapted dual basis pairs two place labels, denoted by − and +. The theorem gives a scalar S with |S|p ≤ √p, weights ut with |ut|p ≤ 1, and a series V with integral factorial-weighted coefficients. The entry satisfies

Θ(X) = exp(−S ∑t,a,b utX−,t,a,bX+,t,a,b) · V(X).

The scalar and weights are common to the allowed translates. Factor the exponential out of their finite sum. The remaining integral combination gives V. To pass to the actual entry, the comparison uses that the chosen scaling generator in each label has norm one at d in the prescribed embeddings.

One paired coordinate. Take the model Θ(X,Y) = exp(−SXY) with vp(p) = 1 and vp(S) = −½. The coefficient of XkYk is (−S)k/k!. The derivative of order (k,k) at zero is (−S)kk!, of valuation −k/2 + vp(k!). For 1 ≤ k < p, the loss is exactly k/2. The minor calculation below bounds how many paired contractions can occur for the prescribed rows. Where the evaluated map is nonzero

At a level-free place the entry estimate bounds the denominator of a rational kernel image in the next local lattice. The rationality assertion adds that applying the complex kernel to an evaluated rational vector gives the evaluation of a rational vector at the next stage. Either vector can map to zero. The construction gives a nonzero evaluation at the distinguished base tuple of a fitted point by using a separate rank argument.

At such a point, write Pt for the quotient projection, ιt for the complex linear injection at the base tuple (and the specified complex map at other tuples), and emb for coordinatewise passage to ℂ. The evaluation identity on a rational vector y is

Θt(jt(ev0,t(y))) = ιt(emb(Pty)).

For the identity, subtract from y a chosen lift of its projection. The difference evaluates in a complementary subspace on which the theta construction vanishes by orthogonality. At the base tuple t₀ the quotient has positive dimension and Pt₀ is onto. Lift its first coordinate vector e₁ to y. Since the base map ιt₀ is injective, ιt₀(emb(e₁)) ≠ 0. This exhibits a nonzero value of the composite. The comparison uses it to show its scalar κ is nonzero. If κ vanished, all the separating linear readings would vanish on this same vector, since their prefactors are nonzero. The contradiction permits division by κ when constructing a common comparison matrix. Individual entries of the local kernel and individual class-pair maps may still vanish.

A nonzero vector reaches the rational quotient

Fix ε > 0. At sufficiently large scale x, with the parameter choice, size and level hypotheses of the construction, take the last definite index i = m − 1. At each of the two levels let P be the finite level group, dK the dimension before enforcing its character, and d₀ the dimension with that character. The action on classes is free. Every nonidentity element has trace zero, so the representation on the full space is a sum of regular representations. Each copy contains the specified character once. Thus |P|d₀ = dK and d₀ ≥ 1. Write εz for the exponent in the size data. The estimate on the discarded types leaves a good subspace of dimension at least (1 − δ)d₀, with δ = exp(−xεz/7) < 1. Its dimension is therefore positive.

Choose a nonzero good vector. The unnormalized character average on this vector gives |P| times the vector. The same average preserves the Hecke summands, so at least one summand has a nonzero projected component. Equality of multiplicities transfers that component to the row space. Let u be the resulting nonzero row, fixed by the prescribed character and central projectors. For the base theta map Θ the adjoint Θ* is injective. The identity ⟨ΘΘ*v,v⟩ = ‖Θ*v‖² makes ΘΘ* injective, hence surjective in finite dimension. Write u = ΘΘ*v. Here “rational” means defined over the construction’s coefficient number field. Such vectors in the adjoint image span it over ℂ. If every rational generator vanished after projection and application of Θ, linearity and equivariance would force their composite to kill u. Both fix u. A rational generator therefore survives, giving positive quotient rank at each level. The adjusted base tuple uses the first level.

Check the finite character count with two group elements

For P = {1, s} acting on its complex regular representation, s interchanges the basis vectors e₁ and es. The sign projector (1 − s)/2 has image spanned by e₁ − es. The full dimension is two and the character dimension is one. On that line the unnormalized average 1 − s acts by two.

Which tests can be fixed for every row?

Fix the admissible grid, its Weil data and row volume, and a nonzero smooth input w. For each nonzero row t, the bottom period and Bessel ascent give some column Ψ, test datum Φ, real vector ρ and coefficient functional ξ with a nonzero convergent period. By linearity of the integral, a period that is nonzero on a span must be nonzero on at least one of its spanning vectors.

The top weight-gap result gives a single function A(ρ, ξ) for this w. With t, Ψ and Φ fixed, the period for every ρ, ξ equals A(ρ, ξ) · lt,Ψ,Φ, where the second factor is independent of ρ, ξ. Choose any successful test on a first nonzero row and keep its (ρ₀, ξ₀). Then A(ρ₀, ξ₀) ≠ 0. For any further nonzero row, some successful test has lt,Ψ,Φ ≠ 0, and those Ψ, Φ work with the same (ρ₀, ξ₀). The column and test datum may vary with the row. In the fitted model the columns span the allowed column space for each test datum. If all its coordinate readings ψb(t) vanish, linearity and convergence force every one of these tested periods to vanish. Hence the simultaneous kernel of the readings is zero.

How a bottom period can detect a prescribed row

Fix the grid, its Haar measures and a nonzero row t. A row turns a smooth vector into an automorphic function on the bottom unitary group, which we call Y. The first core group V comes from adjoining a line to its Hermitian space. Write ι for the embedding of Y in V that fixes this line. For a core function F and a row function u, their initial period is the integral of their product over the rational quotient of Y, with the row measure,

P₀(F,u) = ∫[Y] F(ιh) u(h) dh.

The two function values enter bilinearly. The adjoint theta map in the preceding positive-rank argument acts on multiplicity spaces. Here the question is which functions have a nonzero period. Fix ε and CF ≥ 6510. Above a threshold depending on these parameters, the argument works for every grid satisfying the size, level and model conditions. The threshold is chosen before the row.

Start with the vector w′ supplied by the real-place estimates and put φ = t(w′). There are a bound b for |φ| and a point x with |φ(x)| > b/2. The construction chooses a scale 0 < s ≤ ½. If the lattice at x had a vector violating the prescribed product-of-lengths bound, the short-vector estimate for a cusp form would give |φ(x)| ≤ b/2. Thus every nonzero vector in an ideal multiple of that lattice satisfies the bound. It transfers to the larger lattice in V.

To build F, translate a matrix coefficient by ι(x⁻¹), restrict its finite part to the level, and sum its rational translates. This is a Poincaré series. Unfolding its integral against φ groups the translates into cosets of the rational stabilizer of the added vector z₀. The identity coset gives cφ(x) for a scalar c ≠ 0 supplied by the real and finite data. Distinct cosets carry z₀ to distinct vectors z. A nonidentity coset can contribute only when z − z₀ is a nonzero vector of the lattice multiplied by the level ideal 𝔪. This is where its length matters.

Let n be the Hermitian rank of V, f the number of real places of the totally real field, and Q the loss exponent in the coefficient estimate. Put R = sf√Norm(𝔪). Summing the decaying contributions over those nonzero vectors gives the following bound. The depth choice guarantees R ≥ 2 exp(Q + (6n + 9)f) and R > 1.

∑nonidentity cosets |contribution| ≤ b|c| exp(Q + (6n + 9)f)/R ≤ b|c|/2 < |cφ(x)|.

Absolute convergence justifies unfolding, and the strict last inequality prevents cancellation. The Poincaré series is realized as an evaluation of a cusp form y in the required core multiplicity space. We now have a nonzero initial period, so far at the vector w′.

Where can the bottom cusp form be large enough to separate a row?

In the bottom period the chosen evaluation point must satisfy two demands. The value of the cusp form must exceed half its largest possible size, and the transported row lattice must have a lower bound on its lengths. Once the family has reached the size threshold in the depth theorem, the same depth works for every nonzero row with the prescribed data. The point at which one evaluates can depend on the row.

First fix the row. Let t be a nonzero row map, let w = ⊗τwτ be the packet tensor, and set φ = t(w). Each wτ is nonzero. Choosing a linear functional with value one on each factor shows that their tensor is nonzero. Why must its image under this particular map also be nonzero? Schur orthogonality expresses the integral of two row values as a scalar times the corresponding tensor inner product. If t killed w, pairing with all pure tensors would force that scalar to vanish. All images of pure tensors under t would then have zero squared norm on the automorphic quotient. Continuity and invariance would make them identically zero, contradicting t ≠ 0.

Rapid decay at order zero gives an upper bound for |φ|. Thus B = supy|φ(y)| is finite and positive. The definition of the supremum gives an x with |φ(x)| > B/2. This step only requires approaching the supremum. Multiplying t by a scalar multiplies B by its modulus.

What is the length condition at x? Let Λx be the rational lattice obtained by transporting the finite lattice by x. The archimedean norm ‖w‖τ,x is measured after applying the inverse of the τ-component of x and the chosen frame. With f = [F ∶ ℚ] real places and s > 0, the condition is simultaneous in the ideal and the vector.

∏τ ‖w‖τ,x ≥ sf √N(𝔪)   for every nonzero ideal 𝔪 of 𝒪E and every nonzero w ∈ 𝔪Λx.

To see where the ideal norm enters, write λ for the least normalized size of a nonzero submodule of Λx. For w ∈ 𝔪Λx, choose 0 ≠ a ∈ 𝔪 and write (a) = 𝔪𝔟. The line module 𝔟(w/a) lies in Λx. Its submodule generated by w has index N(𝔪). The rank-one height formula then gives λf√N(𝔪) ≤ ∏τ‖w‖τ,x. Consequently failure of the displayed condition forces λ < s.

Why is a cusp form small at a point with a short line? Suppose the rank is n ≥ 1, the lattice is self-dual, and q ≥ 1 bounds the smaller of the two signature dimensions at every real place. For λ < s ≤ 1/2, the canonical lattice filtration supplies an isotropic step. Its increasing size parameters run from λ to 1/2 in at most q steps. The product of the consecutive ratios (smaller divided by larger) is 2λ, so some ratio is at most (2λ)1/q. This explains the fractional power in the estimate.

Let U be the unipotent radical associated to this isotropic step. For any u ∈ U(𝔸), strong approximation at the finite places and the two real roundings express ux as a rational translate of x followed by a finite congruence motion and two real exponentials. If φ is left rationally invariant and right invariant at principal congruence level (g), g ≥ 1, only the two real motions affect its value. Assume that on every real one-parameter subgroup, right translation by exp(hX) changes φ by at most L|h| times the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the Lie algebra element in the chosen frame, uniformly in the base point. The reduction bounds the two real motions together by n²√f · g · rd(E)(2λ)1/q/4 in the summed Euclidean norms. Summing the placewise variations costs at most another √f by Cauchy–Schwarz. Here rd(E) = |disc(E)|1/[E∶ℚ].

Cuspidality makes the average of φ(ux) over the rational unipotent quotient zero. With probability Haar measure, φ(x) is therefore the integral of φ(x)−φ(ux). The variation estimate bounds this integral, giving the following inequality after enlarging the constant.

If the length condition fails,   |φ(x)| ≤ L n² f g rd(E) (2s)1/q.
Check the fractional exponent on a two-step flag

For the increasing sequence 1/32, 1/8, 1/2, both successive ratios are 1/4. Their product is 1/16 = 2λ. The square root in the bound for q = 2 is exactly 1/4. Replacing that square root by 2λ would require one ratio to be at most 1/16, which this sequence excludes. This numerical example checks the ratio argument used to select the isotropic step.

Use the same depth across rows. The real packet supplies a kernel whose convolution with φ is a nonzero scalar multiple of φ. Translate the kernel inside that identity, subtract the original identity, and use |φ| ≤ B. The packet's bound on the integral of the absolute kernel difference gives the directional estimate with L = exp(Q)B after cancelling the nonzero scalar. The loss Q is fixed before choosing t.

At the bottom rung g is the product of the prescribed two level primes, n is the bottom rank and q is the signature bound used by the construction. The depth hypothesis chooses one 0 < s ≤ 1/2 such that exp(Q)n²fg rd(E)(2s)1/q ≤ 1/2. Failure of the length condition would force |φ(x)| ≤ B/2 at every such failure. Hence every point with |φ(x)| > B/2 satisfies the condition for all ideals. The same depth must also leave sf√N(𝔪) large enough at the period level 𝔪 for the nonidentity terms. This simultaneous choice is what makes the point usable in the separating period.

How can one identity term dominate infinitely many translates?

In the bottom period, the identity coset contributes cφ(x). To exclude cancellation, the proof needs the sum of the absolute sizes of all the other contributions to be smaller than |cφ(x)|. Each coset q moves the distinguished vector z₀ to a vector z(q). Two representatives with the same image differ by an element fixing z₀, precisely the subgroup by which the cosets were formed. Thus the displacements w = z(q) − z₀ are all distinct. Only the identity gives zero. The integral for one coset supplies its decay at infinity. The finite-place test makes the term vanish unless w belongs to the prescribed ideal multiple of the lattice.

At each infinite place τ the chosen frame gives ‖z₀‖τ = 1 and ‖z(q)‖τ ≥ 1. The triangle inequality gives 1 + ‖w‖τ ≤ 2 + ‖z(q)‖τ ≤ 3‖z(q)‖τ. This explains the 3 in the weight below. Write n ≥ 1 for the complex vector dimension and f ≥ 1 for the number of places. After taking out the common factor b|c|exp(Q), the unfolded bound asks us to sum

W(w) = ∏τ (3/(1 + ‖w‖τ))2n+5.

Where is the saving? The lattice estimate assumes ∏τ ‖w‖τ ≥ R > 1 for every nonzero lattice point. Use it twice. First apply it to the difference between any two points. At some place their distance must be at least 1, so the products of open radius-½ balls around distinct points are disjoint. Next put h(u) = (1 + ‖u‖)−(2n+4). Within the ball around wτ we have 1 + ‖u‖ ≤ (3/2)(1 + ‖wτ‖). This bounds the weight at the centre by (3/2)2n+4 times the weight at u. Integrate this inequality over each product of balls and add. Disjointness bounds the total by the integral over the whole space divided by the common ball-product volume.

That integral is finite in each copy of ℂn. In polar coordinates the radial integrand is r2n−1/(1 + r)2n+4 ≤ (1 + r)−5, whose integral from zero to infinity is 1/4. The one-place integral divided by the volume of a radius-½ ball is at most n4n/2. The weight W still contains one spare inverse factor per place. Here the product bound enters for the second time, now on the point itself. The product of these factors is at most 1/R. Combining the factors gives, for every finite set F of nonzero lattice points,

∑w∈F W(w) ≤ exp((6n + 9)f)/R.
Can one coordinate stay short?

In two copies of ℂ take the additive subgroup generated by (½, 12). A nonzero multiple indexed by m has product of lengths 6m², so R = 6 works. For adjacent multiples the first radius-½ disks overlap, but the second disks are 12 units apart at their centres. The product boxes are therefore disjoint. At m = 1 the spare inverse product is 1/((1 + ½)(1 + 12)) = 2/39 ≤ 1/6. This small subgroup tests both uses of the product estimate.

Return to the period. Since the summands are nonnegative, the uniform bound on finite sums passes to the sum over all nonidentity cosets. Restoring b|c|exp(Q) and using the depth condition R ≥ 2exp(Q + (6n + 9)f) bounds their total by b|c|/2. At the selected evaluation point |φ(x)| > b/2 and c ≠ 0. The identity term is strictly larger than the entire possible cancellation. This supplies the nonzero period needed at the first rung.

Which derivatives determine the lowest-type coefficient?

A matrix coefficient of an infinite-dimensional representation will be replaced by an integral on a compact group. The difficulty is to prove that the integral represents the same function. Fix G = U(p,s), m = p + s, q = min(p,s) and K = U(p) × U(s). Denote the diagonal signature matrix by J. Keep the coordinate order in which the Harish-Chandra parameters λ₁ > ⋯ > λm decrease, and record the sign of each coordinate in that order. Each λa − (m−1)/2 is integral. Suppose |λa − λb| ≥ h when the signs differ, with h ≥ 120mq3/2. When both signs occur, this gives an opposite-sign gap γ > 2m, for instance γ = h. When there is only one sign the gap condition is vacuous and any γ > 2m serves.

Let π be the unitary discrete series with these data. Denote its lowest K-type by S, with highest weight Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. Here ρn and ρc are the half-sums of the positive roots between opposite and equal signs respectively. The large-gap multiplicity-one theorem says that the sum of all copies of this lowest type is itself one finite-dimensional irreducible K-space. Write Π for the orthogonal projection onto S. We seek the operator x ↦ Ππ(g)x on S. The later branching projection in the identity term has a different target, the representation of a smaller unitary group.

Uniqueness from derivatives at the identity. Consider a smooth difference F(g) of two proposed operators on S. Suppose it transforms on both sides by K, so F(k₁gk₂) = π(k₁)F(g)π(k₂) on S, and F(1) = 0. One further set of first-order equations is required. Write Dab for differentiation along g exp(tX), extended complex-linearly to the matrix unit Eab. Arrays (vab) of vectors in S encode the noncompact first derivatives, with entries only in opposite-sign positions. Under the simultaneous compact action on the directions and the vectors, their lowering part is the sum of compact types of highest weight Λ + ea − eb with b < a of opposite signs. The first-order condition near the identity is

∑a,b Dab[F(g)vab] = 0   for every array in the lowering part.

Under these hypotheses every iterated derivative of F at 1 vanishes. The derivative of order zero is the value F(1) itself. For the coefficient below, averaging projections onto the compact translates of a highest-weight line gives I/dim S, so the normalized average and the compressed representation both start at the identity on S. Now assume all derivatives through order j−1 vanish. Commuting two adjacent derivatives replaces their difference by a bracket, a derivative of lower order. The order-j derivative is therefore symmetric in its j directions. Compact covariance removes any compact direction by differentiating the action on the input or output. The remaining derivative defines a compact-equivariant linear map T from arrays of j noncompact directions with coefficients in S to S. Applying the other j−1 derivatives to the displayed equation shows that T kills arrays obtained by inserting a lowering array in one slot with the other indices fixed.

Why must T vanish on the rest? Work in the orthogonal complement of its kernel. Permutations preserve T, so a vector f in that complement is symmetric. Orthogonality to the inserted lowering arrays says that every one-slot slice of f lies in the complementary raising part. Let CK be the compact Casimir and κ its scalar on S. The Casimir estimate on a raising slice gives a mixed term of at least (γ − 2m) times its squared norm. Summing over the slices recovers ‖f‖². There are j identical slot contributions by symmetry, each counted twice in the Casimir of a tensor product, and the Casimir on the direction indices is nonnegative. Consequently

Re ⟨f, CKf⟩ ≥ [κ + 2j(γ − 2m)] ‖f‖².

Equivariance gives T(CK − κ)f = 0, so pairing with f gives the left side exactly κ‖f‖². Since j ≥ 1 and γ > 2m, we get f = 0. This proves the induction from the assumed value F(1) = 0. The compact-type inputs here are the splitting of the one-slot array into raising and lowering types and the stated Casimir bound on each raising type.

The formal argument stores ordered derivatives as words in matrix units. The Lie brackets give the adjacent transpositions used in the induction. Its Casimir inequality is for symmetric arrays whose one-slot slices lie in the raising submodule.

An integral formula for the compressed operator

Choose a highest-weight unit vector w in S. Let d = dimℂ S, and give K Haar probability measure. Write Δa(Z) for the leading principal minor of size a, and put μa = λa + (m+1−2a)/2 for 1 ≤ a ≤ m, with μm+1 = 0. These are integers. Set Φ(Z) = ∏a=1m Δa(Z)−(μa−μa+1) wherever the minors are nonzero. Take a Hermitian X with XJ = −JX. Then exp X belongs to G and is positive definite, as is each compact conjugate. For arbitrary u, v ∈ S, the compression formula is

⟨v, π(exp X)u⟩ = d ∫K Φ(k−1 exp(X) k) ⟨v, π(k)w⟩ ⟨π(k)w, u⟩ dk.

Identify the value and derivatives. At X = 0, Φ(1) = 1. Averaging the projections onto the lines ℂπ(k)w gives an operator commuting with K. Its eigenspaces are invariant, so irreducibility makes it scalar. Its trace is 1, hence it equals I/d. This explains the multiplier d and makes the proposed operator agree with Ππ(1) on S.

For the comparison near 1 one uses the compact-equivariant extension from positive matrices by polar decomposition. Its local expression at a group element g uses Φ of the entrywise conjugate of k−1gk. On the positive ray the principal minors are real and this is exactly the displayed integral. Near 1 the minors are uniformly separated from zero for k in the compact group, so they may be differentiated under the integral. In the conjugated coordinates the derivative is a sum indexed by a row c and column b. Terms with b < c have zero scalar derivative coefficient by triangularity of the leading minors. For c ≤ b, the highest-weight component of a lowering array paired with the rotated vector w is zero. Thus the integral satisfies the lowering equation. The representation coefficient satisfies it as well. Indeed the map taking (vab) to ∑ dπ(Eab)vab intertwines the compact action. A nonzero image of a lowering component would give π a compact type with smaller value of ‖μ + 2ρc‖² than at μ = Λ, contradicting its minimality. The uniqueness result for derivatives now applies to the difference.

From the identity to the whole ray. Fix X and replace it by tX. On the integral side the minors depend analytically on t. At each real t their positive minimum over K permits integration of a locally convergent power series. On the representation side, the analytic-vector estimate for the lowest type gives constants B, C ≥ 0 with ‖dπ(X)ku‖ ≤ Ck(B+k)k‖u‖. Division by k! gives a Taylor series of positive radius, and unitarity gives the same derivative bound after translating along the ray. Hence the scalar difference is real analytic on ℝ. Each of its derivatives at 0 is a linear combination of the ordered derivatives already shown to vanish. The Taylor series is zero on a neighbourhood of 0. If this zero interval had a finite endpoint, continuity of every derivative and the convergent Taylor series there would extend it. The difference is therefore zero at t = 1, proving the formula.

A two-coordinate check. For U(1,1) take λ = (241/2, −241/2), so the gap 241 exceeds the required 240. The compact group U(1) × U(1) has one-dimensional types. With u = v = w, the two compact coefficients multiply to 1. Take X with zeros on the diagonal and ones off the diagonal. The leading minor of exp(tX) is cosh t and its determinant is 1, even after compact conjugation. The integral is (cosh t)−242. Its value at zero is 1, its first derivative is zero, and its second derivative is −242. At t = log 2 it equals (4/5)242. This example tests the compression formula in rank one. The subsequent period estimates impose their own dimension conditions.

Lean correspondence

The compact average on the positive part is extended by polar decomposition. Near the identity the argument uses entrywise conjugation, written z.map star. The equality on the positive ray follows from analyticity after the two local lowering equations have been compared.

Which compact types can occur in one derivative?

The uniqueness argument for the derivatives separates two kinds of noncompact directions. The distinction is visible in one derivative before we symmetrize several of them. Keep the coordinates in decreasing parameter order, and let εa be the sign of coordinate a. Put m = p + s, K = U(p) × U(s), and let S be the irreducible finite-dimensional unitary K-space of highest weight Λ. Write ea for the ath coordinate weight. The complexified noncompact directions are the matrix units Eab for which εa ≠ εb. A vector in their tensor product with S is an array ∑ Eab ⊗ vab. Set its equal-sign entries to zero.

Let this array be a nonzero highest-weight vector of weight μ. Choose a nonzero coefficient vab with maximal a − b. The diagonal action on Eab has weight ea − eb, so the coefficient has weight μ − ea + eb. To find its weight inside S, apply any compact raising operator Ecd, with c < d and equal signs. Its action on the full array vanishes. In position (a,b) that action is

Ecdvab + δac vdb − δbd vac = 0.

When a = c, the second term has index difference d − b > a − b. When b = d, the third has difference a − c > a − b. Both vanish by maximality. Thus every compact raising operator kills the selected coefficient. In the irreducible space S it has highest weight Λ. We conclude μ = Λ + ea − eb.

Finite-dimensional unitary representations split into irreducibles by successively taking invariant orthogonal complements. Group together all copies of each highest weight. The preceding calculation puts every occurring weight in one of two lists. The case a < b gives the raising part, b < a the lowering part. Distinct ordered opposite-sign pairs give distinct shifts. The two parts are consequently orthogonal and exhaust the array space. A particular candidate weight can have no summand. If one sign is absent, the noncompact direction space is zero and both lists are empty. P. Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, proposition 25.5 and corollaries 25.11 and 35.2 on highest weights and complete reducibility[11].
