The Casimir on one noncompact direction

For compact matrix units write Dcd for the infinitesimal action in a representation. Fix the normalization C = ∑εc=εd DcdDdc, summing over ordered pairs, including the diagonal. On an irreducible space of highest weight η this Casimir acts by

κ(η) = ‖η + ρc‖² − ‖ρc‖².

Here ρc is half the sum of the roots ec − ed with c < d and equal signs. On a highest vector the diagonal terms give ∑ ηc². For each such pair the raising operator kills that vector, so the two orders together contribute the commutator Dcc − Ddd, with eigenvalue ηc − ηd. The sum is κ(η). This scalar holds on the entire irreducible space because C commutes with the compact action. Indeed ∑ Ecd ⊗ Edc pairs a basis of each matrix block with its dual for the conjugation-invariant trace pairing, so the sum and its product are invariant.

On the array the generator is Pcd + Dcd. The first operator acts on the matrix position by commutator and the second acts on the coefficient in S. They commute. Expanding the Casimir and exchanging c,d in one cross term gives Ctotal = Cposition + Ccoefficient + 2Ω, where Ω = ∑εc=εd PcdDdc.

To compute the position term, apply the double commutator [Ecd, [Edc, Eab]] to an opposite-sign direction. Its two middle matrix products vanish because they would require the row and column of Eab to lie in the same sign block. The outer products give EccEab and EabEdd. In the sum the first contributes once for each index in the block of a, the second once for each index in the block of b. The blocks have total size m. Thus Cposition acts by m, and Ccoefficient acts by κ(Λ). On a summand of highest weight μ the mixed operator Ω has eigenvalue

cab = (κ(μ) − m − κ(Λ))/2,   μ = Λ + ea − eb.

How much of the weight gap survives?

For the lowest compact type, Λ = λ + ρn − ρc, where ρn is half the sum of the positive opposite-sign roots. Expanding the square in κ after adding ea − eb adds twice the difference of the two coordinates of Λ + ρc, plus 2. Hence

cab = λa − λb + (ρn)a − (ρn)b + 1 − m/2.

For a < b of opposite signs, assume λa − λb ≥ γ. Twice each coordinate of ρn counts opposite-sign indices after it minus those before it. Each coordinate lies between −m/2 and m/2. This gives cab ≥ γ + 1 − 3m/2 ≥ γ − 2m. For a general raising array, write it as the orthogonal sum of its isotypic components. The real part of its inner product with Ω applied to it is the sum of the corresponding eigenvalues times the squared component norms. It is therefore at least (γ − 2m) times its squared norm.

A check with interleaved signs. In dimension three take (+,−,+) and λ = (721,360,0). Then both half-sums equal (1/2,0,−1/2), so Λ = λ. The direction E23 tensored with a highest vector gives a highest vector of weight μ = (721,361,−1) because the only compact raising operator E13 commutes with E23. The change in the sum of coordinate squares is 722, and the change in the compact-root term η₁ − η₃ is 1. Thus κ(μ) − κ(Λ) = 723, and Ω acts by (723 − 3)/2 = 360. The two opposite-sign gaps are 361 and 360, so the uniform lower bound for γ = 360 is 354.

In a symmetric derivative of order j, fixing the other j − 1 positions gives a one-position slice. Once the lowering components have been removed, the preceding inequality applies to every such slice. Their squared norms sum to the squared norm of the whole array. By symmetry each of the j positions contributes the same lower bound, and the Casimir expansion counts each mixed term twice. This supplies the gain 2j(γ − 2m) in the uniqueness proof.

How does a gap between two weights make a matrix coefficient small?

The compression identity expresses the coefficient as an average over the compact group K. The part of its integrand that changes as we move away from K is a product of determinants. We first estimate this product at each point of the average.

Write J for the diagonal matrix of signs defining the unitary group in dimension m, and q for the smaller of the numbers of positive and negative signs. Suppose q ≥ 1. Choose a Hermitian matrix X with JX = −XJ. For k ∈ K put Y = k−1Xk and t = ‖X‖F = ‖Y‖F. The matrix Y also interchanges the two sign spaces. Let Δℓ(s) be the determinant on the first ℓ rows and columns of exp(sY), numbering coordinates in decreasing order of the weights λ₁ > ⋯ > λm. Exp(sY) is positive definite, so all these determinants are positive for real s. For consecutive weights set bℓ = λℓ − λℓ+1 + 1. Suppose the weight difference across each pair of opposite signs is at least h ≥ 0 in absolute value. Then

∏ℓ=1m−1 Δℓ(1)−bℓ ≤ exp(−(h/8) min{t², t/√(2q)}).

What one cut measures. Let P be orthogonal projection onto the first ℓ coordinates, and let A be the corresponding diagonal block of Y. Every diagonal entry of Y vanishes, so Δℓ′(0) = tr A = 0. Expanding the determinant of the block of I + sY + s²Y²/2 through second order gives Δℓ″(0) = tr(PY²P) − tr(A²). Hermitian symmetry cancels the entries with both indices in the block. What survives is the squared size of the entries crossing its boundary, Vℓ = Σj≤ℓ<i |Yij|².

To turn this derivative into a bound at s = 1, diagonalize Y in an orthonormal basis. Cauchy–Binet applied to the compressed exponential writes Δℓ(s) = ΣI wI exp(s yI), where yI is the sum of the ℓ eigenvalues selected by I. The weights are squared absolute minors of the change of basis. They sum to Δℓ(0) = 1. Thus the first two derivatives give a random variable with mean zero and second moment Vℓ. The off-diagonal sign blocks have rank at most q each. At most 2q eigenvalues are nonzero and their squares sum to t². Cauchy–Schwarz gives |yI| ≤ R = √(2q)t.

If t = 0 the product is 1. Otherwise put a = min{1, 1/R}. On [−1,1] the cubic Taylor lower bound for the exponential gives exp(x) ≥ 1 + x + x²/3. Averaging at x = a yI yields Δℓ(a) ≥ 1 + a²Vℓ/3. The added term lies in [0,1/3], where log(1+x) ≥ 3x/4 by integration of 1/(1+x). Concavity of x ↦ xa gives Δℓ(a) ≤ Δℓ(1)a. Together these give log Δℓ(1) ≥ aVℓ/4.

Why the weights add up. An entry in row i and column j with j < i contributes at cuts ℓ = j, …, i−1. The corresponding weights sum to λj − λi + i − j. For a nonzero entry the two coordinates have opposite signs, so this sum is at least h. Each conjugate pair has one entry below the diagonal, giving Σℓ bℓVℓ ≥ ht²/2. Multiplication by a/4 proves the product bound, since at² = min{t², t/√(2q)}. For example, an entry at (4,2) appears at cuts 2 and 3. The intermediate weight λ₃ cancels.

A two-cut check. In dimension three take signs (+,+,−), weights (2,1,0), and place log 2 at entries (1,3) and (3,1) of Y, leaving all other entries zero. Exponentiation gives cosh(log 2) = 5/4 on the first and third diagonal entries and 1 on the second. Both leading minors are 5/4 and both weights bℓ equal 2. Their product with negative exponents is (4/5)⁴. This small gap tests the determinant calculation before the large-gap hypothesis is needed for compression.

Why does the compact average preserve that decay?

Let π be the unitary discrete series with admissible parameter λ, and let S be its lowest K-type. Write d = dim S, choose a unit highest-weight vector w in S and give K Haar measure of mass one. The compression identity applies when h ≥ 120m q3/2. Its scalar factor at k−1exp(X)k has absolute value equal to the preceding product. The full determinant contributes 1 because tr X = 0. Denote the uniform product bound by D(t).

Write fx(k) = ⟨x,π(k)w⟩. Substituting X = 0 and testing the compression identity against x in both slots gives d∫K|fx|² = ‖x‖² for every x ∈ S. For two vectors u, v ∈ S, take absolute values in the integral at X and apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the two functions on K. Each function has norm ‖fx‖₂ = ‖x‖/√d. Hence

|⟨v,π(exp X)u⟩| ≤ dD(t) ‖fv‖₂ ‖fu‖₂ = D(t) ‖v‖ ‖u‖.

This also controls every group element g. The positive matrix g*g satisfies J(g*g)J = (g*g)−1. Its positive square root is exp X, with X Hermitian and JXJ = −X by diagonalization. Then k = g exp(−X) is both unitary and signed unitary, so k ∈ K. Moving π(k) to the first slot replaces v by a vector of the same norm in S. The singular values sj of g are the eigenvalues of exp X, so the argument of D is t = (Σj (log sj)²)1/2.

How many powers of the Frobenius norm are available for integration?

The integral over the stabilizer uses the ordinary Frobenius norm F = ‖g‖F. The preceding bound uses logarithms of singular values. Here is the conversion, with the constants later spent in the restricted period integral.

Lowest-type coefficient estimate. Suppose m ≥ 3 and the opposite-sign parameters of π are separated by at least h = 1000m³. For any unit vector v₀ in its lowest K-type and any g in the signed unitary group,

|⟨v₀,π(g)v₀⟩| ≤ exp(100m³) F−40m².

First take q ≥ 1. The stated h exceeds 120m q3/2 since q ≤ m. Set M = min{t², t/√(2q)}. The estimate on the compact average gives log of the upper bound equal to −125m³M. Each singular value is at most exp(t), hence F² = Σ sj² ≤ m exp(2t). Also t ≤ 1 + mM. This is immediate when t ≤ 1. For t ≥ 1 both mt² and mt/√(2q) are at least t. Using log m ≤ m, we obtain

40m² log F ≤ 20m³ + 40m² + 40m³M ≤ 100m³ + 125m³M.

Rearranging and exponentiating proves the estimate. If q = 0 the group is compact and all singular values are 1. Then F = √m, and the right-hand side is at least 1 by log m ≤ m. Unitarity bounds the coefficient by 1. This argument uses one representation. The choice of a translate with a large projection needs a second representation on the stabilizer.

Why does a translated coefficient become small away from the stabilizer?

The bottom period contains one integral for each translate. Its size depends on how far the translate moves a distinguished vector z. Start at a single real place, in coordinates where z is a positive unit coordinate vector. Write G for the unitary group of the signed Hermitian form in m = n + 1 variables, and H for the unitary group on its orthogonal complement. The embedding ι extends each element of H by the identity on z. Put ℓ(g) = ‖gz‖₂ and let ‖·‖F denote the Frobenius norm. Because g preserves the signed form, ℓ(g) ≥ 1. Right multiplication by ι(h) leaves gz unchanged.

Local coefficient estimate. Let π and σ be the discrete series on G and H in the real branching construction. Here n ≥ 3, the smaller signature has at least one negative direction and at least as many positive as negative directions. Both lists of Harish-Chandra parameters have absolute values at most B, descend in steps of at least 2 and have gaps of at least 1000m³ between entries of opposite signs within either list. The signed lists satisfy the branching condition both as given and after lowering any one entry of the longer list by 1. In decreasing order of the combined entries, successive distinct levels with no entry strictly between them obey this rule for each pair of entries at the two levels. Their signs agree exactly when the entries come from different lists.

Choose a lowest K-type unit vector v₀ in π, where K is the maximal compact subgroup fixed by the signed coordinates. Put v = π(g₀)v₀, with ‖g₀‖F ≤ (8mB)10m, and Φ(X) = ⟨v,π(X)v⟩. For the model Haar measure μ₀ on H, write V₀ = μ₀{h : ‖h − 1‖F ≤ 1/4} and ℬ(C) = exp(Cm⁴ log(8mB)). Then for every g ∈ G the restricted translate is absolutely integrable and

∫H |Φ(gι(h))| dμ₀(h) ≤ V₀ ℬ(1000) ℓ(g)−(2n+7).

Where the two powers go. The large-gap estimate for a lowest K-type bounds |⟨v₀,π(X)v₀⟩| by exp(100m³) ‖X‖F−L, with L = 40m². Unitarity replaces X by g₀−1Xg₀ for the vector v. The Frobenius norm of the inverse of a signed unitary matrix equals the norm of the matrix, since the inverse is its conjugate transpose between two diagonal sign matrices. Submultiplicativity now costs at most ‖g₀‖F2L.

Use the unitary decomposition g−1 = ι(u)b, where β = ‖b‖F satisfies β² ≤ m + 2ℓ(g)². To see the decomposition, split gz into its positive and negative parts, of Euclidean lengths a and d. Thus a² − d² = 1. Up to separate ordinary unitary rotations in these two coordinate spaces, the matrix carrying z to gz is the block with rows (a,d) and (d,a), extended by the identity. If d = 0 a rotation alone suffices. The resulting matrix T has squared Frobenius norm m − 2 + 2(a² + d²). Since T−1g fixes z, inversion gives the required factorization with b = T−1.

Put x = ‖gι(h)‖F and s = ‖u−1h‖F. The unchanged column gives x ≥ ℓ(g), and b gι(h) = ι(u−1h) gives s ≤ βx. Reserve A = 4n² + 1 powers for integration on H. Since β ≤ √(3m) ℓ(g),

x−L ≤ s−A βA ℓ(g)−(L−A) ≤ (3m)A/2 s−A ℓ(g)−(2n+7).

The last inequality uses L − 2A ≥ 2n + 7. To integrate the factor s−A, left invariance removes u. In the real space of complex n-by-n matrices, balls of radius r = 1/(8R) around a maximal 2r-separated subset of {‖h‖F ≤ R} have disjoint interiors. Volume comparison in dimension 2n² bounds their number by (1 + 8R²)2n². Every group point in that set lies within 2r of a centre h₀, hence ‖h₀−1h − 1‖F ≤ R·2r = 1/4. Each centre therefore costs at most V₀ in group measure.

On the shell 2j ≤ ‖h‖F < 2j+1, its integral is at most V₀·2−Aj(1 + 32·4j)2n² ≤ V₀·332n²2−j. Summing over j ≥ 0 gives ∫‖h‖F−A dμ₀ ≤ exp(10n²)V₀. The continuous coefficient thus has an integrable majorant. The remaining factors exp(100m³)‖g₀‖F2L(3m)A/2exp(10n²) fit inside ℬ(1000) by the stated bound on g₀ and B ≥ 1.

A rank-four check. Put the block with rows (5/4, 3/4) and (3/4, 5/4) on one positive and one negative coordinate and use the identity on the other two. Since (5/4)² − (3/4)² = 1, this is signed unitary. Taking the positive coordinate in that block as z gives ℓ(g)² = 17/8. Here n = 3, A = 37 and L = 640. Of the 566 remaining powers the estimate uses 13, giving the factor (8/17)13/2 in its upper bound.

Where can the smaller representation be seen inside the larger one?

Keep the signed unitary groups H ⊂ G, the positive unit vector z fixed by H, and the real branching assumptions. Write m = n + 1 for the larger dimension and X = 8mB. Fix a lowest compact-type unit vector v₀ for π on G and a lowest compact-type unit vector w₀ for σ on H. The signed interlacing theorem supplies an occurrence of σ in the restriction of π. Its isometric intertwiner is a map i from the space of σ to that of π. Set P = i∗. Then P takes values in the smaller space, while iP is the orthogonal projection onto its copy inside the larger space.

The task is to choose a translate π(g₀)v₀ whose projection has a quantitative lower bound. Consider the nonnegative function F(g) = |⟨iw₀,π(g)v₀⟩|² and the squared column length Y(g) = ‖g−1z‖₂². For Haar measures μ on G and ν on H let dπ, dσ be the corresponding formal degrees. Schur orthogonality says that the squared matrix coefficient of two vectors integrates to the product of their squared norms divided by the formal degree. For our unit vectors this gives ∫F dμ = 1/dπ. The model uses its fixed ambient Haar measure for the estimates below. M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations[12].

Mixed coefficient moment. The branching construction gives the following bound on the average of Y with density dπF.

∫G Y(g)F(g) dμ(g) ≤ X8m/dπ.

Here is how a column of g−1 enters. Tensor π with the dual of the defining representation. Acting on a tensor supported in coordinate l and reading its z-coordinate inserts the matrix entry (g−1)l,z. The discrete-series decomposition of this tensor on smooth vectors writes the resulting coefficient as ∑s al,s(g) over at most m summands, each with one parameter lowered by 1. In each summand, Schur orthogonality gives ∫|al,s|² ≤ X6m/dπ. Three bounds multiply here. The scalar obtained by applying the tensor projection and taking the distinguished coordinate costs at most Xm, the squared projected input with its form normalization costs X4m, and the reciprocal shifted formal degree costs at most Xm/dπ. The component estimate below derives their product.

For each l, the square of the sum costs at most the number of summands times ∑s|al,s|² by Cauchy–Schwarz. Summing over l recovers the whole squared column. The three factors from Cauchy–Schwarz, the sum over s and the sum over l are each ≤ m ≤ X. Thus the exponent is at most 6m + 3 ≤ 8m. This moment controls the mass with a large distinguished column even when left multiplication by the stabilizer makes the full matrix arbitrarily large.

Why does lowering one weight produce the terms of the column moment?

In the mixed coefficient moment the factor (g−1)l,z comes from the dual of the defining representation of G = U(p,q). Let m = p + q = n + 1. A smooth tensor is a column x of m smooth vectors of π. Its group action has coordinate (A(g)x)c = ∑l(g−1)l,cπ(g)xl. We write elv for the column with only one nonzero entry.

Tensor translation theorem used here. Suppose 1 ≤ q ≤ p, π is a discrete series with regular Harish-Chandra parameter λ, and opposite-sign coordinates of λ differ by at least 200m³. For each s for which λ − es remains a regular dominant parameter, there is a discrete series πs of that parameter. On smooth tensors there is one summand for each such s. In the branching application consecutive coordinates differ by at least two, so each lowering preserves strict order. The construction at a regular weight gives square-integrable models for the shifted parameters. Averaging their coefficients gives maps which together detect every smooth column. The calculation with two lowerings proves that one copy of each model suffices.

Write ps for the map that keeps a summand inside the tensor, and rs for its coordinate in the Hilbert space of πs. The first reconstructs x by summation. The second intertwines the group actions. Give the tensor its invariant form [y,x] = ∑lεl⟨yl,xl⟩ with εl equal to +1 or −1 according to the signature. Invariance and Schur's lemma give a scalar cs for the form on one summand. For smooth x,y the identities used below are

∑s psx = x,   rsA(g)x = πs(g)rsx,   [y,psx] = cs⟨rsy,rsx⟩.

The decomposition can be read one coordinate at a time. The differential operator Ω sends x to the column with entries ∑ldπ(Ecl)xl, where Ecl is the elementary matrix. On the s-summand it has eigenvalue λs + (m − 1)/2. The eigenvalues are distinct. The product over other summands of (Ω − κt)/​(κs − κt) therefore keeps precisely the s-coordinate. This argument takes place on the smooth direct sum, where the indicated derivatives exist.

What does one lowering cost in formal degree?

Fix the same Haar measure on the same group for both degrees. The formal-degree formula for a regular discrete series gives dπ = C·∏a<b(|λa − λb|/(b − a)). The positive constant C depends on the signature and Haar normalization. The quantitative version used in this moment applies when both signs occur and the opposite-sign gap is at least 120m³. Lowering one entry by one reduces any gap by at most one, so both parameters qualify under the preceding 200m³ hypothesis. This degree formula is the representation-theoretic input. The comparison below only uses the product. M. F. Atiyah and W. Schmid, §5, p. 25, formal-degree formula following (5.15)[13].

In the ratio dπ/ds, the constant and the denominators cancel. A pair avoiding s contributes 1. For a pair touching s, let h be its gap after the shift. The coordinates lie on the same translate of the integers and the new parameter is regular, so h ≥ 1. Its old gap is at most h + 1 ≤ 2h. There are m − 1 such pairs. With X = 8mB ≥ 4 the reciprocal degree satisfies

1/ds ≤ 2m−1/dπ ≤ 22m/dπ ≤ Xm/dπ.

The middle bound is the one used in the moment. It counts a factor 2 whenever s is the first or second coordinate of an ordered pair. As a check of the ratio alone, lower the second coordinate of (13/2, 7/2, 1/2, −5/2). Its three affected gaps change from (3, 3, 6) to (4, 2, 5). Thus the ratio of the old product to the new one is (3/4)(3/2)(6/5) = 27/20. This finite product example checks the direction of the inequality independently of the large-gap hypothesis.

How much squared mass can one shifted summand carry?

Return to the pair (G,H) and the unit vectors of the mixed moment. Put ξ = iw₀, P = i∗ and κ = 1/dσ for the chosen Haar measure ν on H. The z-coordinate corresponds to the positive line fixed by H. Two estimates for ps enter with different powers of X.

First consider its entries on elv₀. The quantum cofactor identity for the differential matrix writes each entry of the projector as a signed minor of size n = m − 1, divided by a product of n nonzero parameter differences. To see the denominator, put tj = λj − (m − 1)/2. On the s-summand the cofactor matrix at u acts by ∏j≠s(u + tj). Evaluating at −ts kills the other summands and leaves the factor ∏j≠s(λj − λs), of absolute value at least one. A zero projector contributes zero throughout. For a nonzero summand the matching index is determined by its eigenvalue λs + (m − 1)/2, since the λs are distinct. The differential word estimate controls the factors in each term of this cofactor. A word of length j ≤ n in elementary matrix derivatives applied to the unit vector v₀ has norm at most Mj, with M = 8√m(B + n). There are n! permutations in the minor. Expanding its factors, whose scalar parts have size at most 4B, bounds its norm by n!(4B + M)n. The parameter spread gives n ≤ 2B, hence M ≤ 3X, 4B + M ≤ X², and n! ≤ Xn. Every entry thus has norm at most X3n ≤ X4m. Taking x = y = elv₀ in the signed form and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives |cs|‖rs(elv₀)‖² ≤ X4m.

Second, on a smooth vector η the distinguished entry satisfies P((ps(ezη))z) = γsPη, where P is applied after taking the coordinate. Removing the z row and column leaves the quantum determinant of the smaller group. Its action on σ is scalar. The numerator is the product of the n factors μj − λs + 1/2. Each has size at most 2B + 1/2 ≤ X. The same denominator has size at least one, so |γs| ≤ Xn ≤ Xm.

It remains to explain why these two bounds multiply. The coefficient projection on H supplies a smooth test vector η with ⟨η,ξ⟩ ≠ 0. Define b = rs(ezη). Average the coefficient ⟨b,πs(h)a⟩ against φ(h) = conj(⟨w₀,σ(h)w₀⟩). This integrable weight defines a bounded functional of a, hence a vector b′ by Hilbert-space representation. Inversion symmetry and φ ∗ φ = κφ give ‖b′‖² = κ⟨b′,b⟩ by integrating twice. On the fixed positive coordinate, averaging the signed form identity gives κ⟨η,ξ⟩⟨ξ,(psx)z⟩ = cs⟨b′,rsx⟩. At x = ezη this yields |cs|‖b′‖² = κ²|⟨η,ξ⟩|²|γs|.

Now let al,s(g) = ⟨ξ,(psA(g)elv₀)z⟩. Applying the averaged identity at that translated input expresses al,s as a scalar times a coefficient of πs. Schur orthogonality gives its squared integral. The factor κ²|⟨η,ξ⟩|² cancels by the preceding identity, leaving

∫G |al,s|² dμ = |γs| · |cs|‖rs(elv₀)‖² / ds ≤ X6m/dπ.

This equality also covers a vanishing coefficient. Only the positive number κ and the nonzero test pairing were divided out. At m = 4 the scalar, the squared input and the reciprocal degree cost at most 4, 16 and 4 powers of X. The finite sums in the column moment are taken after this estimate. M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations[12].

Which shifted weights give actual spaces of vectors?

In the column moment a matrix entry of the inverse of g multiplies a coefficient of π. Together they are a coefficient of X = V* ⊗ π, where V is the defining representation of G = U(p,q). To integrate its square we want to write it in terms of representations with a known formal degree. A list of candidate eigenvalues tells us how to label the pieces. We also need vectors in each piece and maps which recover every smooth column.

Regular unit shifts. Let 1 ≤ q ≤ p, m = p + q. Order the Harish-Chandra parameters λ₁ > ⋯ > λm and keep the sign attached to each position. These parameters lie on a common translate of the integers. Assume that opposite-sign entries differ by at least h ≥ 200m³. To form the sth candidate, subtract one from λs. The lattice condition is preserved. Only the gap to the next entry can close. Hence the last entry can always be lowered, and an earlier entry can be lowered exactly when its next gap exceeds one. Every opposite-sign gap after the move is at least h − 1. The analytic threshold used below is at most 43m³, so even the additional allowance m² + 3 for coefficient estimates fits inside the original gap.

The model at an allowed weight ν. Write K = U(p) × U(q) for the maximal compact subgroup. The lowest compact type is a finite-dimensional representation of K carrying a distinguished highest weight. For ν, take that type T, its unit highest-weight vector w, and its matrix kernel Ψν. The lowest-type construction gives square-integrable smooth functions g ↦ ⟨w,Ψν(g)v⟩ as v ranges over T. Start with their span, adjoin its derivatives under the complexified Lie algebra, and take the closure in L²(G). The discrete-series realization theorem for this kernel says that right translation preserves this closure, acts unitarily and irreducibly on it, and has parameter ν. Thus a regular lowering supplies an actual Hilbert space, which we call πs. The construction uses the existence and decay of the normalized kernels for the original and shifted weights.

Coefficient comparison at a regular shift. Call a vector K-finite when its compact translates span a finite-dimensional space. Let ρ(g) = (g−1)ᵗ. For K-finite v,w in π and any coordinate pair c,d, the product below has a finite expansion. In the other direction each regular model has a nonzero vector y whose diagonal coefficient ⟨y,πs(g)y⟩ is a finite sum of products of the type on the left.

ρ(g)cd ⟨w,π(g)v⟩ = ∑i ⟨bi,πs(i)(g)ai⟩.

On the space generated by derivatives, the tensor differential splits each input into finitely many eigenvectors. The central-character calculation labels their eigenvalues by shifts. The partial-trace and residue calculation removes the eigenspace of a singular shift. For a surviving eigenvector, the coefficient comparison with the model of that weight supplies one term on the right. Conversely the algebraic embedding of the shifted module realizes a pair of its vectors in tensor coordinates. Expanding the pairing over those coordinates gives the reverse identity. The embedding compares vectors in the two algebraic models before completion. G. Zuckerman, Tensor products of finite and infinite dimensional representations of semisimple Lie groups, on translation by finite-dimensional tensors[14].

How is the kernel defined before any representation exists?

The regular models are built from a function on G alone. At a shifted parameter no discrete series is given in advance, so the compression formula cannot be read as an identity between two known coefficients. Its right-hand side becomes a definition. Fix a parameter λ with the lattice condition, the integers μa = λa + (m+1−2a)/2 with μm+1 = 0, and the minor product Φ(Z) = ∏a Δa(Z)−(μa−μa+1). In other words μ = λ + ρ with ρa = (m+1−2a)/2. Let T be an irreducible unitary representation of K on a space of dimension d, with a unit vector w of highest weight Λ = λ + ρn − ρc, the lowest compact weight. Write P for orthogonal projection onto ℂw and give K Haar measure of mass one. Wherever every compact conjugate k−1xk has nonzero leading minors, set

A(x) = d ∫K Φ(k−1xk) T(k)PT(k)−1 dk.

Replacing k by ck in the integral gives A(cxc−1) = T(c)A(x)T(c)−1 for c ∈ K. This uses only invariance of the measure. At x = 1 every minor equals 1. The average of the projections commutes with T, hence is a scalar by Schur’s lemma, and its trace is 1 because each projection has trace 1. The factor d therefore gives A(1) = I.

From positive matrices to the group. Every g ∈ G factors as g = k exp X with k ∈ K and X Hermitian satisfying XJ = −JX, by the polar decomposition. The factors are unique. Indeed g*g = exp(2X), the exponential is injective on Hermitian matrices, and then k = g exp(−X). Define

Ψ(k exp X) = T(k) A(exp X).

For k1, k2 ∈ K the factorization of k1gk2 is (k1kk2) exp(k2−1Xk2), because k2−1Xk2 is again Hermitian and anticommutes with J. The conjugation rule for A then gives

Ψ(k1gk2) = T(k1) Ψ(g) T(k2),   Ψ(1) = I.

A symmetry and positivity on the noncompact part. The sign matrix J belongs to K and commutes with every element of K, so T(J) is a scalar. Since J exp(X) J = exp(−X), the conjugation rule gives A(exp(−X)) = A(exp X). Now exp X = exp(X/2)* exp(X/2) is positive definite, and so is each compact conjugate. Its leading principal submatrices are positive definite, hence every leading minor is a positive real number and Φ(k−1 exp(X) k) > 0. Moreover ⟨v,T(k)PT(k)−1v⟩ = |⟨T(k)w,v⟩|². Integrating, Ψ(exp X) is a positive semidefinite operator. This positivity is used when a shifted model is placed in the tensor product.

For example, take U(1,1) with signs (+,−), so K consists of the matrices diag(eiα,eiβ) and ρc = 0. Then Λ = μ = (λ1+1/2, λ2−1/2), d = 1 and T(diag(eiα,eiβ)) = ei(Λ1α+Λ2β). For X with zero diagonal and both off-diagonal entries t, every compact conjugate of exp X has first minor cosh t and determinant 1. Hence

Ψ(k1 exp(X) k2) = ei(Λ1(α1+α2)+Λ2(β1+β2)) (cosh t)−(λ1−λ2+1).

At λ = (3/2,−1/2) and t = log 2, the value at exp X is (4/5)³ = 64/125.

Why is the kernel smooth near every point of the group?

Near each point of the group the kernel agrees with a holomorphic function of the inverse matrix. We derive that formula from two directional derivatives of A at positive definite matrices. Write T(Y) also for the complex-linear differential of the compact representation on block diagonal matrices, whose entries between opposite signs vanish.

A Hermitian direction. Let x be positive definite and H block diagonal and Hermitian. The direction Hx + xH is the velocity of exp(tH) x exp(tH). Differentiate A under the integral. At a conjugate z = k−1xk put B = k−1Hk. Let L keep the entries of B below the diagonal, change the sign of those above it, and vanish on the diagonal. Then B + L is lower triangular, B − L is upper triangular, both have diagonal entries Baa, and

Bz + zB = (zL − Lz) + (B+L)z + z(B−L).

Left multiplication by a lower triangular matrix and right multiplication by an upper triangular one rescale each leading minor by the product of the leading diagonal entries. Hence each of the last two directions changes Φ at the rate −∑μaBaaΦ. The matrix L is block diagonal and skew-Hermitian, so the first direction is an infinitesimal compact conjugation. On the representation side the highest weight supplies a matching identity,

T(B)P + PT(B) = [T(L),P] + 2(∑ΛaBaa) P.

Indeed the part of B above the diagonal kills w, the diagonal part multiplies w by ∑ΛaBaa, and T(Y)* = T(Y*) moves the part below the diagonal to the other side of P.

The correction from a moving frame. The matrix L depends on the integration variable k. Integration by parts must therefore differentiate its coefficients as well as the function on which it acts. For two distinct indices a, b of the same sign, use the skew-Hermitian directions Aab = Eab − Eba and Bab0 = i(Eab + Eba). Both one-parameter subgroups stay in K. The integral of either right derivative of a continuously differentiable function vanishes by Haar invariance and differentiation on the compact group. Complex linearity then gives the identity for Eab = (Aab − iBab0)/2.

Differentiating the moving coefficients contributes −4∑a ρc(a)Baa times the integrand. Here 2ρc(a) counts later positions minus earlier positions with the sign of a. This contribution cancels the scalar terms because μ = Λ + 2ρc, as follows from μ = λ + ρ and Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. We obtain

dA(x)(Hx + xH) = −(T(H)A(x) + A(x)T(H)).

One-sided identities. For a skew-Hermitian block diagonal Y, differentiating the conjugation rule gives dA(x)(xY − Yx) = A(x)T(Y) − T(Y)A(x). The Hermitian identity for H = iY, divided by i, gives the corresponding sum. Adding and subtracting, then extending complex-linearly to every block diagonal Y,

dA(x)(xY) = −T(Y)A(x),   dA(x)(Yx) = −A(x)T(Y).

These hold at positive definite x. For z close to such a matrix write z = Z1 + iZ2 with Z1, Z2 Hermitian. Along s ↦ Z1 + sZ2 the defect of each identity is holomorphic for |s| < 2. It vanishes for real s, where the matrix stays positive definite, and hence at s = i by uniqueness of analytic continuation. The identities therefore hold on an open neighbourhood U of the positive definite matrices.

The local formula. By the first identity, t ↦ T(exp tY)A(z exp tY) has derivative zero while the path stays in U. Fix g0 = k0 exp X0. For g = k exp X near g0, write k−1k0 = exp Y with Y small and skew-Hermitian. The polar factors depend continuously on g, so the path exp(−X) exp(tY), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, stays in U. Together with A(exp(−X)) = A(exp X) this gives

Ψ(g) = T(k)A(exp X) = T(k0) A(g−1k0),   g−1k0 = exp(−X) exp(Y).

The right side is a holomorphic function of the matrix g on a neighbourhood of g0. Its restriction to G is therefore smooth. Only continuity of the polar factors was used.

Where does the compact weight correction change an actual derivative?

Take U(2,1) with signs (+,+,−) and λ = (3,1,−2). Then Λ = (3,2,−3), μ = (4,1,−3), and 2ρc = (1,−1,0). In the U(2) block, T is the defining two-dimensional representation times the square of the determinant. Put H = diag(1,−1) in that block and zero in the last coordinate. Since tr(H) = 0, its action on the compact type is just diag(1,−1).

At x = I, a uniformly distributed unit vector u ∈ ℂ² gives the conjugated highest-line projector Pu = uu*. In the direction 2H, differentiation of the scalar minor product contributes −2(μ₁ − μ₂)(u*Hu). Write s = |u₁|². In the sphere coordinates u = (√s exp(iα), √(1−s) exp(iβ)), the induced metric has diagonal entries 1/(4s(1−s)), s, 1−s. Its determinant is 1/4. Thus the rotation-invariant surface measure is proportional to ds dα dβ, so s is uniform on [0,1] and the phases are uniform and independent. The phases kill the off-diagonal terms in the average of Pu(u*Hu). Its first diagonal entry is ∫₀¹ s(2s − 1) ds = 1/6, and the second is −1/6. Multiplication by the normalization d = 2 gives dA(I)(2H) = −4(μ₁ − μ₂)H/6. The prescribed difference 3 gives −2H, exactly the Hermitian derivative identity at A(I) = I. Substituting Λ for μ would give −2H/3.

Why do the Casimir operators act on the kernel through λ?

The realization theorem needs Ψ to be an eigenfunction of the Casimir operator, and the residue argument needs the whole central character. Both statements are proved first for holomorphic functions of a matrix and then transported to G. On matrices z with nonzero leading minors put LXF(z) = dF(z)(Xz), the derivative of F(etXz) at t = 0. Because the variable is multiplied on the left, [LX,LY] = LYX−XY.

The minor product is an extremal vector. Let c be lower triangular and c′ upper triangular, both with nonzero diagonal. The leading block of czc′ is the product of the three leading blocks, so Δa(czc′) = ∏l≤a cllc′ll Δa(z). The exponents of Φ telescope to Φ(czc′) = ∏l(cllc′ll)−μl Φ(z). Differentiating along c = 1 + tEab gives

LEabΦ = 0 for a > b,   LEaaΦ = −μaΦ.

Now compute LEabLEbaΦ. If a < b, the inner operator already kills Φ on a neighbourhood. If a = b, the result is μa²Φ. If a > b, exchange the two operators. The exchanged product vanishes, and the commutator is L applied to Ebb − Eaa, which multiplies Φ by μa − μb. Position a has a − 1 predecessors and m − a successors. Summing over all pairs therefore gives ∑μa² − ∑(m+1−2a)μa = |μ − ρ|² − |ρ|², that is,

∑a,b LEabLEbaΦ = (|λ|² − |ρ|²) Φ.

The compact average. For c ∈ K the function z ↦ Φ(c−1zc) satisfies the same equation. Indeed the tensor ∑Eab ⊗ Eba is unchanged when both factors are conjugated by the same invertible matrix. The set of z for which every compact conjugate has nonzero minors is open because K is compact, and it contains every positive definite matrix. On it, two differentiations under the integral show that A satisfies the equation as well. The projection P plays no role in this step.

Transport to the group. Write Eab also for the complex-linear extension of right differentiation on G. Every complex matrix Z splits as Z1 + iZ2 with Z1 = (Z − JZ*J)/2 and Z2 = (Z + JZ*J)/(2i) in the Lie algebra of G. Then E(Z) differentiates along Z1 and adds i times the derivative along Z2. By the local formula, Ψ(getX) = T(k0)A(e−tXg−1k0) near g0, so EabΨ(g) = −T(k0)(LEabA)(g−1k0). Applying this twice, the two signs cancel and the order of the factors is kept:

∑a,b EabEbaΨ = (|λ|² − |ρ|²) Ψ   on G.

The Casimir scalar here uses μ = λ + ρ. Transport to the group uses the local formula with Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. The gap between opposite-sign coordinates will enter the decay estimate below.

All Gelfand elements. For k ≥ 0 let tr(Ek) be the sum of the products Ea1a2Ea2a3⋯Eaka1. The case k = 2 is the Casimir operator. Put lr = λr + (m−1)/2 and let γk(λ) be the coefficient of Xk+1 in 1 − ∏r(1 − X/(1 − lrX)). Then

tr(Ek)Ψ = γk(λ) Ψ,   tr((E∨)k)Ψ = γk(−λ) Ψ,

where E∨ab = −Em+1−b, m+1−a is the dual family reindexed by the order-reversing permutation. The proof has the same three steps. In the holomorphic step Φ is a highest-weight vector for two families satisfying the commutation relations of the Eab: the family −Em+1−a,m+1−b, with weight μ read backwards, and the transposed family, with weight −μ. On a highest-weight vector the diagonal entries of the matrix Ek act by scalars obeying a triangular recursion, whose sum is γk. Conjugating the family does not change tr(Ek), which takes care of the compact average. On the group each derivative contributes a sign, and the k signs cancel the sign (−1)k of the holomorphic eigenvalue.

The Gelfand elements commute with every Eab. Their scalar action therefore extends from the span of the coefficient functions fu(g) = ⟨w,Ψ(g)u⟩ to the module these functions generate under derivatives. Thus the generated module has infinitesimal character λ. This is the central-character input of the residue calculation. For λ = (3/2,−1/2) we get l = (2,0) and 1 − ∏ = 2X + X² + 2X³ + 4X⁴ + ⋯. Thus γ0 = 2 = m, γ1 = 1 = λ1 + λ2 and γ2 = 2 = |λ|² − |ρ|².

How fast does the kernel decay, and against which weights is it integrable?

Let h be the opposite-sign gap of λ and assume q ≥ 1. For X as above put t = ‖X‖F. Each conjugate k−1 exp(X) k equals exp(Y) with Y = k−1Xk. This matrix is again Hermitian, anticommutes with J and has Frobenius norm t. Its exponential has determinant 1, since Y has zero diagonal. The other exponents of Φ are μa − μa+1 = λa − λa+1 + 1, which are the weights of the minor-product bound. That bound therefore holds at every point of the average:

0 < Φ(k−1 exp(X) k) ≤ D(t) = exp(−(h/8) min{t², t/√(2q)}).

The operator A(exp X) averages the positive operators T(k)PT(k)−1 with positive weights at most D(t), and the same average with weight 1 is the identity. Hence 0 ≤ A(exp X) ≤ D(t)I as self-adjoint operators, and the norm is monotone on positive operators. Since T(k) is unitary,

‖Ψ(k exp X)‖ ≤ exp(−(h/8) min{t², t/√(2q)}).

No factor of d is lost. The kernel decays at the rate of its scalar factor.

Haar measure in polar coordinates. Parametrize the noncompact directions by the block B ∈ ℂp×q of entries between positive and negative positions. Let XB be the Hermitian matrix with that block. The polar map (k,X) ↦ k exp X is a bijection onto G. Transport dk ⊗ 𝒥(X)dX along it, where 𝒥(X) = ∏a<b sinh(ya−yb)/(ya−yb) over the eigenvalues y of X, each factor being 1 when the difference vanishes. The image is invariant under right translation. This reduces to the change of variables for the action of G on the cosets Kg, which the noncompact directions parametrize. It is also invariant under inversion, which sends (k,X) to (k−1,−kXk−1). Hence it is a Haar measure. Every Haar measure is a positive multiple of it. Each ratio sinh u/u is at most cosh u ≤ e|u|. The matrix X has rank at most 2q, and the squares of its eigenvalues add up to t². By Cauchy–Schwarz, ∑|ya| ≤ √(2q) t. Finally ∑a<b|ya−yb| ≤ (m−1)∑|ya|. Consequently, for every Haar measure ν there is a constant C such that every measurable f ≥ 0 satisfies

∫G f dν ≤ C ∫ℂp×q (∫K f(k exp XB) dk) em√(2q) ‖XB‖F dB.

Three thresholds. Put c = √(2q) and r = ‖X‖F. Expanding (r − 1/(2c))² ≥ 0 gives min{r², r/c} ≥ r/c − 1/(4c²), so ‖Ψ(k exp X)‖ ≤ eh/(32c²) e−hr/(8c). After paying the growth factor emcr, a function bounded by a constant times e−δr with δ > 0 is integrable over the finite-dimensional block space. This leaves three conditions.

  • The kernel is integrable when h/(8c) > mc, that is h > 16mq.
  • Its square decays at twice the rate, so the kernel is square integrable when h > 8mq.
  • The exponential series gives ‖k exp X‖F² = ‖exp X‖F² ≤ m e2r. For s ≥ 0 the function ‖Ψ(g)‖² ‖g‖Fs is therefore integrable when h/(4c) − s > mc, that is h > 8mq + 4s√(2q).

The construction of the regular models takes s = 2. It assumes h > max{2m, 16mq + 8√(2q)}, which gives all three conditions. These thresholds are not sharp. On U(1,1) the exact density is proportional to sinh(2t) dt dθ, so the kernel (cosh t)−(λ1−λ2+1) is integrable as soon as λ1 − λ2 + 1 > 2. For integrability alone the general bound here is h > 32. The weighted square-integrability test has its own threshold in the table.

The weighted coefficients of the generated vectors are treated after the realization theorem, in the growth bound for smooth vectors.

Why does right translation act unitarily on the closure of the generated module?

Fix a kernel Ψ of parameter λ and a nonzero vector v0 in its lowest compact type T. For u ∈ T write fu(g) = ⟨v0,Ψ(g)u⟩. Their span V is where the desired representation starts. We shall recover Ψ by taking coefficients of the right action on a Hilbert space H. To construct H, first close V under the infinitesimal operators Eab, obtaining a module M, then take its closure in L²(G). These derivatives exist in Hilbert norm. Indeed the functions are smooth and square integrable, their compact derivatives stay in V by equivariance, and the full Casimir acts there by the kernel scalar. The unweighted derivative estimate proved below puts each iterated derivative in L². Right translation and the fundamental theorem of calculus on each one-parameter subgroup then give the derivatives in norm.

Right translation is unitary on L²(G). The modular character of G is trivial on the compact group and on the exponentials of the noncompact directions. By the polar decomposition it is trivial everywhere, so right translation preserves Haar measure. On compactly supported continuous functions translation is continuous in L² by uniform continuity on compact sets. Density and the isometry extend continuity to every vector.

H is invariant. Since R(g) is continuous, it suffices to send generated vectors into H. Write g = k exp Y. For a nonzero noncompact direction Y, the layer estimate gives a Taylor radius of at least 1/(√2‖Y‖F) at every time, for every generated vector. At time zero the coefficients are iterated derivatives in M, so the Taylor sums lie in H. Now suppose R(exp(t0Y)) sends every vector of M into H. The Taylor coefficients at t0 are translates by this very operator of derivatives in M. They too lie in H, which is closed. Finitely many steps shorter than the same radius reach time one. For the compact factor write k = exp Z. Each layer is finite-dimensional and stable under the derivative along Z, so that series converges for every t. The restriction of R to H is therefore a unitary representation, written σλ.

How far above the lowest type can a compact type lie?

Organize the generated module by derivative layers. L0 = V, and Lk+1 adds to Lk the images of Lk under the noncompact derivatives. Each layer is finite-dimensional and stable under the compact derivatives, and M is their union. Write κ(η) = |η + ρc|² − |ρc|² for the compact Casimir scalar of highest weight η, and let h > 2m be the opposite-sign gap.

Layer bound. Let w ∈ Lk+1 be a nonzero compact highest-weight vector of weight μ, orthogonal to Lk. Then μ − Λ is a sum of k + 1 noncompact roots, and

κ(μ) ≥ κ(Λ) + 2(k+1)(h − m + 1).

Two consequences are used throughout. A compact highest-weight vector of weight Λ in M lies in V, since its components beyond V would violate the bound. A compact highest-weight vector of weight μ lies in the layer of index ⌈(κ(μ) − κ(Λ))/(2(h − m + 1))⌉, so every compact type of M occurs in a bounded layer.

To see the size of one step, lift the new vector to a tensor with one noncompact slot for each derivative. In the compact Casimir each slot pairs with the lowest type. The Dirac inequality excludes the lowering summands, and each surviving slot contributes at least 2(h − m + 1).

Deriving the contribution of a noncompact slot

Lifting to a tensor. Multiplication X1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ Xk+1 ⊗ v ↦ X1⋯Xk+1v sends tensors of noncompact directions with a last factor in V onto Lk+1 modulo Lk. It intertwines the diagonal compact action. Project away from the tensors that land in Lk. Because the projected map is injective and equivariant, w lifts to a nonzero tensor P. This tensor is a compact highest-weight vector of weight μ, and it is orthogonal to every tensor landing in Lk. Among the nonzero coefficients of P, indexed by roots eaⱼ − ebⱼ, choose one maximizing ∑ⱼ(aⱼ − bⱼ). The highest-weight equations kill every compact raising operator on that coefficient, since a compensating term would require a larger index. Its weight in V is therefore Λ. Subtracting it from μ leaves precisely the indicated sum of roots.

Splitting the compact Casimir. On tensors the compact Casimir of the diagonal action is a sum of three terms: the Casimir of the slots, the Casimir on V, and twice the sum over slots of the mixed operator C between that slot and V. The first is nonnegative and the second is κ(Λ). On P the left side is κ(μ). It remains to bound each mixed term from below by (h − m + 1)‖P‖².

Raising and lowering directions. On one noncompact slot tensored with V, the mixed operator acts on the summand of highest weight Λ ± α, with α = ea − eb and a < b of opposite signs, by θ with 2θ = ±2⟨λ + ρn,α⟩ + 2 − m. Since ⟨λ,α⟩ ≥ h and ⟨ρn,α⟩ ≥ 2 − m/2, the raising summands have θ ≥ h − m + 1 and the lowering summands have θ ≤ −h − 1. The lowering part contributes nothing to M. Its image in L1 would contain a compact highest-weight vector of weight Λ − α on which the Casimir acts by |λ|² − |ρ|². The Dirac inequality excludes this. Here the lowered parameter λ − α is still strictly decreasing. Across opposite signs its gap loses at most two, and within each sign the integral compact highest weight preserves strict order after the shift by ρc. The exterior module contains an extremal vector of weight ρhol − ρn, where ρhol is the half-sum for the holomorphic noncompact directions. Tensoring with the lowered compact type gives a highest vector of weight λ − α − ρc + ρhol. On it twice the Dirac square acts by |λ − α|² − |λ|² = 2 − 2(λa − λb) < 0. That square is nonnegative because the Dirac operator is symmetric for a positive form. A slot can be moved to the last position at the cost of lower layers only, since the bracket of two noncompact directions is compact. So a tensor whose slices in one slot are lowering lands in Lk. Orthogonality of P to such tensors puts all its slices in the raising part, where the mixed operator is at least h − m + 1.

What does the layer bound say on U(1,1)?

Take signs (+,−), so ρc = 0, κ(η) = |η|² and Λ = (λ1 + 1/2, λ2 − 1/2). The mixed operator on the two noncompact directions has eigenvalues ±(λ1 − λ2 + 1). For the tensor P = E12⊗(k+1) ⊗ w the slot Casimir is 2(k+1)². Then 2(k+1)² + |Λ|² + 2(k+1)(Λ1 − Λ2) = |Λ + (k+1)(e1 − e2)|² = κ(μ). Dropping the slot term recovers the bound. The Dirac step can be seen directly. Let u have weight Λ − (e1 − e2), and suppose the Casimir acts on u by |λ|² − 1/2. Expanding the Casimir gives 2E12E21u = 2(λ1 − λ2 − 1)u. Infinitesimal unitarity for a noncompact pair then gives ‖E21u‖² = −(λ1 − λ2 − 1)‖u‖² < 0, a contradiction.

Why is the model irreducible, and why are its compact-finite vectors generated?

All three arguments below rest on one fact from the layer bound. A compact highest-weight vector of weight Λ in M lies in V. They also use infinitesimal unitarity, ⟨Eabx,y⟩ = sgn(a,b)⟨x,Ebay⟩, obtained by differentiating the unitarity of R.

The generated module is irreducible. Let N ⊂ M be stable under every Eab. If N meets V nontrivially, irreducibility of V under the compact derivatives gives V ⊂ N, hence N = M. Otherwise let fw be the highest-weight vector of V. On the finite-dimensional, compact-stable space N ∩ Lk, where Lk is the kth layer, the functional ⟨fw,·⟩ is represented by a vector z. By infinitesimal unitarity, the diagonal derivatives act on z by the weight Λ and the compact raising derivatives kill it. So z lies in V ∩ N = 0, and N is orthogonal to fw. The orthogonal of N in M is stable and contains fw, so it is all of M, and N = 0.

The lowest type occurs once in the closure. Let j : V → H be compact-equivariant with j(V) orthogonal to V. Differentiating the equivariance shows that y ↦ ⟨j(fw),y⟩ is again a highest-weight functional of weight Λ on M. It vanishes on V. The representing-vector argument shows that it vanishes on M. The vectors v ∈ V with j(v) orthogonal to M form a compact-stable subspace containing fw, hence all of V. Since j(V) ⊂ H and M is dense in H, j = 0.

The closure is irreducible. Let S ⊂ H be closed and invariant, with orthogonal projection P. Its orthogonal complement is invariant too. On smooth vectors both are stable under the derivatives, which are limits of difference quotients. Hence V ∩ S⊥ is 0 or V. If it is V, then H ⊂ S⊥ and S = 0. If it is 0, apply the previous paragraph to the component of P|V orthogonal to V. It vanishes, so P maps V into V. Each v − Pv then lies in V ∩ S⊥ = 0, so V ⊂ S and S = H.

Compact-finite vectors are generated. Take an irreducible compact type τ in H. Its character average Pτ projects onto the sum of all copies of τ and preserves every finite-dimensional compact-stable layer. The layer bound puts all highest vectors of that type in M in one fixed Lk. Compact invariance puts their whole copies there. Consequently Pτ maps M into Lk. By continuity, density of M and closedness of that finite-dimensional layer, Pτ(H) also lies there. Each type thus has finite multiplicity. A finite-dimensional compact-stable subspace is a sum of finitely many such types and lies in the largest of their layers. This is the compact finiteness used for the embedding of the shifted models.

Why do the coefficient functions reproduce the kernel?

The square integrability of the model and the weighted bound both use one identity. For u, u′ in T and g ∈ G,

⟨fu′,R(g)fu⟩ = ‖fw‖² ⟨u′,Ψ(g)u⟩,

where w is the unit highest-weight vector of T. Normalize Haar measure dk on K to have total mass one and put d = dimℂ T. Compact Schur orthogonality will determine the projection onto the lowest type. Rescaling Haar measure on G multiplies both sides of the displayed formula by the same factor.

The Gram identity. Right equivariance Ψ(xk) = Ψ(x)T(k) gives R(k)fu = fT(k)u. So the map u ↦ fu intertwines two unitary actions of K. Its Gram operator commutes with T and is a scalar by Schur’s lemma. Evaluating on w gives ⟨fu′,fu⟩ = ‖fw‖²⟨u′,u⟩. This is the formula at g = 1.

The residual has no lowest-type component. Project R(g)fu orthogonally onto the finite-dimensional space V; the projection is some fq. The residual x = R(g)fu − fq lies in H and is orthogonal to V. Put a = Ψ(g)u − q. The average B(u′) = ∫K⟨T(k)a,u′⟩R(k)x dk is a compact-equivariant map from T to H. Its image is orthogonal to V, because R(k)−1 preserves V. The lowest type occurs in H only once, by the multiplicity-one argument above, which does not use this formula. Hence B = 0.

Evaluation at the identity. The residual has the continuous representative x(y) = fu(yg) − fq(y). Since B(v0) = 0 in L², the continuous function h ↦ ∫K⟨T(k)a,v0⟩x(hk) dk integrates to zero over every compact set, and so vanishes everywhere. At h = 1, left equivariance gives x(k) = ⟨v0,T(k)a⟩, so ∫K|⟨v0,T(k)a⟩|² dk = 0. Schur orthogonality on K gives d∫K|⟨v0,T(k)a⟩|²dk = ‖v0‖²‖a‖², hence a = 0. Thus the projection of R(g)fu onto V is fΨ(g)u, and the Gram identity gives the formula.

Computing one reproducing coefficient on SU(1,1)

Take Ψ(x) = x11−6 and choose g with diagonal entries 5/4 and off-diagonal entries 3/4. Then (xg)11 = (5/4)x11(1 + z), where z = (3/5)x12/x11. At fixed y = |x11|², the phase of z is uniform and |z| < 3/5. Only the constant term of (1 + z)−6 survives the angular average. With radial Haar measure dy on [1,∞) and angular mass one, the resulting integral is (4/5)⁶∫₁∞y−6 dy = 4096/78125. Dividing by ‖Ψ‖² = 1/5 recovers Ψ(g) = (4/5)⁶.

In what sense is the model the discrete series of parameter λ?

For this large-gap family, the following five properties characterize the representation attached to λ. It is a nonzero irreducible unitary representation. Its coefficients are square integrable. It contains a compact type of highest weight Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. That type is minimal in Vogan's sense: |Λ + 2ρc|² ≤ |μ + 2ρc|² for every compact type μ that occurs. The uniqueness argument below recovers the Casimir scalar from these properties. The constructed space is nonzero because its lowest type embeds, and the preceding argument gives irreducibility and unitarity.

Square integrability. By the reproducing formula, ⟨fw,R(g)fw⟩ is a multiple of ⟨w,Ψ(g)w⟩, which is square integrable by the second threshold. In an irreducible unitary representation one nonzero square-integrable coefficient suffices. Fix y0 and consider the coefficient map x ↦ ⟨y0,σ(·)x⟩ on the vectors where it is square integrable. Its graph is closed and invariant. Let P be its orthogonal projection in H ⊕ L²(G). The first coordinate of P(x,0) defines a positive operator commuting with σ and taking values in the coefficient domain. It is nonzero since the graph contains a pair with nonzero first coordinate. By Schur’s lemma it is a scalar multiple of the identity, so the domain is the whole space and every coefficient of y0 is square integrable. Inversion preserves Haar measure and interchanges the entries up to complex conjugation. Thus, for each fixed y, its coefficient domain already contains y0 ≠ 0. The same graph projection now makes that domain all of H, giving square integrability for every pair.

The lowest type and its minimality. The space V is a compact type of highest weight Λ, and every copy of this particular type in H equals V. Let μ ≠ Λ occur. Choose the first layer Lj+1 containing its highest vector. Subtract its projection to Lj. The nonzero remainder has the same highest weight because this projection commutes with the compact action. The layer bound gives κ(μ) − κ(Λ) ≥ 2(j+1)(h − m + 1), where κ is the compact Casimir scalar. Moreover μ − Λ is a sum of j + 1 noncompact roots, each pairing with ρc to at least −m. Since |x + 2ρc|² = |x + ρc|² + 2⟨x,ρc⟩ + 3|ρc|²,

|μ + 2ρc|² − |Λ + 2ρc|² ≥ 2(j+1)(h − 2m + 1) > 0.

This is where the hypothesis h > 2m is used.

Uniqueness. Conversely, any representation with these five properties is unitarily equivalent to σλ. Minimality excludes compact types of weight Λ − (ea − eb) in the first layer. The Dirac square then makes the Casimir operator act by |λ|² − |ρ|² on the lowest type, and irreducibility spreads this to all smooth vectors. Take a compact isometry φ between the two lowest types. Form the direct sum and generate a closed subrepresentation from the diagonal lowest type {(v,φv)}. In each coordinate the compact type is Λ and the full Casimir acts by |λ|² − |ρ|². The diagonal type inherits both properties. Project the antidiagonal copy {(v,−φv)} onto this generated subrepresentation. That projection is compact-equivariant and remains orthogonal to the diagonal lowest type. Multiplicity one makes it zero. The antidiagonal is thus orthogonal to every group translate of the diagonal. Expanding this inner product gives ⟨φv′,σ(g)φv⟩ = ⟨v′,σλ(g)v⟩ for all g. The translates of the lowest type are total by irreducibility, so R(g)v ↦ σ(g)φv extends to a unitary intertwiner. Combined with the kernel, this proves existence for every parameter with h > max{2m, 16mq + 8√(2q)}. When q = 0 the group is compact and K = G, and this case is treated separately.

Why do the derivatives of a coefficient keep its weighted square integrability?

The weighted bound for generated vectors needs more than the kernel. A coefficient can be square integrable with a weight while its derivatives grow. The following estimate uses compact stability and the Casimir equation to control every derivative with the same weight. Let W be a space of smooth functions on G with three properties. It is stable under the compact derivatives Eij, those with i and j of the same sign. All its members are eigenfunctions of the Casimir operator C for one eigenvalue. Finally, ∫G ‖g‖F4a|w|² dg < ∞ for every w ∈ W, for some fixed a ≥ 0. Then every derivative Ep1⋯Epkw has the same weighted bound, and

∫G EijF · conj(F′) dg = sgn(i,j) ∫G F · conj(EjiF′) dg

for any two such derivatives F, F′. Here sgn(i,j) is +1 for a compact pair and −1 otherwise. The sign comes from conjugation: Eij(conj f) = −sgn(i,j) conj(Ejif), because JEij*J = sgn(i,j)Eji. The argument applies to any dimension of W and any common Casimir eigenvalue.

The estimate comes from the signed second-order operator T = 2CK − C. Integration by parts bounds the weighted first derivatives of u once u and Tu have finite weighted norm. Compact stability keeps T in the same derivative layer, which lets the estimate be iterated.

The cutoff, integration by parts and the bound on one derivative

Cutoffs with bounded derivatives. Measure size by ℓ(g) = log ‖g‖F². On G we have ‖g‖F² ≥ tr(Jg*Jg) = m, so ℓ ≥ 0. The right derivative of ℓ along X is 2 Re⟨g,gX⟩/‖g‖F², which has absolute value at most 2‖X‖F. Let χ be smooth and decreasing, equal to 1 on (−∞,1] and to 0 on [2,∞). The cutoff χ(ℓ/R) has compact support and derivatives of size O(1/R), uniformly on G. This is why the logarithm of the size is used rather than the size. For a smooth function ψ vanishing outside a compact set, ∫G RXψ dg = 0. Indeed G is unimodular, so the integral of ψ(g exp tX) does not depend on t.

A Gårding inequality. Let ρR = χ(ℓ/R)² e2aℓ, so that 0 ≤ ρR ≤ ‖g‖F4a and |EijρR| is at most a constant cij times χ(ℓ/R)e2aℓ once R ≥ 1. Integrate the derivative of ρRu conj(Eiju) along Eij. The Leibniz rule and the conjugation rule give

∫ρR|Eiju|² = −∫(EijρR) u conj(Eiju) + sgn(i,j)∫ρR u conj(EjiEiju).

Sum over all pairs i, j, both compact and noncompact. The last terms combine into ∫ρR u conj(Tu) with T = ∑ sgn(i,j)EjiEij = 2CK − C, where CK is the compact Casimir. Bound the first terms by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and absorb half of the left side. Write ‖u‖a for the weighted norm. The weighted integral of ∑|Eiju|² against ρR is then at most (1 + ∑cij²)‖u‖a² + ‖Tu‖a², uniformly in R. As R grows, ρR increases to the full weight, and monotone convergence shows that every Eiju is weighted square integrable whenever u and Tu are.

Induction on the length of a derivative. Let Vk be the span of all derivatives of members of W by words of length at most k. Moving a compact derivative to the right through a word changes the word only by words of the same length, by the commutation relations, so CK preserves Vk. The Casimir operator commutes with every Eab, so it acts on Vk by the eigenvalue of W. Hence T maps Vk to itself. If Vk is weighted square integrable, the inequality applies to every u ∈ Vk and puts Vk+1 in the same space. The adjoint identity then follows by the same integration by parts with the cutoff χ(ℓ/R) alone. Its error term is O(1/R) times an integrable function, and dominated convergence removes the cutoff.

Which Casimir controls the derivative on U(1,1)?

For f(g) = g11−k with an integer k ≥ 2 one finds E11f = −kf, E12f = E22f = 0 and Cf = (k² − k)f, while Tf = (k² + k)f. At a = 0 the summed identity reads ∑‖Eijf‖² = ⟨f,Tf⟩, so the noncompact derivative has ‖E21f‖² = k‖f‖². In polar coordinates with x = cosh²r, Haar measure is proportional to dx. The two sides are k²∫1∞(x−1)x−k−1dx = k/(k−1) and k∫1∞x−kdx.

Weighted coefficients of the generated vectors. The signed column pairing and the embedding of the shifted models assume that ‖g‖F⟨y,R(g)x⟩ is square integrable for all x, y ∈ M. Take a = 1/2, so the weight is ‖g‖F². Fix y in V and let W consist of the coefficients ⟨y,R(·)x⟩ with x ∈ V. By the reproducing formula these are multiples of coefficients of Ψ. The third threshold with s = 2 makes them square integrable with this weight. The space W is stable under the compact derivatives and consists of Casimir eigenfunctions, so the lemma applies. A derivative of a coefficient is the coefficient of the derivative, ⟨y,R(·)Eabx⟩ = Eab⟨y,R(·)x⟩. Hence the claim holds for y ∈ V and all x ∈ M. The substitution g ↦ g−1 exchanges the two vectors, because g−1 = Jg*J has the same Frobenius norm and Haar measure is invariant under inversion. A second application of the lemma, now in the other slot, covers every pair.

Why does the column differential have finitely many eigenvalues?

Let M be the module generated by the coefficient functions of the kernel, and consider columns f = (f1,…,fm) with entries in M. Write x[c] for the column whose only nonzero coordinate is x, in position c. On V* ⊗ π the matrix Eab acts by (Tabf)c = Eabfc − δcbfa. The column differential of the residue calculation is (Df)r = −∑s Ersfs. Expanding the tensor Casimir gives ∑TabTba = (Casimir on each entry) + m + 2D. The Casimir acts on M by the scalar |λ|² − |ρ|², so D commutes with every Tab. The space of columns is infinite-dimensional. Three facts nevertheless give a polynomial in D that vanishes on it.

A finite-dimensional stable piece. Let V be the span of the coefficient functions, a copy of the lowest compact type, and let Vm be the columns with entries in V. Each diagonal operator Tcc commutes with D. Hence the compact weights occurring in the spaces Dj(Vm) lie in a finite set, fixed by the minimal polynomials of the Tcc on Vm. Organize M by derivative layers. The zeroth layer is V, and the kth adds one noncompact derivative to the previous layer. The Casimir gap shows that a compact highest-weight vector of a given weight lies in a layer whose index is bounded by the compact Casimir difference divided by 2(h − m + 1). Choose a layer L containing every compact highest-weight vector of M whose weight is an allowed weight shifted by a unit vector. Suppose Dj(Vm) had a component orthogonal to Lm. Projecting away from Lm is compact-equivariant, so that component would contain a compact highest-weight vector. Its extreme nonzero coordinate would be a compact highest-weight vector of M of a shifted allowed weight. It would lie in L while being orthogonal to L, which is impossible. Thus the sum W of all Dj(Vm) is finite-dimensional and stable under D.

A positive invariant form. For columns f, f′ put Q(f,f′) = ∑∫G conj(φ(f)) φ(f′) dg, where φ runs over the coefficients of the column action against y ⊗ eξ, with y in a basis of V and ξ a coordinate. Each coefficient is a sum of products of a matrix entry of (g−1)ᵗ with ⟨y,R(g)fc⟩. That entry is at most ‖g‖F in absolute value, so the weighted bound of the preceding section makes Q finite. It is positive definite. If Q(f,f) = 0 every coefficient vanishes, and then f = 0 because M lies in the closed span of the translates of V. Right invariance of Haar measure makes each Tab adjoint to ± Tba, with the sign of the product of the two coordinate signs. The two signs multiply to 1 in the tensor Casimir, so D is symmetric for Q.

The nodal polynomial. A symmetric operator for a positive definite form on the finite-dimensional space W has real eigenvalues and no nilpotent part. Let N(X) = ∏b∈B(X − b) over its spectrum B on W. Then N(D) kills W, which contains Vm. The kernel of N(D) is stable under every Tab. A space of columns stable under every Tab and containing Vm contains all columns, because (Eabx)[c] = Tab(x[c]) + δac x[b]. Hence N(D) = 0 on every column. Lagrange interpolation at the points of B writes each column as a finite sum of eigenvectors of D, and every eigenvalue of D lies in B. Only the quadratic Casimir was used. Identifying which numbers occur is the work of the residue calculation, which uses the whole central character.

The partial traces of the powers. The partial trace of an operator S on columns is the operator x ↦ ∑c(S(x[c]))c on M. The operator D multiplies columns by the matrix (−Ers), whose entries are operators on M. Hence Dk multiplies them by the kth power of that matrix, with the factors kept in order. Taking the partial trace gives the trace of this power, (−1)ktr(Ek). The central character evaluates it on M as (−1)kγk(λ). Put X = −z in the series defining γk. Since 1 + z/(1 + lsz) = 1 + z/(1 − asz) with as = −λs − (m−1)/2, this proves the identity used in the residue calculation:

ptr(Dk) = coefficient of zk+1 in ∏s(1 + z/(1 − asz)) − 1.

A finite-dimensional model shows the mechanism without any analysis. Take m = 2 and replace M by ℂ² with Eab the matrix units, so λ = (3/2,−1/2). Then D(ej[i]) = −δij ∑r er[r]. Columns are 2 × 2 matrices here. The eigenvalue −2 occurs on the line spanned by the identity matrix and 0 on the traceless matrices. These are −λs − 1/2 for s = 1, 2. The partial traces of Dk for k = 0, 1, 2, 3 are 2, −1, 2, −4. The series (1 + z/(1+2z))(1 + z) − 1 = 2z − z² + 2z³ − 4z⁴ + ⋯ has the same coefficients.

How does a collision in the weights remove an eigenspace?

On the tensor columns generated by the lowest compact type, take D = −Ω, where Ω is the column differential used in the final projector. The minus sign comes from the action of a matrix on covectors. If position s survives, its candidate eigenvalue for D is as = −λs − (m − 1)/2. These numbers are distinct even when shifting a weight would create a tie. To determine which candidates are present, take the partial trace of an operator on columns, the sum of its diagonal operator entries. It acts on the original representation space.

Here are the two representation-theoretic ingredients. On the generated columns, the finite spectral decomposition of D gives projections Pb at a finite set of real values b, and each partial trace equals a scalar cb times the identity. Second, the central character prescribes the partial trace of each power Dk. Its value is the coefficient of zk+1 in ∏s(1 + z/(1 − asz)) − 1. We can compare these two evaluations using ordinary polynomials.

Introduce u = 1/z. The product becomes ∏t(1 + 1/(u − at)) − 1. Its partial fraction at as has numerator rs obtained by multiplying by u − as and evaluating there. The difference between the rational function and the sum of these partial fractions has no poles and tends to zero at infinity, so it vanishes. Expanding 1/(u − a) as z/(1 − az) now gives, for k ≥ 0,

∑b cb bk = ∑s rs ask,   rs = ∏t≠s (λs − 1 − λt)/(λs − λt).

To isolate a value v, take the union of the two finite supports. For each other value w multiply by the polynomial factor (X − w)/(v − w). The resulting polynomial is one at v and zero everywhere else on the union. Linear combinations of the power identities therefore equate the total weight at v on both sides.

One analytic fact is essential at this point. For the spectral projections here, a zero partial-trace scalar forces the entire projection to vanish. The coordinate calculation below proves this fact. In the coefficient model, testing the projection on one lowest-type vector gives the scalar as a sum of squared norms of representing vectors divided by a positive formal degree. If the scalar vanishes, all those vectors vanish. Every projected coefficient of a column supported on that test vector then vanishes. Vary the lowest-type vector and apply the commuting differential action to reach the generated columns. This positivity argument is what turns a statement about a trace into one about vectors.

If λs − 1 = λt, one numerator of rs vanishes. The interpolation and positivity show that there is no nonzero eigenvector at as. Conversely, when a lowering is regular every factor is nonzero, so the matching spectral projection is nonzero. For (6001,6000,0) the three partial-trace scalars are 0, 5999/3000 and 3001/3000. Their sum is 3, as it must be for the partial trace of the identity on three columns. Only the last two shifts contribute to the coefficient expansion.

How can a signed pairing detect every column?

To decide whether a shifted eigenspace is empty, we need a test that detects a nonzero vector even if its signed length vanishes. Write J = diag(ε₁,…,εm), where εb = ±1 records the signature of U(p,q). On an m-tuple of vectors in π put B(f,h) = ∑b εb ⟨fb,hb⟩. We take inner products linear in the second entry. For signature (+,−), the column (x,x) has signed length zero, even for a nonzero x. Pairing it with (x,−x) gives 2‖x‖².

Fix a nonzero vector y in the lowest compact type of π and its formal degree d for the chosen Haar measure. Let A(g) = (g−1)ᵗ on the dual defining representation. For derivative-generated columns define zf,b(g) = ⟨y,π(g)fb⟩ and Φ(f)(g) = JA(g)zf(g). Each coordinate is in L² by the weighted coefficient estimate for the separated original parameter. This use of the weight matters because A(g) may grow. Denote by J also the operation that changes signs coordinatewise on L²(G)m.

⟨Φ(f), JΦ(h)⟩ = (‖y‖²/d) B(f,h).

Indeed A(g)*JA(g) = J. This follows by taking inverses and conjugating the defining relation g*Jg = J, since J is real and J² = I. Thus the signed pointwise inner product reduces to that of zf and zh. Integrate and apply Schur orthogonality in π separately to each coordinate. Finally take the pair (Jf,f) in the identity. If Φ(f) vanishes, then (‖y‖²/d)∑‖fb‖² vanishes as well. This proves injectivity. Duflo and Moore, orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations, in the unimodular case[12].

Why is the partial trace a sum of ordinary squared norms?

Let P be the projector for one tensor eigenvalue. On generated columns it is idempotent, commutes with compact translations and tensor derivatives, and satisfies B(Pf,h) = B(f,Ph). Suppose its partial trace is cI. We want the sign of c. The ordinary Hilbert space where we can compute norms is the closure HP of the span of Φ(Pf). Right translation R(g) preserves this space. To see why, let V be the finite-dimensional lowest compact type. The starting space ΦP(Vm) is finite-dimensional and compact-stable. It generates every Φ(Pf) by derivatives. Indeed a tensor derivative is the sum of its actions on the matrix slot and the coefficient slot. Subtract the first action, which only mixes matrix coordinates, and induct on the number of coefficient derivatives. The tensor Casimir on these projected generators has scalar cπ+m+2z, where cπ is the original Casimir scalar and z is the tensor differential eigenvalue. Its three terms come from the coefficient slot, the matrix slot, and twice their mixed operator. Symmetry on the unitary coefficient space makes this scalar real whenever the image is nonzero. The derivative-closure theorem applies to their derivatives. In particular the ordinary orthogonal projection Q onto HP commutes with these unitary translations.

Write eby for a column with y in slot b only. Set ub = Φ(Peby), κ = d/‖y‖² and wb = κQJub. Each wb reads one coordinate of a translated vector:

vb(g) = ⟨wb, R(g)v⟩   for almost every g,   v ∈ HP.

For a generator v = Φ(Pf), its translate is the coefficient column of the translated tensor vector, since both are evaluated by replacing x with xg. The components of the translated tensor are in the closed original representation space and its coefficient functions remain in L² by right invariance of Haar measure. These are exactly the hypotheses of the signed pairing calculation. Pair this with JΦ(eby) in the signed column identity. Multiplying by κ gives exactly the value of coordinate b at g. We may first replace eby by Peby. Indeed B((I−P)η,Pf) = 0 by idempotence and signed symmetry, hence JΦ((I−P)η) is perpendicular to the closed space containing the translate. Its orthogonal projection is zero. For a limit of generators the coordinates converge in L², and along a subsequence almost everywhere. On the other side the inner products converge uniformly in g, since R(g) is an isometry. For the subsequence, choose successive L² errors at most 2−2j. The sets with error greater than 2−j then have summable measures, so their tail unions have measure tending to zero.

Computing ⟨y,(ptr P)y⟩ slot by slot gives c‖y‖² = ∑b εb B(Peby,Peby). The signed column identity makes each B on the right equal to ⟨ub,wb⟩. Expand these last inner products by coordinate. The integral comparing (ub)a and (wb)a is the complex conjugate of the integral with a,b exchanged. To see this, use the displayed coordinate formula for both functions and change g to g−1 in Haar measure. Unitarity exchanges the slots of two coordinate readers. For the mixed pair, ⟨wa,R(g)ub⟩ = κ⟨ua,R(g)Jub⟩ = ⟨ua,R(g)wb⟩. In the first equality we may drop Q because R(g)ub belongs to its range. In the second we may insert it because R(g−1)ua also belongs to its range. Conjugation then exchanges the indices at g−1. On summing, the sign εb now acts on the coordinate b inside each vector. Thus

c‖y‖² = ∑a ⟨Jua, wa⟩ = κ ∑a ‖QJua‖²,   c = (1/d)∑a ‖wa‖².

If c = 0, all coordinate readers vanish, so every element of HP has every coordinate zero almost everywhere. In particular Φ(Pf) = 0 for each generated column f. Injectivity of Φ gives Pf = 0. This proves the positivity and the vanishing criterion used at the colliding weight.

When does one shifted representation fill the projected space?

Suppose a copy of a shifted irreducible square-integrable representation has already been placed in HP. Write H′ for this nonzero closed invariant subspace, E for orthogonal projection onto it, and d′ for its formal degree in the same Haar measure as d. We can measure exactly how much of each coordinate reader lies in this copy. For v ∈ H′ every translate belongs to H′, so ⟨wb,R(g)v⟩ = ⟨Ewb,R(g)v⟩. Integrate its squared modulus using Schur orthogonality in H′, sum in b, and choose v nonzero to cancel ‖v‖². This gives ∑‖Ewb‖² = d′. The trace formula and Pythagoras now give an exact remainder:

d c − d′ = ∑b ‖(I − E)wb‖² ≥ 0.

At equality every wb lies in H′. Take v in HP perpendicular to H′. For every g we have ⟨R(g−1)wb,v⟩ = 0, so every coordinate of v vanishes almost everywhere. Hence HP = H′. For a regular lowering the formal-degree product gives d′/d equal to the residue at that shift. This proves saturation in the Hilbert coefficient space once the algebraic embedding has supplied the copy. Identifying individual algebraic tensor vectors in its image additionally uses compact finiteness in this copy.

For a finite example take the four-element group of pairs of bits and normalized counting measure. On the constants together with the character χ(a,b) = (−1)a, the function w = 1 + χ represents evaluation at the identity. Its squared norm is 2. Projection onto the constants leaves a reader of squared norm 1, the formal degree of the trivial representation. The difference 1 measures the second character. Restrict the original space to constants alone and the difference vanishes.
