How is a regular shifted model placed among the columns?

Fix G = U(p,q), 1 ≤ q ≤ p, and m = p + q. Take a regular lowering λ′ = λ − es under the gap hypotheses for the shifted models. Both parameters must lie in the range of the kernel construction. The initial opposite-sign gap is at least 200m³, and lowering one entry costs at most one. Thus both gaps exceed the threshold for the weighted coefficient estimates. For each parameter use its positive kernel, a nonzero initial vector in its lowest compact type and the resulting derivative module, denoted M and M′. Their Hilbert closures carry π and πs. We will embed M′ into the columns of M by a complex-linear map ι intertwining the derivatives and K. Its image will be exactly the eigenspace of D at as = −λs − (m−1)/2.

A compact map and a positive pairing. Write T, T′ for the lowest compact types and Ψ, Ψ′ for their kernels. Their weights satisfy Λ′ = Λ − es. By the Pieri rule the compact type of weight Λ′ occurs in T ⊗ V*, and interchanging the two tensor factors gives a nonzero K-equivariant map ι0 ∶ T′ → V* ⊗ T. For an orthonormal basis (bi) of T′ consider

I = ∑i,j ∫G conj⟨ι0bi,(ρ(g) ⊗ Ψ(g))ι0bj⟩ ⟨bi,Ψ′(g)bj⟩ dg,

with ρ(g) = (g−1)ᵗ. The integral converges by the weighted bound, since |ρ(g)cd| ≤ ‖g‖F. Write g = k exp Y. The equivariance of the two kernels and of ι0 removes k, because the sum over an orthonormal basis does not change under a unitary change of basis. What remains is tr(SΨ′(exp Y)) with S = ι0*(ρ(exp Y) ⊗ Ψ(exp Y))ι0. Here ρ(exp Y) = exp(−Yᵗ) is positive definite, and the two kernels are positive semidefinite at exp Y by the first section. So S ≥ 0 and the trace of a product of two positive operators is nonnegative. At g = 1 the integrand is ∑‖ι0bj‖² > 0. By continuity Re I > 0.

From the pairing to a projection. The integrand of I pairs a coefficient of the column action with a coefficient of Ψ′. By the reproducing formula of the realization theorem, coefficients of Ψ′ are inner products in the closure of M′. Hence some coefficient of the column action, φ(f)(g) = ∑c⟨ηc,(A(g)f)c⟩ with A(g) the column action, has a nonzero component in that closure. Each such φ(f) is smooth and square integrable by the weighted bound. Let p(f) be its orthogonal projection onto the closure of M′. A finite-dimensional K-stable subspace of that closure lies in M′, so p maps columns into M′. It commutes with the derivatives and with K, and it is not zero.

The signed adjoint. Let jc = ±1 be the sign of coordinate c. For x ∈ M′ define ιx by ⟨(ιx)c,y⟩ = jc⟨x,p(y[c])⟩ for y ∈ M, with the column notation y[c] of the spectral splitting. The right side vanishes on all compact types above some level, so compact finiteness of M supplies a representing vector in M. The signs are what make ι commute with the derivatives. On smooth vectors the formal adjoints satisfy Eab* = jajbEba, and the column action carries the same pair of signs. The kernel of ι is a submodule of the irreducible module M′. It is not everything because p ≠ 0, hence ι is injective.

The eigenvalue. The tensor Casimir acts on ι(M′) by |λ′|² − |ρ|² = |λ|² − |ρ|² − 2λs + 1. By the expansion of the tensor Casimir it also equals |λ|² − |ρ|² + m + 2D there. Since m + 2as = 1 − 2λs, we get Dι = asι.

Filling the eigenspace and the ratio of formal degrees. Let P be the Lagrange projection onto the as-eigenspace given by the spectral splitting. The residue calculation gives its partial-trace scalar rs = ∏t≠s(λs − 1 − λt)/(λs − λt). Take the formal degrees d of π and d′ of πs for one Haar measure on G. For the lowering, the copy of πs accounts for a contribution d′/d to the partial trace. The degree defect gives d′/d ≤ rs. Equality forces every projected column Pf into ι(M′). For the reverse estimate start from πs, tensor with V and raise λ′ + es = λ. The same argument now places the original degree in the numerator and gives d/d′ ≤ ∏t≠s(λs − λt)/(λs − 1 − λt) = 1/rs. Hence

d′/d = rs,   ι(M′) = {f : Df = asf}.

Indeed rs ≥ d′/d > 0, so taking reciprocals in the reverse estimate gives the missing inequality rs ≤ d′/d. In the finite model of the spectral splitting the two eigenspaces are the line of the identity matrix and the traceless matrices. Their dimensions divided by dim ℂ² = 2 are 1/2 and 3/2. These equal r1 = (3/2 − 1 + 1/2)/2 and r2 = (−1/2 − 1 − 3/2)/(−2), so dimensions play the part of formal degrees.

How does an embedding of derivative modules become an identity on the group?

Work in the two unitary models above and let ι ∶ M′ → Mm be any complex-linear injection intertwining the derivatives and K. Write (A(g)F)c = ∑d ρ(g)cdR(g)Fd for the column action on the Hilbert space. Although ι is defined on derivative vectors, their coefficients agree on the whole group. Given a column f, there exists z ∈ M′ such that for every x′ ∈ M′

∑c ⟨fc,(A(g)ιx′)c⟩ = ⟨z,R(g)x′⟩   for all g ∈ G.

Conversely, given z ∈ M′, one can choose a single column f for all x′ and g.

The identity element. For the first identity, the functional y ↦ ∑c⟨fc,(ιy)c⟩ on M′ vanishes on compact types above some level. Indeed f lies in finitely many derivative layers, the compact Casimir is symmetric on columns, and ι intertwines it. Compact finiteness then gives a representing vector z, which does not depend on x′. For the converse, injectivity makes ⟨ιy,ιy′⟩ a definite form on each finite-dimensional eigenspace of the compact Casimir. Solving ⟨ιy0,ιy⟩ = ⟨z,y⟩ there gives the column f = ιy0.

The coefficient identity extends from 1 along a compact one-parameter subgroup and then along a noncompact one. At each point the two orbit series have equal Taylor coefficients because ι intertwines the derivatives. Their radii admit a lower bound independent of the point and the vector, so finitely many steps cover each segment. This reaches every element of G by polar decomposition, since g = exp(Z) exp(Y) with Z skew-Hermitian in the compact blocks and Y Hermitian in the noncompact directions.

Why the orbit series propagate the identity along a segment

Suppose a pair f, z gives the identity at h for every y ∈ M′. Along a compact or noncompact direction X, the coefficient of tk on either side at h exp(tX) is that identity applied to Xky/k!. On columns the derivative includes the factor exp(−tXᵗ) from the dual defining representation. In a compact direction the generators preserve a finite-dimensional layer, so its exponential series is entire. For a noncompact Y, the sum of the squared noncompact derivatives of a vector is the quadratic form of the compact Casimir minus the full Casimir. The former is bounded on layer j by a quadratic in j, and the latter acts by a scalar. Iteration gives

‖Yky‖ ≤ ‖Y‖Fk ∏l<k(C + √2(j+l)) ‖y‖   for y in the jth layer.

After division by k!, the product bound gives convergence for |t| < 1/(√2‖Y‖F + 1), regardless of the initial layer j. Taylor’s formula with remainder identifies the series with the orbit on this interval. Translation by h then preserves the convergence.

Back to the comparison. Take z = x′ = y in the converse identity. Then ⟨y,πs(g)y⟩ = ∑c,d ρ(g)cd⟨fc,R(g)(ιy)d⟩, a finite sum of products of an entry of ρ(g) and a coefficient of π. This is the reverse direction of the coefficient comparison. For the forward direction, split a column into eigenvectors of D. Each surviving eigenvector lies in the image of ι for its shift, and the first identity converts its coefficient into a coefficient of πs.

How do identities of scalar functions recover a smooth column?

Fix an allowed shift and write σ = πs. Let A(g) denote the action on the smooth columns of X. Fix a coordinate b, a smooth vector w in π and a vector y in σ. Use the inverse action to define a scalar test fb,x(g) = ⟨w,(A(g−1)x)b⟩. Take inner products linear in the second slot. Against the same Haar measure as the formal degree, set

Pb,w,yx = ∫G fb,x(g) σ(g)y dg.

The gap bound supplies coefficient decay of order m² + 2. The single finite-dimensional matrix factor uses one power of the group size. The remaining majorant of order −(m² + 1) is integrable and its constant for fixed w is bounded by a finite sum of derivative norms of x. Since σ is unitary, the norm of the integrand is |fb,x(g)| ‖y‖. Substituting g = hu gives P A(h) = σ(h)P by left invariance. The derivative-norm estimate makes P continuous on smooth columns, so applying it to the smooth orbit of x gives the smooth orbit of Px.

Every regular model is detected. Compact-finite vectors in these discrete series are smooth, so their one-coordinate columns can enter the averaging map. Take the nonzero y in the reverse coefficient identity. Evaluate that identity at g−1 and multiply by ⟨y,σ(g)y⟩. The left side integrates to ‖y‖⁴/dσ by Schur orthogonality. Every term on the right is ⟨y,Px⟩ for one of the maps above and a column supported in one coordinate. The positive left side implies at least one such map is nonzero.

Together the maps detect every column. Suppose every map to every regular model kills a smooth column x. Choose a nonzero K-finite w in π. For a fixed coordinate c, multiply each fb,x by ρ(g)cb⟨w,π(g)w⟩ and sum over b. By the forward coefficient identity every integral is a finite sum of pairings with images of x, hence zero. Before integration, the factors ρ(g) and ρ(g−1) multiply to the identity. The single surviving coordinate gives, by mixed Schur orthogonality,

0 = ∫G ⟨w,π(g)w⟩ ⟨xc,π(g)w⟩ dg = ‖w‖² ⟨w,xc⟩ / dπ.

The common kernel is invariant. Apply the same calculation to A(h)x and multiply its vector of coordinate pairings by ρ(h)−1. This yields ⟨w,π(h)xc⟩ = 0 for every h. The closed span of the translates of the nonzero vector w is an invariant subspace, hence is the whole irreducible space of π. Each coordinate vanishes. M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, Schur orthogonality for square-integrable representations[12].

Why does one map per regular shift suffice?

Let B be the shifted model πs and T the original π. Translating B by the defining representation V raises the same coordinate back to λ. The averaging argument for this direction gives a nonzero map V ⊗ B → T. Tensor adjunction turns it into an inclusion κ from B into V* ⊗ T. In coordinates adjunction sends a map f to b ↦ ∑ded ⊗ f(ed ⊗ b), where the two bases are dual. Evaluation in each basis direction recovers f. The smooth kernel theorem makes this map injective. Indeed, if it killed a nonzero smooth vector, equivariance would kill its entire orbit span. Smooth approximation by that span controls any prescribed finite list of derivatives. Continuity in those derivative norms would then make the map zero on every smooth vector.

To bound the number of maps V* ⊗ T → B, use adjunction once more. A candidate now reads I from T to V ⊗ B. Apply I to each T-coordinate of κ. Reordering the two finite factors gives a map Φ from B to V ⊗ V* ⊗ B. Contracting the first two slots takes the trace of its matrix of vectors. This makes an endomorphism of B, hence a scalar by Schur's lemma. To see why the scalar determines I, suppose it is zero.

Write C(λ) for the scalar of the quadratic Casimir, the sum of squared coordinates of λ minus a rank-dependent constant. On Φ the total Casimir has scalar CB, and the partial Casimir on the V and B slots has scalar CT by construction of I. Expanding the square of the three-slot differential gives the sum of the two partial Casimirs, with one copy of the B-Casimir subtracted because both partials contain it, plus a cross term between the two finite slots. On a matrix of vectors that cross term is −2 times the map sending its trace to a scalar diagonal matrix. Indeed on the dual factor the generator Eab acts by −Eba. Thus on Φ the expansion reads Ctotal = CV,B + CV*,B − CB. On each row the partial Casimir for V* ⊗ B would have scalar 2CB − CT.

But the maps separating this last tensor have targets at regular second lowerings. Subtracting one in position s changes the sum of squares by −2λs + 1. A second subtraction in position t gives

C(λ − es − et) − [2C(λ − es) − C(λ)] = 2(λs − λt) + 2δst.

For t = s the difference is 2. For distinct positions it is nonzero by strict ordering. An intertwiner commutes with the Casimir, so its image of each row must be zero. Joint separation gives Φ = 0. Since κ is nonzero, one of its coordinates takes a nonzero value, which I must kill. The kernel theorem for smooth discrete-series intertwiners then gives I = 0. We have injected the space of candidate maps into the scalars. Existence from the preceding argument makes its dimension exactly one.

Choose one nonzero projection Ps per regular shift. Compositions with inclusions of other weights vanish because their central characters differ. Some projection detects a nonzero vector in the sth inclusion, hence its own projection does. Normalize that inclusion so the matching composition is the identity. Subtract ∑sκsPsx from a smooth column x. Every chosen projection kills the difference. Multiplicity one makes every map to every model a multiple of a chosen projection, so joint separation kills the difference itself. This is the smooth direct sum on which the cofactor projector is evaluated.

How large is one derivative after the vector has already been differentiated?

The projector onto a shifted summand involves a minor whose entries are differential operators. Applying the first operator can take a vector out of its lowest compact type. To estimate a product of operators, we therefore follow the spaces reached at each order.

Let π be a unitary discrete series of G = U(p,q), with m = p + q ≥ 2, and K = U(p) × U(q). Its Harish-Chandra parameter λ has strictly decreasing coordinates that belong to the same translate of the integers. Assume |λa| ≤ B and |λa − λb| ≥ 100m³ for coordinates with opposite signature. Write ρ for the half-sum of the positive roots ea − eb with a < b. The same-sign roots contribute ρc and the opposite-sign roots contribute ρn. The lowest compact-type and infinitesimal-character theorems give a unique smooth compact type of highest weight Λ = λ + ρn − ρc and the full Casimir eigenvalue ‖λ‖² − ‖ρ‖². We use these statements as inputs. The discrete-series input requires a gap strictly greater than mpq + 1. Since pq ≤ m², the stipulated gap suffices. M. F. Atiyah and W. Schmid, Corollary (6.13) and Theorem (8.5), on infinitesimal characters and lowest compact types[13]. In the large-gap range both statements are also consequences of the kernel realization, through the uniqueness of the model.

Denote the lowest compact type by V₀. Write Dab = dπ(Eab) for the complexified derivative in an elementary matrix direction. Define Vk+1 as the span of Vk and DabVk for opposite signs. Compact derivatives preserve each layer. Each layer is finite dimensional and decomposes orthogonally into compact types. The compact weight estimate proved in the chapter on discrete-series derivatives says that each highest weight μ in Vk satisfies ‖μ − Λ‖ ≤ √2k. Each noncompact step can add a root of length √2, so the bound grows with the number of steps.

Energy bound. If x ∈ Vk and 0 ≤ k ≤ S, then

∑a,b ‖Dabx‖² ≤ 64m(B + S)² ‖x‖².

Indeed, Dab∗ = Dba on equal-sign directions and equals −Dba on opposite-sign directions, as identities of pairings on smooth vectors. Write Ω for the full sum ∑a,bDabDba and ΩK for the same-sign part. Then twice the compact sum minus the full sum gives every squared norm a positive sign. On a compact type of highest weight μ, ΩK has eigenvalue ‖μ + ρc‖² − ‖ρc‖². Thus its quadratic form on the whole layer is at most (R² − ‖ρc‖²)‖x‖² for R = ‖Λ + ρc‖ + √2k. Compact Casimir and its extension from each compact type to its span.

The factors in 64 can now be checked. Strict order and the integer differences give m − 1 ≤ 2B, hence m ≤ 4B. Each coordinate of ρn and ρ has absolute value at most m/2. Consequently R ≤ √m(B + m/2) + √2k ≤ 3√m(B + S) and ‖ρ‖² ≤ 4m(B + S)². Substituting the two Casimir eigenvalue estimates and discarding the nonpositive terms gives 2R² + ‖ρ‖² ≤ 22m(B + S)². The stated constant 64 makes the one-step factor after taking square roots equal to 8√m(B + S).

From one derivative to every word in a projector minor

Derivative-word bound. Let v₀ be any vector in the lowest compact type, and let X₁,…,Xr be complex m-by-m matrices with Frobenius norms at most one. For every integer S ≥ r,

‖dπ(X₁) ··· dπ(Xr)v₀‖ ≤ [8√m(B + S)]r ‖v₀‖.

For one direction write dπ(X)x = ∑a,bXabDabx. The triangle inequality followed by Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its norm by ‖X‖F(∑‖Dabx‖²)1/2. This is at most 8√m(B + S)‖x‖ in each layer that is reached. Its value lies in the next layer. Reading the word from right to left gives one such factor per derivative. The empty word leaves the starting vector unchanged. This explains why the exponent is the actual word length r, even when a larger S serves many words.

In the cofactor estimate, set n = m − 1 and S = n. The lowest vector has norm one, each matrix unit has Frobenius norm one, and the branching gap of 1000m³ implies the 100m³ hypothesis above. A product from a minor of size n contains at most n derivatives. Each remaining scalar factor has size at most 4B. Summing over which factors act by differentiation gives (4B + 8√m(B + n))n per permutation. The n! permutations then give the bound used for a single projector entry. The splitting of the signed form and the positive quantity |cs|‖rs(elv₀)‖² come from the signed form identity.

As a check on the order of the operators, take the defining representation of the compact group U(4). Its lowest compact type is the entire defining space, with Λ = (1,0,0,0) and λ = Λ + ρ = (5/2,1/2,−1/2,−3/2). Acting on e₄, the word E₁₂E₂₃E₃₄ gives e₁. Reversing the word gives zero. Here ‖λ‖² − ‖ρ‖² = 9 − 5 = 4, which agrees with ∑‖Eabe₄‖² = 4. With S = 3 and B = 5/2, the estimate permits 88³ for the norm. This compact example tests the word and energy formulas. The indefinite branching pair imposes additional signature and interlacing hypotheses.

How does the chosen translate affect the period derivative?

The vector finally inserted into the period coefficient is v = π(g₀)v₀, where the branching construction chooses g₀. Here the argument uses real Lie derivatives. Write C = 8mB and let v₀ have norm one. For m ≥ 3 and opposite-sign separation at least 1000m³, the independent one-place estimate gives, for a word of length r ≤ m + 2 in real Lie directions Yi, an upper bound ∏i(C²‖Yi‖F) on the norm of its value on v₀.

Indeed the one-place estimate, with its weight budget set to b = √B, gives a cost βP = (√m)B + (3/2)m3/2 + 3P after P derivatives. Here m ≥ 3 implies B ≥ 1, and a word of the indicated length has at most m + 1 previous derivatives. The three terms are bounded respectively by (mB)², (3/2)(mB)² and 2(mB)². Their sum is at most C². Multiplying the bounds for the successive real directions proves the assertion.

Suppose Y is a direction of the smaller unitary group with ‖Y‖F ≤ 1. Its image Y′ in the larger Lie algebra acts as zero on the distinguished line and has the same Frobenius norm. Differentiating exp(tY′)g₀ = g₀ exp(t g₀−1Y′g₀) twice moves both derivatives back to v₀. Put R = ‖g₀‖F. Since g₀−1 = Jg₀∗J for the diagonal signature matrix J, it has the same Frobenius norm. Submultiplicativity gives ‖g₀−1Y′g₀‖F ≤ R². The period argument therefore uses

‖dπ(Y′)²π(g₀)v₀‖ ≤ (C²R²)².

For a check choose one positive and one negative coordinate and set the corresponding block of g₀ to ((5/4, 3/4), (3/4, 5/4)). It preserves diag(1,−1). Fix two further coordinates, one the distinguished positive line. Choose Y′ to be i times the diagonal projector onto the positive coordinate of the block. Its norm is one. Conjugation gives the block (i/16)((25,15),(−15,−9)), of Frobenius norm 17/8. The four-dimensional matrix gives R² = 25/4, so the bound covers this increase. In the period proof the second derivative controls a Taylor remainder for the coefficient. Decay in the subgroup variable then makes the resulting bound integrable.

Why do the columns of the differential minor have successive shifts?

The shifted tensor estimate needs an explicit entry of a projector. Its numerator is a determinant-like sum of differential operators. Since their order matters, begin with the exact convention. Let V be the common complex space on which the operators Eab act, for 0 ≤ a,b ≤ N. In the application V is the space of smooth vectors and the matrix size is m = N + 1. The complexified elementary generators satisfy the matrix-unit commutation laws

[Eab, Ecd] = δbcEad − δdaEcb.

Here [A,B] = AB − BA, and δ is the Kronecker delta. Set Tab(u) = Eab + δabu Id. For row and column lists a and b of length k, let Q(a,b∣u) be the sum over row permutations σ of their signs times the ordered product of the factors Taσ(h),bh(u − h), in the order h = 0,…,k − 1 from left to right. The rightmost operator acts first. The empty minor is the identity. Reindexing σ gives alternation in the rows.

To interchange two adjacent columns c,d, keep fixed every factor before and after these positions and pair the two assignments of their rows p,q. Write x and y for the two column parameters. The sum of the old alternating pair and the pair with its columns interchanged has the following middle factor

Tpc(x)Tqd(y) − Tqc(x)Tpd(y) + Tpd(x)Tqc(y) − Tqd(x)Tpc(y).

Expanding the factors shows exactly what the shift pays for. Put L = δpcEqd − δqdEpc − δqcEpd + δpdEqc. The purely scalar terms cancel. The mixed terms give (x − y)L. The terms with two generators give [Epc,Eqd] + [Epd,Eqc] = −L. Consecutive parameters satisfy x − y = 1, so the middle factor vanishes with the surrounding factors in their original order. Adjacent swaps generate all permutations. Thus the minor is alternating in its columns and a repeated column makes it zero. A. I. Molev, Yangians and their applications, §2.6, formulas (2.24)–(2.25) and the quantum minors[15].

Which side of the matrix does the comatrix multiply?

Let D(u) be the full minor on the ordered lists 0,…,N. Define a matrix C(u) of operators by putting in entry (i,j) the factor (−1)i+j times the minor obtained by deleting row j and column i, keeping the remaining lists in increasing order. Its size-N minor always starts with parameter u. Let E denote the matrix with entries Ejl acting on columns in Vm. Then the identity used in the projector is

C(u) ((u − N) Id + E) = diag(D(u),…,D(u)).

Fix an output row i and an input column l. Form the full minor with its column list equal to 0,…,N with i omitted, followed by l. Group the permutations according to the row j assigned to that last column. Moving row j to the last position takes N − j switches, and the last operator stays on the right. The contribution is (−1)N−j times the minor without row j and column i, multiplied on the right by Tjl(u − N). Multiplying the whole expansion by (−1)N−i gives precisely the (i,l) entry on the left above.

If l ≠ i, the chosen column list contains l twice, so its full minor vanishes. If l = i, moving the last column back to its original position takes N − i switches. That sign cancels the factor outside the sum, leaving D(u). This proves the claimed multiplication identity without commuting the cofactor past its last factor. A. I. Molev, Definition 2.26 and Proposition 2.27, equations (2.30)–(2.31)[16].

For a two-by-two check, the upper-right entry of the product is (u + E₁₁)E₀₁ − E₀₁(u − 1 + E₁₁) = [E₁₁,E₀₁] + E₀₁ = 0. Using u in both columns would leave −E₀₁. This is already nonzero for the defining representation.

How does evaluation select one shifted summand?

Now specialize the algebraic identity to the signed discrete series in the smooth tensor decomposition. Its infinitesimal character gives the scalar action D(u) = ∏j(u + tj) Id with tj = λj − N/2. This scalar action is the representation-theoretic input in this step. One can read off the shifts on a highest-weight vector of weight μ. In a nonidentity row permutation, take the rightmost column j whose row has moved. Its assigned row is less than j. The columns to its right have fixed rows and act diagonally on the vector. The raising operator in column j therefore kills that term. The identity permutation gives the scalar ∏j(u + μj − j). In the Harish-Chandra parameter λ = μ + ρ the jth coordinate of ρ is N/2 − j, which yields the displayed factors. The centrality of the coefficients and the infinitesimal character of the discrete series make this same scalar applicable on its smooth vectors. The tj have distinct values. A. I. Molev, Casimir elements for glN, formula (4.37) and Corollary 4.6.2, the Harish-Chandra image of the Capelli determinant[17].

On any nonzero eigenvector Y of E with eigenvalue κ, the left factor in the comatrix identity is multiplied by u − N + κ. Setting u = N − κ forces one of the factors on the right to vanish, so κ = N + ts for a unique s. On the corresponding eigenspace the identity becomes (u + ts)C(u)Y = ∏j(u + tj)Y. For u ≠ −ts cancellation gives C(u)Y = ∏j≠s(u + tj)Y. Both sides are vector-valued polynomials of degree at most N, since every cofactor contains exactly N affine factors. Their coefficients lie in a finite-dimensional span. In each coordinate these polynomials agree at infinitely many points, so they also agree at −ts.

Applied to a vector in a different shifted summand, this same product still contains u + ts and vanishes there. On the s-summand it is the nonzero scalar below. Decomposing a smooth tensor x into its summands thus gives

psx = C(−ts)x / ∏j≠s(tj − ts).

The differences are the nonzero integers λj − λs, so the reciprocal denominator has absolute value at most one. For an input supported in one coordinate the numerator is a single signed minor, the one estimated by the differential word bound. The construction uses a direct sum of eigenspaces on smooth tensors. A repeated root would invalidate this division.

A projector with a negative denominator. Take the defining two-dimensional representation, with the usual elementary matrices on basis e₀,e₁. Its full minor is (u + E₀₀)(u − 1 + E₁₁) − E₁₀E₀₁ = (u² − 1) Id. Thus (t₀,t₁) = (1,−1). On a column (v,w) the operator E gives (v₀ + w₁)(e₀,e₁), where the subscripts denote coordinates. Its eigenvalues are 2 and 0. The sum of the two diagonal elementary matrices equals Id, whence C(−1) = −E. Dividing by t₁ − t₀ = −2 gives the projector E/2. It sends (e₀,0) to (e₀,e₁)/2 and kills (e₀,−e₁).

How does a bound on one column locate a translate of bounded matrix norm?

Bounded translate. There exists g₀ ∈ G such that

‖g₀‖F ≤ X10m,   ‖Pπ(g₀)v₀‖ ≥ X−100m³.

Take Y₁ = 2X8m and S = {g : Y(g) ≤ Y₁}. The moment bound gives ∫G∖SF ≤ 1/(2dπ), so at least half the mass lies in S. Put U = {h ∈ H : ‖h − 1‖F ≤ 1}, and let C be the ambient ball ‖g‖F² ≤ 64m(m + Y₁)². The radius here is specified by the squared Frobenius norm.

For g ∈ S, choose a signed-unitary matrix b taking z to g−1z with ‖b‖F² ≤ 16(m + Y₁)². Such a matrix is obtained by rotations in the positive and negative subspaces and a two-dimensional signed-unitary block, as in the column decomposition. Then gb fixes z, so gb = ι(h₀) for some h₀ ∈ H. If h = h₀u with u ∈ U, then ι(h)−1g = ι(u)−1b−1 belongs to C. Indeed ‖ι(u)‖F² ≤ 4m, and inverse signed-unitary matrices have the same Frobenius norm. Each g ∈ S therefore contributes at least ν(U) to the integral of the indicator of C over these h. Multiply by F(g), integrate and change variables by left translation. Tonelli's theorem gives

ν(U) ∫S F dμ ≤ ∫C ∫H F(ι(h)k) dν(h) dμ(k).

Equivariance of i and Schur orthogonality on H make the inner integral exactly ‖Pπ(k)v₀‖²/dσ. Two quantitative comparisons fix the scale. Integrating the decaying subgroup coefficient of w₀ gives 1/dσ ≤ Dν(U), with D = X67m². Covering the ambient ball by translates of the identity neighbourhood of radius (100m(B + 1))−2 gives dπμ(C) ≤ K, with K = 4X24m³. The formal degree times the measure of that small neighbourhood is at most 4. T. Tao, An Epsilon of Room, I, Theorem 1.1.23 (Tonelli)[18].

If ‖Pπ(k)v₀‖² were smaller than 1/(4DK) throughout C, multiplying the displayed double integral by dπ would give at most ν(U)/4 on the right and at least ν(U)/2 on the left. Since 0 < ν(U) < ∞, one g₀ in C has projected squared norm at least 1/(4DK). The parameter gap implies X ≥ 16. The numerical inequalities 64m(m + 2X8m)² ≤ X20m and 4DK = 16X67m²+24m³ ≤ X200m³ give the asserted bounds after taking square roots. For the first inequality use m + 2X8m ≤ 3X8m and 576m ≤ X4m. In particular ℬ(100)‖Pπ(g₀)v₀‖ ≥ 1 for ℬ(100) = X100m⁴, the common scale of the period estimates.

For m = 4 the moment calculation costs 27 powers of X and allows 32. The coefficient before the squared projection is 16X2608, since 67·16 + 24·64 = 2608. The bound 16 ≤ X then gives 4DK ≤ X2609, within the allowed X12800.

Why does the projected vector yield a positive diagonal period?

Set v = π(g₀)v₀, p = Pv ≠ 0 and ρ = π restricted to H. Inner products are linear in their second argument. The preceding absolute-integral estimate at the identity makes h ↦ ⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩ integrable. On the smaller Hilbert space define the coefficient operator

⟨a,Tb⟩ = ∫H conj(⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩) ⟨a,σ(h)b⟩ dν(h).

Inversion of Haar measure on this unimodular group gives T = T∗. The coefficient of v is bounded and integrable, hence square-integrable. In an orthonormal basis of the smaller space, Schur orthogonality makes the matrix coefficients of σ an orthonormal family of functions after multiplication by √dσ. For every finite part of this family, subtract the orthogonal projection of the coefficient onto its span. The squared norm of the remainder is nonnegative. This gives Bessel’s inequality and bounds the sum of squares of all entries of T by the squared L² norm of the coefficient divided by dσ. Keeping finitely many of these entries gives a finite-rank operator. By Cauchy–Schwarz the squared operator norm of the discarded part is at most the sum of its squared entries, which tends to zero. Thus T is compact.

The lower estimate is Re⟨a,Ta⟩ ≥ |⟨p,a⟩|²/dσ. One way to see why the projection appears is to average ρ against the conjugate coefficient of w₀, multiplied by dσ. This is an orthogonal projection by Schur convolution, and fixes iw₀. Its quadratic form therefore dominates |⟨·,iw₀⟩|². For a in the span of translates of w₀, a change of variables in the two coefficient integrals transfers this inequality to T. That span is dense by irreducibility, so continuity gives the lower estimate for every a.

In an eigenbasis of the compact self-adjoint T, the quadratic form at p is the sum of the eigenvalues weighted by the squared coordinates of p. If all eigenvalues were smaller than ‖p‖²/(2dσ), this sum would be at most ‖p‖⁴/(2dσ). The preceding lower estimate gives at least ‖p‖⁴/dσ. Thus there is a unit eigenvector w with eigenvalue c₁ ≥ ‖p‖²/(2dσ) > 0. Inserting b = w into the defining integral gives c₁⟨a,w⟩, the diagonal term of the period. MIT 18.102, Lecture 22, Theorem 232 (compact self-adjoint spectral theorem)[19].

The construction also gives a smooth w. The form ∫⟨y,ρ(h)v⟩⟨σ(h)w,a⟩ dν represents ⟨Ay,a⟩ for a bounded operator from the larger space to the smaller one. Its norm bound is ‖w‖(∫|⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩| dν/dσ)1/2 by the coefficient Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Schur orthogonality. Left invariance makes A equivariant. At y = v the eigenvector identity, conjugated, says Av = c₁w. Dividing the intertwiner by c₁ maps the smooth vector v to w, which is therefore smooth.

Check on a circle. To test this last operator identity, take normalized Haar measure on the unit circle, σ trivial, ρ(t) = diag(1,t) and v = (3/5,4/5). Embed σ as the first coordinate. Then Pv = 3/5 and dσ = 1. The coefficient of v is 9/25 + (16/25)t. Its conjugate integrates to 9/25, so the eigenvalue is 9/25 and the guaranteed lower bound is 9/50. This example checks the normalization of the diagonal integral independently of the large-gap estimates.

Which signed parameters give a copy of the smaller representation?

Let G = U(p,q), let z be a positive unit coordinate, and let H = U(p − 1,q) fix z. Write m = p + q = n + 1. At each position of the Harish-Chandra parameters λ of G and μ of H, record its sign in the Hermitian space and its group of origin. Merge the two decreasing lists in numerical order. The signed interlacing rule requires neighbouring entries from different groups to have the same sign, and neighbouring entries from the same group to have opposite signs.

Occurrence theorem used here. Suppose 1 ≤ q ≤ p, n ≥ 2, and each parameter is strictly decreasing in its Harish-Chandra lattice (in rank r, each entry belongs to ℤ + (r − 1)/2). Within each group require an absolute gap of at least 200m³ between entries of opposite sign. If the merged list obeys the signed rule, every pair of unitary discrete-series models π and σ with these signed parameters admits a nonzero bounded map j from the space of σ into the space of π with jσ(h) = π(h)j on H. He’s branching theorem gives the occurrence criterion for discrete series. The argument below follows the descent used for this separated range. Hongyu He, Definition 1 and Theorem 0.1[20].

Where the descent starts. Denote an entry of the merged target list by ax, and set dx = 2ax + K, choosing an integer K large enough to make all directions positive. These are distinct integers in the same order as the target. The signed frame theorem realizes the two lists of directions as an ambient diagonal operator and its compression to the smaller space after conjugation. The distant-parameter occurrence estimate then supplies an actual smaller parameter μ′ occurring under λ + t dG, with |μ′j − t dH,j| ≤ C√t for sufficiently large admissible t. Take t to be a large integer square. The displacements on the two sides are bG,i = t dG,i and bH,j = μ′j − μj. They are integers by the parameter lattices. The error from t dx is bounded by C√t + max |ax|. Consecutive predictions differ by at least t and the smallest prediction is at least t. Taking t large makes every displacement nonnegative, with bx ≤ by whenever ax < ay. Thus the offsets decrease weakly as we read the displayed lists from largest to smallest. The chosen starting pair therefore has an occurrence.

How to choose a step. The current entries are ay + by. Among the positions with bx > 0, choose the one with the smallest target entry. Lower its displacement by one. Every smaller position now has displacement zero, and every larger one has displacement at least the old bx. This proves monotonicity after the change. At either stage regularity and both gap bounds follow because monotone displacements can only enlarge a difference of target entries.

In particular, an entry from the other group cannot be the midpoint of this step. A smaller target entry has zero displacement and lies strictly below ax, the lowest possible endpoint. A larger one is already strictly above the starting value. The two ranks have opposite integral and half-integral lattices, so there are no equal target entries between groups. A step on the λ side therefore satisfies

λscurrent − ½ ≠ μjcurrent for every j.

The one-step argument below transports the occurrence across this lowering. A μ-step uses derivatives transverse to the smaller group. It assumes an occurrence before the step, admissible parameters on both sides of the step, and μj − ½ distinct from every current λs. It translates σ, proves that a projected smooth vector in the smaller tensor is nonzero by applying words in the infinitesimal operators, and uses Schur orthogonality to exclude absence of the shifted σ. At the starting pair the trial vector supplies the estimate that locates a constituent. At each smaller-group move the transverse derivative identity transfers it. Each step reduces ∑xbx by exactly one. When it reaches zero the occurrence is at the prescribed parameters.

Why is there still a nonzero coefficient after lowering λ?

Write λ, μ for the current parameters. Assume they satisfy the rank, signature, regularity and gap hypotheses above, that λ − es still satisfies them, that the midpoint condition holds, and that σ already occurs in π restricted to H. The tensor translation theorem supplies a shifted ambient model πs of parameter λ − es, its smooth tensor projection ps, its coordinate map rs into that model, and its signed-form scalar cs. We must show that σ occurs in πs restricted to H.

Use the normalized test at an existing occurrence. Fix Haar measure ν on H, let κ be the reciprocal formal degree of σ for ν, and choose a unit vector w in its lowest compact type. Set φ(h) = ⟨w,σ(h)w⟩∗, where the star means complex conjugation. The coefficient is integrable under the stated smaller-group gap. We use the following coefficient projection for the known occurrence. There is an isometric H-intertwiner i and a smooth ambient vector η with ⟨η,iw⟩ ≠ 0 such that, for every ambient vector y,

∫H φ(h) ⟨η,π(h)y⟩ dν = κ ⟨η,iw⟩ ⟨iw,y⟩.

Let P = i* and put η into the single positive tensor coordinate z. Write y₀ = (ps(ezη))z and b = rs(ezη). The cofactor identity selects ps. In its z,z entry the deleted coordinate leaves precisely the infinitesimal operators of H. The adjoint P intertwines those operators on the smooth vectors. With the smaller rank one less than the larger, their scalar shifts differ by ½. The specialized identity gives

DsPy₀ = ΓsPη,   Ds = ∏k≠s(λk − λs),   Γs = ∏j(μj − λs + ½).

Regularity gives Ds ≠ 0. The noncrossing condition makes each factor of Γs nonzero. Pair with w and use the adjoint relation. Since ⟨iw,η⟩ ≠ 0, this gives ⟨iw,y₀⟩ ≠ 0. For h ∈ H, the group fixes the positive coordinate z. Evaluating the signed tensor form with first vector ezη therefore gives cs⟨b,πs(h)b⟩ = ⟨η,π(h)y₀⟩. Multiply by φ and integrate.

cs ∫H φ(h) ⟨b,πs(h)b⟩ dν = κ ⟨η,iw⟩ ⟨iw,y₀⟩ ≠ 0.

Consequently the integral itself is nonzero. Absolute convergence follows from φ ∈ L¹ and |⟨b,πs(h)b⟩| ≤ ‖b‖². The coefficient criterion below gives a bounded H-intertwiner into πs. Unitary equivalence of models with a fixed signed discrete-series parameter transports it to every pair of realizations. This proves the λ-step.

A signed example. For G = U(3,1) and H = U(2,1), take T = 64,000 and target lists λ = (6T + ½, 4T + ½, 3T + ½, ½) of signs (+,+,−,+), and μ = (5T, 2T, T) of signs (+,−,+). The merged sequence is G+, H+, G+, G−, H−, H+, G+. Both lists have opposite-sign gaps at least T. To check a single step, give all seven entries displacement one. The selected position is the last λ, currently 3/2. Its midpoint is 1, below all three current μ entries. Here Ds = 72T³ and Γs = 10T³. The compression multiplies Pη by exactly 5/36, and the step lowers the displacement sum from seven to six.

To see why the order of the moves matters, change the last target μ in this example from T to 1. The signs, the merged order and the stated gap bound all survive. With the seven displacements again equal to one, the last λ and μ now stand at 3/2 and 2. Moving μ first would put its midpoint 3/2 exactly on λ. The prescribed move lowers λ to ½. The step from μ = 2 to 1 can now pass through 3/2 with all ambient entries clear of its midpoint.

How does a single nonzero integral produce a bounded intertwiner?

Let ρ be the restriction of the shifted representation to H. Use the Hilbert inner product linear in its second argument. For any ambient vectors a,b, write I(a,b) = ∫ φ(h)⟨b,ρ(h)a⟩ dν. Keep the irreducible square-integrable σ, its nonzero unit vector w, its integrable coefficient φ, and its Schur constant κ > 0. We construct a bounded intertwiner J with ⟨b,Jw⟩ = I(a,b).

Take the subspace of vectors y for which h ↦ ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ is integrable. This subspace contains w, and left invariance of ν makes it stable under σ. Its closure is the whole representation by irreducibility. On this dense subspace define

Jy = ∫H ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ ρ(h)a dν(h).

The vector integral converges since ρ is unitary. To bound its norm, expand ‖Jy‖² as a double integral and write the second group variable as ht. For each fixed h, left invariance of Haar measure leaves dν(t) unchanged. The two σ coefficients become the conjugate of ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ and the coefficient ⟨σ(ht)w,y⟩. Their product is absolutely integrable in the original two variables and the remaining coefficient of ρ has modulus at most ‖a‖². Fubini and Schur orthogonality for σ now integrate out h, giving ‖Jy‖² = ‖y‖² κ I(a,a). This bounds J on its dense domain. Left translation in the vector integral gives Jσ(g) = ρ(g)J, and both sides extend continuously. At y = w its coefficient against b is exactly I(a,b). A single nonzero value therefore forces a nonzero bounded intertwiner. Applied to the preceding step, the two test vectors both equal the shifted vector b. Duflo and Moore, orthogonality of square-integrable representations, pp. 209–243[12].

How can a distant ambient representation predict a smaller weight?

The descent in the signed parameters needs a starting pair at which the smaller group actually occurs. Write G = U(p,q), H = U(p−1,q) and n = p+q−1. The subgroup fixes a positive unit vector. Choose distinct signed directions d in the big space and d′ in the small one, with the signed interlacing rule. The compression calculation below supplies a fixed g ∈ G for which the small diagonal matrix with entries d′ is the upper block of g diag(d) g⁻¹ in the subgroup coordinates.

Fix a scale t ≥ 1 at which λ + td is a regular Harish-Chandra parameter with opposite signs separated by at least 200(n+1)³. Let π be a discrete series with that parameter. Write Dab for the derived action of the matrix unit in the smaller block. For a smooth vector x define its error in following the small diagonal by

Qt(x) = ∑a,b ‖Dabx − δabtd′ax‖².

Take a unit highest-weight vector v in the lowest compact type of π. Its diagonal weights are L + td, where L = λ + ρnoncompact − ρcompact and each ρ is the half-sum of the indicated positive roots. We claim that η = π(g)v has Qt(η) ≤ C₀t for one constant independent of the scale and the chosen model. For a compact root the raising operator kills v, and commuting it with the opposite lowering operator bounds the latter’s squared norm by the absolute difference of the two weights. For noncompact roots the sum of the squared norms is the difference of the compact and full Casimir scalars. This follows by summing the signed adjoint identity for each pair of opposite matrix units. The two quadratic scalars have the same leading term t²∑ di², so their difference is affine in t. Thus every off-diagonal derivative of v has norm at most √(P+Rt) for fixed nonnegative P,R. Lowest compact type.

Conjugate the small matrix unit by g⁻¹ and call the resulting big matrix Y. Its diagonal contribution to the derivative on v is ∑ Yii(Li + tdi). The compression identity gives ∑ Yiidi = δabd′a by taking a trace. The entire order-t term is exactly the prescribed center in the displayed error. What remains has norm at most (∑ |Yij|)√(P+Rt) + ∑ |YiiLi|. Squaring, using (a+b)² ≤ 2a²+2b², and summing the n² terms proves the claim.

How can a compact-finite trial vector retain the same error?

The preceding translate is smooth. The next step needs a vector that lies in a finite-dimensional space under the maximal compact subgroup of H. We can approximate η in a finite sum F of smooth compact types of G. The density used here follows by projecting a smooth vector onto its compact types by character integration and applying the Peter–Weyl theorem. Each projection is smooth by differentiation under the compact integral. P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups, lecture 4, Corollary 4.7[21]. Let x be the orthogonal projection of η onto F and w = η − x. The subspace F is stable under the compact Casimir ΩK. If c is the scalar of the full ambient Casimir, the signed adjoint identity from the preceding argument gives

∑i,j ‖DGijw‖² = Re ⟨(2ΩK − c)η, w⟩ ≤ A‖w‖,   A = ‖(2ΩK − c)η‖.

Indeed twice the sum over compact pairs minus the signed sum over all pairs is the unsigned sum. Replacing w by η inside the first slot adds a vector of F, orthogonal to w. The superscript G includes all ambient matrix units. The corresponding sum over the smaller block is bounded by this full sum. Put B = ∑a|td′a|². For this particular scale choose F large enough that ‖w‖ is less than min(1/2, t/(4A+1), t/(4B+1)). Then the derivative sum for w and the scalar error B‖w‖² are each at most t/4. Applying the elementary square bound twice to x = η − w gives Qt(x) ≤ 2C₀t + 4(t/4) + 4(t/4). Since ‖x‖ ≥ 1/2, we obtain

x ≠ 0,   Qt(x)/‖x‖² ≤ Ct,   C = 8C₀ + 8.

Restriction to H leaves the vector and its norm unchanged and identifies the derivatives in the small block. Since its compact subgroup lies in the big compact subgroup, x is compact-finite on restriction. The approximating subspace can depend on t and π. The constant in the quotient is common to all of them.

Why does the trial vector give an actual discrete constituent?

Distant occurrence. Suppose the entries of d′ are decreasing with gaps at least one. For all sufficiently large t with λ + td admissible as above, each ambient discrete series π at that parameter contains, on restriction, a discrete series with some smaller parameter μ′ satisfying the following estimate. The constants are uniform in π. If another realization of that same smaller discrete series is chosen, it too admits a nonzero bounded intertwiner into π.

|μ′a − td′a| ≤ (√(2C) + J + n)√t,   J = ⌈C⌉ + 1.

Set ξ = td′, S = Ct and s = √(2S). The proof follows one vector through three steps. First, select a nonzero compact component whose error is at most the trial bound. Its weight ν records how the diagonal torus acts, and its compact Casimir scalar κ measures the sum of its compact derivative squares. The invariant cutoff gives the lower bound κ − 2S for the full Casimir on every unit vector in a space stable under differentiation. A vector with the original compact data survives in that space.

Next, raise the compact weight to a highest weight L at distance at most s from ξ. Now lower across opposite signs when the first derivative layer supplies the required next highest vector. Each lowering moves a coordinate by at most one and costs at least 2(t−2(s+J))−2n−2 in compact Casimir. For J = ⌈C⌉ + 1 the cost of J moves would exceed 2S for sufficiently large t. The Casimir lower bound forces a stopping type.

Finally, convert its compact weight to the parameter μ′ by the half-root shift. This costs at most n per coordinate. The three errors add to √(2Ct)+J+n, which gives the displayed estimate for t ≥ 1. At large enough separation a discrete series of this parameter exists. The isometry on translates of the terminal type puts a copy inside the restriction. The integer descent can then start at a large square scale and return to the requested pair. Hongyu He, Theorem 0.1 on signed branching[20].

Constructing a compression with the prescribed signs

Let D = diag(di) in a basis of squared lengths εi = ±1. Seek a positive unit normal z so that the compression of D to z⊥ has the specified eigenvalues d′a and signs ε′a. In the merged decreasing list all values are distinct. Multiply each sign coming from the smaller group by −1. The signed interlacing rule says these modified signs alternate. There are n+1 positive modified signs and n negative ones, so the first sign is positive.

Form the two monic polynomials P(X) = ∏i(X−di) and R(X) = ∏a(X−d′a). Canceling each pole gives the partial fractions below. After multiplication by P, both sides agree at all n+1 roots of P and have degree at most n, proving equality. Leading coefficients give ∑ ci = 1.

R(X)/P(X) = ∑i ci/(X−di),   ci = R(di)/P′(di).

The sign of ci is (−1) to the number of entries above di, by counting negative factors. Thus it equals εi. Take zi = √|ci|. Its signed squared norm is ∑ ci = 1. For each small root u = d′a put v(u) = (uI−D)⁻¹z. Its pairing with z is R(u)/P(u) = 0. Since Dv(u) = uv(u) − z, its projection onto z⊥ is uv(u). Distinct roots give orthogonal vectors by self-adjointness of the compression. Their signed squared norms are ∑ ci/(u−di)² = −R′(u)/P(u). Counting signs of factors again gives ε′a, including the minus sign for the small group. Normalize these n vectors and append z at the distinguished positive coordinate. The inverse of this isometric basis change is the g required in the moment calculation.

For U(2,1) take the big directions (5,4,3) with signs (+,−,+), and the small directions (2,1) with signs (+,−). The residues of (X−2)(X−1)/((X−5)(X−4)(X−3)) are 6, −6 and 1. The normal (√6,√6,1) has signed squared norm 1. The two vectors from the resolvent have signed squared norms 1/6 and −1/24. Thus both the eigenvalues and the signature of the compressed block can be read directly from this one rational function. For these directions take λ = (2,1,0). At every sufficiently large integer t, the ambient parameter λ + t(5,4,3) has minimum opposite-sign gap t + 1. The occurrence estimate then gives a constituent within C√t of (2t,t) in each coordinate.

Which compact component inherits the trial bound?

The trial estimate bounds the sum of the squared errors in all matrix directions at once. The first task is to find a vector with one definite weight to which the estimate still applies. Write μ = td′, S = Ct, and let Dab act in the smooth restricted representation. The full Casimir Ω sums DabDba over the smaller group. Its compact counterpart ΩK sums only over pairs with the same sign. On a finite-dimensional compact-stable space containing the trial vector x, ΩK and all diagonal derivatives are commuting Hermitian operators. A diagonal commutator assigns the opposite weights to Dab and Dba, so their product has weight zero.

Decompose x into joint eigenvectors, grouping components with identical eigenvalues. To see why their energies add, expand the sum of derivative squares as a quadratic form. Its operator on smooth vectors is 2ΩK − Ω − 2∑a μaDaa + ‖μ‖²I. The signed adjoint of each matrix unit gives the first two terms. Ω commutes with every derived matrix unit, by cancellation in the commutator with the sum defining Ω. Thus this energy operator preserves all joint eigenvalues. Different joint eigenspaces are orthogonal, so their cross terms vanish even when the energy operator takes a vector outside the finite space. Simultaneous diagonalization here follows by diagonalizing one Hermitian operator and repeating on its invariant eigenspaces for the others.

Consequently the quotient for x is a weighted average of the component quotients, with weights proportional to the squared norms. Choose a nonzero component y with quotient at most S. Write ν for its diagonal weight and κ for its compact Casimir eigenvalue. The three contributions to its quotient are

Qμ(y)/‖y‖² = ‖ν−μ‖² + (κ−‖ν‖²) + Re ⟨(κI−Ω)y, y⟩/‖y‖².

The first term is the diagonal error. The second sums squared compact off-diagonal derivatives divided by ‖y‖². The third does the same for the opposite-sign derivatives. Each is nonnegative and at most S. The last inequality gives control on this one vector. Following a sequence of derivatives will require a bound throughout an invariant subspace.

A compact calculation. In the defining action of U(2) on ℂ² take μ = (1,0). Here Ω = ΩK = 2I, because ∑a,b EabEba = 2I. Both coordinate vectors have compact off-diagonal energy 1 and noncompact energy 0. Their diagonal errors are respectively 0 and 2, giving total quotients 1 and 3. The trial vector e₁+e₂ has quotient 2. Taking its first joint component improves the bound while fixing the weight.

A bounded inverse on the Hilbert space

Fix κ from the selected component and put U = κI − Ω. Work on the dense space of smooth vectors in the Hilbert space of the restricted representation. Write R = 2S > 0. In finite dimensions the function 1/(1+(u/R)²) is large near u = 0 and small far away. To use the same idea for the possibly unbounded derivative U, first construct a bounded operator T from

B = I + U²/R²,   Re ⟨Bz, z⟩ = ‖z‖² + ‖Uz‖²/R².

The identity follows from symmetry of Ω on smooth vectors. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖Bz‖ ≥ ‖z‖, so the assignment Bz ↦ z is a well-defined contraction. Why is the range of B dense? Let M be the closure of the range of B and Q its orthogonal projection. A group translation conjugates the two matrix units in each Casimir term. The tensor ∑ Eab ⊗ Eba is invariant under simultaneous conjugation because these bases are dual for the invariant trace pairing tr(XY). Thus translations preserve the range, and their inverses do too. Unitarity gives invariance of M and its perpendicular, so Q commutes with the group. R. Melrose, Functional Analysis, §9 on closed subspaces[22].

Any bounded operator commuting with the group takes smooth orbit maps to smooth orbit maps. Differentiation shows that it commutes with each derivative, hence with B on smooth vectors. For such z this gives BQz = QBz = Bz. Injectivity of B forces Qz = z. By density, M is the whole Hilbert space. Extend the contraction Bz ↦ z by taking limits of Cauchy sequences. The resulting operator T is self-adjoint because ⟨z, Bw⟩ = ⟨Bz, w⟩, and it commutes with the group by the same dense-range argument. On smooth vectors we therefore have both TBz = z and BTz = z.

A Casimir bound on every smooth vector of the cut

In the finite-dimensional picture a derivative eigenvalue u with |u| ≤ R gives an inverse eigenvalue at least 1/2. Use this threshold on the bounded self-adjoint operator T. Let A = T − ½I, and form its positive and negative parts P = max(A,0), N = max(−A,0). The continuous functional calculus assigns operators to these scalar functions by uniform polynomial approximation on the spectrum. It respects multiplication, takes the square of a real function to the square of a self-adjoint operator, and preserves commutation with group translations. Applying these facts to the two functions and to their square roots gives A = P − N, NP = 0, and both parts positive. R. Melrose, Functional Analysis, Theorem 3.5 and Remark 3.1[23].

Let W consist of the smooth vectors killed by N. It is stable under every derivative because N commutes with the group. For z in W, also Bz belongs to W. On that vector A equals its positive part. The identity TBz = z gives ½‖Bz‖² ≤ Re ⟨z, Bz⟩ ≤ ‖z‖ ‖Bz‖. Thus ‖Bz‖ ≤ 2‖z‖. Substitution in the preceding square identity yields

‖Uz‖ ≤ R‖z‖,   Re ⟨Ωz, z⟩ ≥ (κ−2S)‖z‖²   (z ∈ W).

This lower bound will apply at every step when roots move the starting weight. The existence of a starting vector in W still requires the estimate on y.

Why a vector of the original weight survives

Restrict the calculation to the smooth eigenspace ΩK = κ. There U is nonnegative as a quadratic form because its expectation is the sum of the squared opposite-sign derivatives. Both U and T preserve this eigenspace. Put V = U/R and x = Ty, so that y = (I+V²)x. The scalar inequality 1−1/(1+v²) ≤ v/2 for v ≥ 0 follows after clearing the denominator from v(1−v)² ≥ 0. On smooth vectors there is a direct version with no choice of eigenbasis. Put w = (I−V)x. Expansion using symmetry of V gives

Re ⟨Vy, y⟩ − 2 Re ⟨y−x, y⟩ = Re ⟨Vw, w⟩ + Re ⟨V(Vw), Vw⟩ ≥ 0.

Because Re ⟨Uy, y⟩ ≤ S‖y‖² and R = 2S, we get Re ⟨Ty, y⟩ ≥ ¾‖y‖². Hence Re ⟨Ay, y⟩ is strictly positive. If Py vanished, this expectation would equal −⟨Ny, y⟩ ≤ 0. Thus Py is nonzero, and NP = 0 places it in W. Applying P to the finite compact-stable space of y gives another finite compact-stable space. Commutation with derivatives shows that Py has weight ν and compact Casimir κ. These facts supply the starting vector for compact raising.

The constant ¾ is attained when U/R = diag(0,1) and y = (1,1). The two inverse eigenvalues are 1 and ½, so their mean is ¾. The middle coordinate in the example below has U/R = 1. It is retained by the kernel condition, while the coefficient of this coordinate in Py is zero. The distinction matters because the theorem uses the entire stable space for subsequent derivatives and a single nonzero vector to start them.

A compact highest vector within square-root distance

Take the surviving vector of weight ν in the cutoff W. A compact raising move applies a derivative Dab with a < b of the same sign, provided the resulting vector is nonzero. Its new weight is ω + ea − eb when the old one is ω. This follows by commuting the derivative with each diagonal unit. If F is the finite compact span of y, the starting vector Py lies in P(F). Every subsequent compact derivative stays in that finite-dimensional compact-stable space, which is contained in W because NP = 0. They preserve the compact Casimir eigenvalue κ because ΩK commutes with compact derivatives.

At any visited weight ω, the diagonal derivative squares are part of the sum defining κ on that vector, so ‖ω‖² ≤ κ. Meanwhile ∑c cωc decreases by b−a ≥ 1 at each move. It has a lower bound on the ball ‖ω‖ ≤ √κ. The chain must end at a nonzero vector annihilated by every compact raising operator. Call its highest weight L. Each move increases the pairing with the decreasing target μ by μa − μb ≥ 0. Expanding the square now controls how far the final weight can be from μ.

‖L−μ‖² = ‖ν−μ‖² + ‖L‖² − ‖ν‖² − 2⟨L−ν, μ⟩ ≤ S + (κ−‖ν‖²) ≤ 2S.

The two terms bounded by S are precisely the diagonal and compact off-diagonal errors already available before the cutoff. Their sum was itself bounded by S in the original energy decomposition. The separate estimates suffice for the radius √(2S) used in the descent. We have found a compact highest vector at coordinate distance at most s = √(2S) from the target. Its compact Casimir scalar is cK(L) = ‖L+ρK‖² − ‖ρK‖² = κ, where ρK is the half-sum of the positive compact roots. Indeed, in the Casimir sum the diagonal terms contribute ‖L‖², and each positive compact root contributes La−Lb by commuting the raising operator to the right.

Why opposite-sign lowering must stop

A compact highest vector lies in a finite sum of irreducible compact types. Within its finite compact span, the orthogonal complement of any stable subspace is stable by the compact adjoint relations. Splitting repeatedly gives irreducible summands. Projecting the highest vector onto one where it is nonzero preserves its weight and all its raising equations. Start with this type inside the invariant cutoff W. For a type of highest weight M, its first layer is spanned by the type and the vectors obtained by applying one noncompact derivative. Commuting a compact derivative past a noncompact derivative shows this layer is compact-stable and finite-dimensional.

If the layer contains a nonzero compact highest vector of weight M − ea + eb for a < b of opposite signs, select its irreducible summand and continue. All these spaces lie in W. Each coordinate changes by at most one on each move. Assume μa − μb ≥ τ for all a < b. For up to J moves every coordinate is within s+J of μ, so Ma−Mb ≥ τ−2(s+J). On subtracting the root α = ea − eb, expand the compact scalar to obtain

cK(M) − cK(M−α) = 2⟨M+ρK, α⟩−2 ≥ 2(τ−2(s+J))−2n−2.

Here ‖α‖² = 2 and each coordinate of ρK has absolute value at most n/2 by counting compact roots. Write h for the lower bound in the display. The full Casimir expectation on every unit highest vector in W is at least κ−2S, and its compact Casimir is at least this expectation by the noncompact square identity. After J moves the compact scalar would be at most κ−Jh. If Jh > 2S this is impossible. A terminal type therefore occurs in fewer than J moves, with highest weight L′ within s+J of μ in each coordinate. For example, with n = 2, τ = 1000 and S = 2 one can take J = 1. A single lowering would decrease the compact scalar by at least 1982 while the cutoff permits at most 4. Under those hypotheses the first compact type already has the terminal property.

To recover the parameter, each coordinate of L′ is an integer. Indeed the corresponding diagonal circle acts on that weight by exp(iθL′a), which is periodic with period 2π. Put μ′ = L′ + ρK − ρnoncompact. Each half-sum has coordinates bounded by n/2, and their difference has the required parity. In coordinate a, subtracting (n−1)/2 from the difference yields minus the number of earlier coordinates of the same sign minus the number of later coordinates of the opposite sign. In particular each μ′a belongs to ℤ+(n−1)/2. The separation assumption ensures strict decreasing order and enough gap for the representation theorem.

μ′a−μ′b ≥ τ−2(s+J)−2n   (a < b),   |μ′a−μa| ≤ s+J+n.

In the distant-parameter argument τ ≥ n³ + 4n + 2 + 2(s+J). The gap in the display exceeds n³ + 2n + 1. The identification of the terminal type uses precisely the absence of these highest vectors in the first layer. Its conclusion embeds every discrete-series model at μ′. To obtain an actual constituent one also needs such a model to exist. The large-gap existence step supplies such a model once the scale is sufficiently large. A. Knapp and P. Trapa, Representations of Semisimple Lie Groups, Lecture 7, Harish-Chandra’s discrete-series theorem[24].

Which Casimir eigenvalue does the stopping type carry?

The descent inside the spectral subspace has found a finite-dimensional compact type V among the smooth vectors of the restricted representation τ. Its stopping weight L′ and the parameter μ′ constructed from it will be written L and μ throughout this identification. Write H = U(r,s), n = r+s and K = U(r) × U(s). Order the coordinates by decreasing parameter. The first derivative layer is the span of V and all EabV for coordinates of opposite signs. The stopping condition says that this layer contains no nonzero compact highest vector of weight L−(ea−eb) for any such pair a < b.

Write ρc and ρn for the half-sums of compact and noncompact positive roots, and ρ = ρc+ρn for the full half-sum. The candidate parameter is μ = L−ρn+ρc. Casimir of the stopping type. If μ is strictly decreasing and the stopping condition holds, every v ∈ V satisfies

Ωv = (‖μ‖² − ‖ρ‖²)v.

To see how the absence of a lower weight determines a scalar, introduce an exterior algebra S with a generator for each pair consisting of a positive coordinate and a negative coordinate. Exterior multiplication adds a generator and contraction removes it. The spinor highest-weight lemma for this exterior tensor supplies a nonzero tensor x ∈ V ⊗ S of compact highest weight β = μ−ρc+θ for the diagonal compact action. Here θ has value s/2 on positive coordinates and −r/2 on negative ones. The two halves of the Dirac operator pair one noncompact derivative with exterior multiplication or contraction. Both preserve the diagonal compact highest-weight equations. On the representation factor they change the sum of the positive-coordinate weights by −1 and +1 respectively.

The first-layer weight lemma used at this point is as follows. At diagonal highest weight β, a nonzero tensor in the first layer with changed positive-coordinate sum would supply a compact highest vector of weight L−(ea−eb) for opposite signs and a < b. Indeed, expand the tensor in the exterior basis and choose a nonzero coefficient whose exterior weight has least dot product with μ. The compact raising equations force this coefficient to be highest because an additional term would come from a strictly smaller dot product. The first layer allows the original weight or a change by one noncompact root. The changed positive-coordinate sum excludes the original weight. An upward change by ea−eb with a < b would put the exterior weight at θ−ρn−(ea−eb). Its dot product with μ would be smaller than the minimum ⟨θ−ρn,μ⟩. To find that minimum, sum the negative values μi−μa over positive coordinates i and negative coordinates a. These are precisely the exterior generators to include in a subset with least dot product. The surviving possibility is exactly the forbidden lowering. Applying this lemma to each half gives Dx = 0.

In this exterior model the Dirac square acts on the tensor of highest weight β by 2D²x = −(Ω ⊗ 1)x + (‖β+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖²−2⟨θ,β⟩)x. This is the compact Casimir minus the full Casimir with the displayed correction for the exterior action. Each sign block of ρc sums to zero, so ⟨θ,ρc⟩ = 0. Ordering the positive coordinates first and the negative coordinates next gives the vector ρc+θ as a permutation of ρ, so ‖ρ‖² = ‖ρc‖²+‖θ‖². Substitution gives (Ω ⊗ 1)x = (‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖²)x. At least one exterior coordinate of x is nonzero, so at least one vector of V has this eigenvalue. Its eigenspace inside V is compact-stable because Ω commutes with every compact derivative. Irreducibility of V makes that eigenspace all of V. The factor 2 and the term involving θ come from the exterior-action convention in this calculation. For the twisted Dirac square and its specialization after the weight shift, see R. Parthasarathy, Proposition 3.1[25] and Proposition 3.2[26].

For U(1,1), take signs (+,−) and μ = (41/2,−39/2). Here ρc = 0 and θ = ρn = ρ = (1/2,−1/2), so L = β = (21,−20). The compact scalar in the tensor is 21²+20² = 841. The linear correction is 2⟨θ,β⟩ = 41. The resulting 800 agrees with (41²+39²−2)/4. This checks the scalar at a stopping type of these weights. The root descent supplies the stopping condition in the occurrence proof.

Why does the exterior tensor contain a compact highest vector of weight β?

The stopping-type calculation and the Dirac step of the layer bound use the following lemma. Coordinates are ordered by decreasing μ, with r positive and s negative ones, and a compact operator Eab is one whose two coordinates have the same sign. Let V be finite-dimensional and irreducible under the compact operators, with a highest-weight vector of weight L = μ+ρn−ρc for a strictly decreasing μ. Only the compact commutation relations are used, and V needs no positive form. The exterior algebra S has one generator eia for each positive coordinate i and negative coordinate a. The compact operators act on the generators as on the root vectors Eia, and on products as derivations. For positive a, b, the operator Eab sends eby to eay, and for negative a, b it sends eia to −eib.

Lemma. V ⊗ S contains a nonzero compact highest-weight vector x of weight β = L+θ−ρn = μ−ρc+θ. Here θ, written ρhol in the kernel chapter, has value s/2 on positive coordinates and −r/2 on negative ones.

The extreme vector. The wedge products eT over sets T of generators form a basis of S, and eT has weight ∑(i,a)∈T (ei−ea). For the form in which this basis is orthonormal, contraction is adjoint to exterior multiplication, so Eab* = Eba on S. Let T0 consist of the generators eia with a < i, whose negative coordinate comes first. The weight of eT0 is θ−ρn. On a positive coordinate c both equal the number of negative coordinates before c, and on a negative coordinate c both equal minus the number of positive coordinates after c. Every compact lowering operator kills eT0. For positive coordinates b < a, the operator Eab replaces a factor eby by eay. Then y < b < a, so eay is already a factor and the product vanishes. Two negative coordinates are handled in the same way. Thus eT0 is a lowest-weight vector of weight ν = θ−ρn.

Dominance. The weight L+ν is again dominant for the compact operators. Take coordinates a < b of the same sign with no coordinate of that sign between them, and let k be the number of coordinates of the opposite sign between them. Then ρc,a−ρc,b = 1, ρn,a−ρn,b = k and θa = θb, so La−Lb = μa−μb+k−1. This difference is a nonnegative integer m, by the 𝔰𝔩₂-string through the highest vector of V. Since μa > μb, we get m > k−1, hence m ≥ k and (L+ν)a−(L+ν)b = m−k ≥ 0. This is the only use of strict decrease.

The component lemma below, applied to V, to S and to its lowest vector eT0, now gives the tensor x of weight L+ν = β.

What does the lemma give for U(2,1)?

Take signs (+,−,+) and μ = (2,0,−1). Then ρc = ρn = (½,0,−½), so L = μ, while θ = (½,−1,½). The generators are e12 and e32, and T0 = {e32}, of weight (0,−1,1) = θ−ρn. The compact group U(2)×U(1) acts on the coordinates 1, 3 and on the coordinate 2. There V has highest weight ((2,−1),0), and β = (2,−1,0) is the weight ((2,0),−1). The two generators span the standard representation of U(2) tensored with the weight −1 of U(1). By the Pieri rule, (2,−1) ⊗ (1,0) contains the component of highest weight (2,0), so β occurs in V ⊗ S in exterior degree one. The dominance margin is m−k = 3−1 = 2 = β1−β3.

Why does a lowest weight added to a highest weight give a component of the tensor product?

The component lemma is the following. Let V be finite-dimensional and irreducible under the compact operators, with a highest-weight vector w of weight Λ. Let U be a finite-dimensional space with a positive form, on which the compact operators satisfy the same relations and Eab* = Eba. Suppose that f ∈ U is a nonzero lowest-weight vector of weight ν and that Λ+ν is dominant. Then V ⊗ U contains a nonzero highest-weight vector of weight Λ+ν. For compact groups this is the component of Parthasarathy, Ranga Rao and Varadarajan[27]. The proof uses the commutation relations and two facts about a highest-weight vector w. The module it generates is spanned by products of lowering operators applied to w, and in it the weight Λ occurs only on the line ℂw. Indeed the commutation relations move raising operators to the right, and every nonempty product of lowering operators strictly lowers the weight.

An auxiliary module. Within each sign block the coordinates of Λ differ by integers, and so do those of ν, by 𝔰𝔩₂-strings through w and f. Hence the fractional part t of Λ+ν is constant on each block, and the integral part ⌊Λ+ν⌋ is dominant. Take the irreducible representation of U(r)×U(s) with highest weight ⌊Λ+ν⌋, and add ta to each diagonal operator Eaa. The commutation relations survive because t is constant on blocks. The result is a module T with a positive form for which Eab* = Eba, and with a highest-weight vector wT of weight Λ+ν. It need not integrate to the group, and only these relations are used. The construction of the terminal compact model gives an explicit realization of this integral representation.

A graph. Let U* carry the dual action. The functional ⟨·,f⟩ is a highest-weight vector of weight −ν, because Eab* = Eba turns the lowering equations for f into raising equations. Thus x0 = wT ⊗ ⟨·,f⟩ is a highest-weight vector of weight Λ in P = T ⊗ U*, where again Eab* = Eba for the product form. Let Γ ⊆ P ⊕ V be the submodule generated by (x0,w), a highest-weight vector of weight Λ. If Γ met 0 ⊕ V nontrivially, irreducibility of V would put (0,w) in Γ. By the second fact, (0,w) would then be a multiple of (x0,w), which is impossible because x0 ≠ 0. So Γ is the graph of an equivariant map from the submodule Z generated by x0 to V, sending x0 to w. The orthogonal complement of Z is a submodule because Eab* = Eba. The map therefore extends by zero to an equivariant Φ : P → V with Φ(x0) = w.

The tensor. Choose a basis (ei) of U with dual basis (ei*), and put xi = Φ(wT ⊗ ei*). The tensor ∑i xi ⊗ ei is the image of wT under the equivariant map T → V ⊗ U corresponding to Φ. It is therefore a highest-weight vector of weight Λ+ν. It is nonzero, because pairing its second factor with f gives ∑i ⟨ei,f⟩ xi = Φ(x0) = w.

Why does the stopping parameter have a discrete-series model?

The stopping type gives a regular Harish-Chandra parameter μ for H = U(r,s). To compare its coefficients with those of a discrete series, we need one such representation at μ. Its required lowest compact weight is L = μ + ρn − ρc on K = U(r) × U(s). Write n = r + s.

Number the coordinates from zero in decreasing order of μ. In La, the correction to μa is (n−1)/2 − a, minus the number of later coordinates of that sign, plus the number of earlier ones of that sign. This counts the two half-sums of roots, and μa + (n−1)/2 is an integer by the lattice condition. If a < b are consecutive positions within one sign block, the later count drops by one and the earlier count increases by one. Hence

La − Lb = μa − μb + (b−a) − 2 ≥ 0.

Indeed, successive μ-coordinates differ by at least one, so μa − μb ≥ b−a. The compact weight is therefore integral and dominant on each block. To realize it, set C = ∑a|La| and add C to every entry. In a block with shifted entries b1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ bd ≥ 0, put bd+1 = 0. Take bi − bi+1 copies of the highest vector in the ith exterior power. Each contributes one to the first i coordinates. Their tensor generates the irreducible module with highest weight (b1, …, bd). Apply this construction to both blocks and take the tensor product. Multiplying the action of (k₊, k₋) by (det k₊ det k₋)−C subtracts C from every torus exponent. This unitary scalar character preserves the invariant subspaces, giving an irreducible type of weight L. Highest weights in exterior tensor powers.

How does one determinant correct both sign blocks?

On U(2) × U(1) take the compact weight (2, −1 | −4), with the bar separating the blocks. Here C = 7, and the shifted weight is (9, 6 | 3). On U(2), three copies of the first exterior vector and six copies of the determinant vector give exponents 9 and 6. On U(1) the character is z ↦ z³. The determinant of the full diagonal element is z₁z₂z₃, so the exponent in the last block changes from 3 to −4 as well.

z₁⁹ z₂⁶ z₃³ (z₁z₂z₃)⁻⁷ = z₁² z₂⁻¹ z₃⁻⁴.

If one sign is absent, H itself is compact. The representation just constructed has a single compact type and its continuous coefficients are square integrable for finite Haar measure. If both signs occur, put u = min(r, s) and let h be a lower bound for the absolute gaps between opposite signs. For h > max(2n, 8n u), the compact type supplies a nonzero highest vector, the normalized kernel is square integrable, and the representation generated by its coefficients is a discrete series of parameter μ.

The single sufficient bound h > 8n² + 2n works in either signature since u ≤ n. At the distant scale t, distinct coordinate centers are at least t apart. Each coordinate of μ lies within A√t of its center for a fixed A. Every opposite-sign gap is thus at least t − 2A√t, which eventually exceeds the bound. We may now choose a model σ at μ. The coefficient identity on the stopping type and the isometry on its translates will put this model inside the restriction.

Why do the two compact types have matching coefficients on the whole group?

Choose any discrete-series model σ at the regular stopping parameter μ, using the existence just proved. Its lowest compact type W has the same highest weight L. The discrete-series parameter theorem gives the Casimir scalar ‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖² on its smooth vectors. On the restricted ambient representation τ the stopping-type calculation gives the same scalar on V. The highest-weight classification on the two compact unitary factors gives a compact intertwiner from V onto W. Its adjoint times itself is a positive scalar by irreducibility, so it can be rescaled to a unitary map φ. Hongyu He, signed Harish-Chandra parameters[28] · P. Etingof, highest weights for the general linear group, §27[29].

Matching the compact types has so far determined their inner products only at compact group elements. The parameter gap now does additional work. The orthogonality lemma for a separated lowest type has the following hypotheses. In a unitary representation take a smooth, compact-stable irreducible type of weight μ+ρn−ρc on which Ω has the prescribed scalar. Require every gap across signs to exceed nrs+1. If a compact intertwiner from this type into the Hilbert space has image orthogonal to the type, its image is orthogonal to every group translate of the type. The preceding descent yields gaps exceeding n³+2n+1 for μ, which suffices. The finite-layer estimate and the passage to translated orthogonality below prove the lemma from the one-position and analytic estimates.

Apply it to the direct sum τ ⊕ σ. Inside that sum take the diagonal compact type of vectors (v,φv). It has scalar ‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖² because both components do. The map (u,φu) ↦ (u,−φu) commutes with the compact action and has image orthogonal to the diagonal, since φ preserves inner products. The lemma gives orthogonality to (τ(g)v,σ(g)φv) for every g ∈ H. Taking the difference of the two component pairings gives

⟨u,τ(g)v⟩ = ⟨φu,σ(g)φv⟩   (u,v ∈ V).

At the identity this says that φ preserves inner products. At arbitrary g it describes how far translates of the compact type point in each of its original directions. Those values determine the lengths of finite sums of translates, which is what allows the compact map to extend to the required Hilbert spaces.

How do equal coefficients put the smaller representation inside the restriction?

Let Cτ be the closed span of vectors τ(g)v with v ∈ V and g ∈ H. Define Cσ in the same way using φV = W. For a finite list of pairs (gi,vi), let xi = τ(gi)vi and yi = σ(gi)φvi. By unitarity the inner product of xi and xj is the coefficient of gi⁻¹gj on vi, vj. The coefficient identity gives the same entry for the two y vectors. Write M for this common matrix of inner products. Then

‖∑ aixi‖² = a*Ma = ‖∑ aiyi‖².

A relation among the x vectors has squared norm zero, hence gives a relation among the y vectors. Subtracting two presentations shows that sending each x to its matching y defines a linear map on the span. The same identity makes it an isometry. It extends by completion to U from Cτ to Cσ. Its image is complete and contains the dense span of the y vectors, so it is onto. Left multiplication by h sends every label (g,v) to (hg,v) on both sides. Thus U intertwines on the spans and, by continuity, on their closures. This norm argument is the same one used to recover a cyclic representation from its coefficients. K. Kremnizer, Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction, Theorem 4.1[30].

On the model side, Cσ is closed, invariant and contains the nonzero space W. Irreducibility of σ makes it its entire Hilbert space. On the ambient side, Cτ is precisely the closure generated from V by derivative words. One inclusion uses the analytic-vector invariance theorem. For these compact-finite smooth data with fixed Casimir, the derivative closure is group-invariant and contains V. For the reverse inclusion, a smooth vector in a closed invariant subspace has every real derivative in that subspace by difference quotients. Complex linearity and repetition put every derivative word on V in Cτ.

j = inclusion ∘ U⁻¹,   jσ(h) = τ(h)j.

This is the direction needed in branching. The source of j is the whole discrete series. Its image is a closed copy of that series in the restricted ambient space. The construction works for each chosen model of μ. The coefficient test can now start with this map.

Three generators of a plane. In a two-dimensional Euclidean model let y₁, y₂, y₃ be unit vectors at angles 0°, 120° and 240°. In ℝ³ take x₁ = (2,−1,−1)/√6 and its two cyclic permutations in order. Each family has diagonal inner products 1 and off-diagonal inner products −1/2. The relation with all three coefficients equal to 1 has zero norm in both families. Every permutation of the three labels acts by an isometry on each plane. The map j sends yi to xi and intertwines those permutations. In the ambient ℝ³ its image is exactly the plane of coordinate sum zero. This example isolates the role of relations, the direction of the embedding and its possible proper image.
