Can the original highest weight appear again in a later derivative layer?

The comparison of compact types uses a fact about one representation. Let V be a nonzero irreducible smooth compact type of H = U(r,s), with highest weight L = μ+ρn−ρc and full Casimir scalar ‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖². Assume μ is strictly decreasing, the opposite-sign gaps are at least h, and h > nrs+1 with n = r+s. The claim is that every compact highest vector of weight L among the derivative words on V already belongs to V.

Set F₀ = V. Build Fk+1 by adding to Fk all vectors Eabu, with u ∈ Fk and a,b of opposite signs. Each layer is finite-dimensional. Commuting a same-sign matrix unit past an opposite-sign unit introduces only opposite-sign units, so induction shows that all layers are stable under compact derivatives. Every derivative word belongs to some layer. Let Pk be the orthogonal projection onto Fk. The adjoint of a compact matrix unit is again a compact matrix unit, so the perpendicular of each layer is compact-stable as well. The projections commute with the compact derivatives and preserve the highest-weight equations. P. Etingof, compact orthogonal complements, §2.1[31].

Write cK(γ) = ‖γ+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖² for the compact Casimir of highest weight γ. The quantitative estimate needed here concerns a nonzero compact highest vector w in Fk orthogonal to Fk−1, with k ≥ 1 and highest weight γ. It gives

cK(γ) − cK(L) ≥ 2k(h−n+1).

To obtain the factor k, represent w modulo the previous layer by an array A of coefficients in V, indexed by words of exactly k noncompact matrix units. Applying the words and projecting off Fk−1 maps these arrays onto the new orthogonal layer. Choose the preimage perpendicular to the kernel. The map respects the compact action, so its restriction to the kernel’s perpendicular is an isomorphism of compact modules. Hence A is nonzero and has highest weight γ.

Apply the mixed Casimir estimate for a single position. In this perpendicular space, the mixed term between the compact action on V and the action on any one word position has expectation at least (h−n+1)‖A‖². More explicitly, hold all the other positions fixed. In this one-position space the mixed operator splits into negative and positive eigenspaces, with positive eigenvalues ≥ h−n+1. The evaluation of a negative slice shows that an array with only negative components at that position evaluates into the previous layer. Test the chosen A against its own negative component, supported on just the fixed slice. This test lies in the kernel just removed. Their inner product is the squared norm of that component, hence is zero. Only positive slices remain. Summing their squared norms over all choices of the other positions gives ‖A‖². Expand the compact Casimir for the diagonal action on the array. Its part on V contributes cK(L)‖A‖². Its part on the word indices is nonnegative, being a sum of squared norms. Twice the mixed expectation occurs at each of the k positions. The total expectation is cK(γ)‖A‖² because A is highest. Dividing by ‖A‖² proves the estimate.

Now let u have weight L and satisfy the compact highest-weight equations in some Fm. Decompose it as P₀u plus the successive differences (Pk−Pk−1)u. A nonzero difference would again be highest of weight L. Its compact Casimir would have to exceed the same scalar by 2k(h−n+1). This is positive when both signature indices are nonzero, since then rs ≥ 1. If one index is zero there are no noncompact derivatives at all. In either case u = P₀u ∈ V.

A rank-two calculation. Continue the U(1,1) example with L = (21,−20) and gap 40. Take an orthonormal sequence e₀, e₁, … of weights (21+j,−20−j). Set E₁₂ej = √((j+1)(41+j)) ej+1 and E₂₁ = −E₁₂*. Their commutator on ej is (41+2j)ej, as required by the two diagonal weights. Starting with e₀, layer k is the span through ek. Its new line has compact Casimir increment 82k+2k², compared with the lower bound 78k. For k = 1 these numbers are 84 and 78. The full Casimir stays 800 because the two noncompact products cancel the growth of the compact scalar.

Why does orthogonality to the compact type persist under translation?

Keep the type V and its gap from the layer estimate. In its unitary representation τ, let B be a linear map from V to the Hilbert space that commutes with the maximal compact group K. Assume its image is orthogonal to V. We will prove that for every g ∈ H and u,v ∈ V,

⟨Bu,τ(g)v⟩ = 0.

Fix a nonzero highest vector u₀ of weight L in V. On a finite layer Fk, the functional x ↦ ⟨Bu₀,x⟩ is represented by the vector z = PkBu₀. Since V is a finite-dimensional compact representation, compact equivariance makes B commute with differentiation along its compact action. The layers are finite-dimensional and stable under this action because exponentiating a compact generator preserves its layer, and the two compact unitary factors are generated by such exponentials. Thus Pk also commutes with K. The compact highest-weight equations of u₀ carry over to z. By the layer estimate, z belongs to V. Since Bu₀ is orthogonal to V,

‖z‖² = ⟨Bu₀,z⟩ = 0.

The translates of u₀ by K span V by compact irreducibility. Commuting PkB past each translate gives PkBu = 0 for every u ∈ V. This works for every finite layer, so Bu is orthogonal to their union. For fixed u, the subspace perpendicular to Bu is closed, so it contains the Hilbert closure of the whole derivative module.

It remains to put τ(g)v in that closure. We apply the invariance theorem for a smooth finite-dimensional compact type of fixed full Casimir. For any vector of its derivative module and any noncompact Hermitian tangent direction Y, translation by exp(Y) lies in the closure of that module. The derivative bounds give a time step valid in every layer. On the compact subgroup each finite layer is already invariant. Every g has a polar decomposition g = k exp(Y). Applying the assertion to exp(Y), followed by the bounded operator τ(k), puts τ(g)v in the derivative closure. This proves the displayed orthogonality. For the diagonal compact type in the comparison of two representations, the orthogonal map B changes the sign of the second coordinate.

Which directions have positive mixed Casimir?

Fix the compact type V of highest weight L = μ+ρn−ρc in U(r,s). Put n = r+s. The coordinates of μ are strictly decreasing, and any two of opposite signs differ by at least h > nrs+1. A derivative in one noncompact position has a matrix index and a coefficient in V. The mixed Casimir measures the interaction of their two compact actions. We need its sign when one position of a longer word varies and every other index stays fixed.

The highest-weight calculation for one position puts each irreducible summand at weight L+ea−eb, with a,b of opposite signs. The Casimir formula gives the mixed eigenvalue θab = μa−μb+(ρn)a−(ρn)b+1−n/2. Throughout this calculation, the order of the two indices refers to their order in μ.

Suppose a < b. Let Ua count opposite-sign indices after a and Db those before b. Both counts are at least one because each includes the other endpoint. The total number of indices of sign opposite to a plus the analogous number for b is exactly n. Subtracting the two half-sum coordinates therefore gives (ρn)a−(ρn)b = Ua+Db−n/2 ≥ 2−n/2. Inserting this lower bound in the two possible orders yields

θab ≥ h+3−n ≥ h−n+1,   θba ≤ −h−1.

When both signs occur, rs ≥ 1 and the first bound is positive. If one sign is absent there are no such directions. The two sums of irreducible summands are orthogonal by compact unitarity. Thus on the positive sum the mixed expectation is at least (h−n+1) times the squared norm. In the U(1,1) example, the gap is 40. The two directions have eigenvalues 41 and −41, and the positive bound used in the layer estimate is 39.

What happens when a negative direction acts on the compact type?

The evaluation map Φ sends an array ∑ Eab ⊗ vab to the vector ∑ Eabvab in the representation. At this step assume that the full Casimir acts on V by c = ‖μ‖²−‖ρc+ρn‖². Centrality carries the same scalar to all derivative words. We show that Φ sends the whole negative sum to zero.

Evaluation commutes with the compact action by the product rule. Hence an irreducible summand with nonzero image would supply an isomorphic compact type in the image. By the sign calculation, a negative summand would give a nonzero compact highest vector of weight γ = L−α for α = ea−eb, a < b of opposite signs. Pair the full Casimir with this vector w. A same-sign pair contributes (γi−γj)‖w‖² for i < j because its raising derivative kills w. For an opposite-sign pair, use [Eij,Eji] = Eii−Ejj and Eij* = −Eji. The contribution becomes −(γi−γj)‖w‖²−2‖Ejiw‖². Add the diagonal contribution ‖γ‖²‖w‖² and discard the final negative squares. Dividing by ‖w‖² gives

c ≤ ‖γ+ρc−ρn‖²−‖ρc−ρn‖².

For γ = L−α the right side minus c is 2−2(μa−μb)+4⟨ρc,ρn⟩. To bound the last term, twice the absolute value of each compact half-sum coordinate is at most n. Twice the absolute value of each noncompact half-sum coordinate is at most its number of opposite-sign indices. Those numbers sum to 2rs, counting each opposite-sign pair twice. It follows that 2⟨ρc,ρn⟩ ≤ nrs. The difference is at most 2(1−h+nrs) < 0. This contradicts the ceiling and proves the one-position vanishing.

For a word of length k ≥ 1, suppose every slice at a specified position belongs to the negative sum. If that position acts directly on the coefficient, fixing the other letters factors the evaluation through Φ, so it vanishes. To bring any specified position next to the coefficient, interchange adjacent letters. Each error is a commutator, a linear combination of single matrix units replacing two letters. It therefore belongs to Fk−1. This proves that the original evaluation is zero in Fk/Fk−1, exactly the quotient tested in the highest-weight argument.

In U(1,1) the hypothetical lower weight is (20,−19). The ceiling would bound the full scalar 800 by 20²+19²−39 = 722. In the two-letter word E₂₁E₁₂e₀ the lowering letter acts last in time. Reversing the order gives zero because E₂₁e₀ = 0. The original word equals the commutator on e₀, namely −41e₀. It vanishes in the new quotient while retaining a nonzero value in the original type.

How quickly can repeated noncompact derivatives grow?

Translation by exp(Y) will be recovered from the derivatives in direction Y. For this argument V may be any finite-dimensional compact-stable space of smooth vectors with a common real full Casimir scalar c. Let Fk be its layers of derivative words. Choose R ≥ 0 bounding ‖ν+ρc‖ for the finitely many diagonal weights ν of V. A noncompact matrix unit shifts a weight by ea−eb, of length √2. Acting on a weight basis of V therefore spans Fk by vectors whose shifted weights have norm at most R+√2k.

Every compact highest weight in this finite layer satisfies the same bound. Split the layer orthogonally into irreducible compact types and apply the compact Casimir formula on each one. For x in the layer, the compact Casimir expectation is at most ((R+√2k)²−‖ρc‖²)‖x‖². Subtract the full expectation c‖x‖². The compact terms cancel, and every opposite-sign pair has adjoint sign −1, giving a sum of squared norms. With d = ‖ρc‖²+c, this proves

∑εa ≠ εb ‖Eabx‖² ≤ ((R+√2k)²−d)‖x‖².

Let Y be a Hermitian off-block matrix in the real Lie algebra, with Frobenius norm S = (∑|Yab|²)1/2. Write T = ∑ YabEab on smooth vectors. The triangle and Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities bound ‖Tx‖ by S times the square root of the displayed energy. Put A = R+√max(0,−d). The square root is at most (A+√2k)‖x‖, as one sees by squaring. Since T sends Fk into Fk+1, iteration gives, for v ∈ Fk,

‖Tmv‖ ≤ Sm ‖v‖ ∏0 ≤ j < m (A+√2(k+j)).

For the unit vector e₀ of weight (21,−20) take R = 29. At depth zero the energy bound is 29²−800 = 41. Directly, only E₁₂ contributes, with squared norm 41. The growth in later layers enters one factor at a time in the product.

How do local Taylor expansions control an entire group translate?

Let W be the Hilbert closure of the union of the derivative layers. Write U(t) = τ(exp(tY)) for the unitary one-parameter group in the direction above. The desired assertion is U(1)W = W. The argument uses one step size for vectors from every layer.

Fix v ∈ Fk. Differentiating U(t+δ)v = U(t)U(δ)v at δ = 0 gives U(t)Tv. Repetition gives the mth derivative U(t)Tmv, of constant norm ‖Tmv‖ by unitarity. To bound the Taylor remainder after degree m−1, pair it with its own unit direction using the real part of the Hilbert inner product. The scalar Taylor remainder bound gives the vector remainder norm at most |δ|m‖Tmv‖/m!. A zero remainder already satisfies the bound. MIT 18.014, Chapter O, Theorem 2, Taylor’s formula with Lagrange remainder[32].

Multiply the product bound by |δ|m/m!. Each majorant is the preceding one times |δ|S(A+√2(k+m−1))/m, which tends to |δ|S√2. When this is below one the majorants eventually decrease at least geometrically, even if the first several grow. The remainder tends to zero. The limit of the multiplier is independent of the initial layer k.

U(t+δ)v = ∑m ≥ 0 (δm/m!) U(t)Tmv,   |δ|√2S < 1.

Choose an integer N > √2S and set δ = 1/N. At time zero all algebraic vectors belong to W. Suppose that at time j/N every algebraic vector has its translate in W. In the Taylor series for the next time each coefficient is such a translate, because every Tmv belongs to a finite layer. Finite sums and their norm limit belong to the closed subspace W. Induction reaches time one. Continuity extends the inclusion to all of W. Applying the same argument to −Y gives equality.

In U(1,1) take Y with both off-diagonal entries one and diagonal zero. Then S = √2 and N = 3 works. Each step has limiting multiplier 2/3.

For a general group element, one can find the required direction directly. Let J be the diagonal signature matrix and set P = g*g. The defining equation g*Jg = J gives Jg*J = g−1, hence JPJ = P−1. Diagonalize the positive definite matrix P and put Y = (log P)/2, taking real logarithms of its eigenvalues. Conjugating by J exchanges P and its inverse, so JYJ = −Y. Thus Y is Hermitian with zero same-sign blocks. Its exponential preserves J because exp(Y)J = J exp(−Y). Now k = g exp(−Y) preserves J and satisfies k*k = exp(−Y)P exp(−Y) = I. It follows that k commutes with J and lies in the block compact group. This proves the polar decomposition g = k exp(Y). Compact translation preserves each derivative layer because it conjugates off-block matrices to off-block matrices and preserves V. Thus τ(g) preserves W, supplying the last step in the translated orthogonality argument.

How can lowering the smaller parameter preserve the occurrence?

Keep the ambient discrete series π of G = U(p,q) fixed. Suppose the smaller discrete series σ of H = U(p−1,q) already occurs in its restriction. We want to replace μ by μ − ej. Assume the separated chamber hypotheses at both endpoints, including the opposite-sign gaps of at least 200(n+1)³, where n is the size of the defining matrices of H. Assume also that the midpoint μj−½ differs from every ambient entry λs. The first task is to find a vector in the desired summand of the smaller tensor.

Let J be the given nonzero bounded intertwiner from σ into π. By unitarity its adjoint intertwines in the reverse direction. Put P = J*/‖J‖, so ‖P‖ = 1. Write z for the fixed positive coordinate and Eab for the ambient complexified matrix-unit derivatives. On a smooth ambient vector η form the column Φ whose ath entry is P Eazη. Conjugating the matrix unit by the embedded h−1 changes its row coordinate while fixing its column z. Thus

Φ(π(h)η)a = ∑b (h−1)b,a σ(h) Φ(η)b.

This is the action on σ tensored with the dual defining representation of H. By regular tensor translation, the lowered parameter gives a smooth summand with projector pj and map rj into its Hilbert model σ′. For q > p−1, apply the translation theorem to the negated smaller Hermitian form. Both smaller signs occur because p ≥ q ≥ 1 and p+q ≥ 3. Negating the form gives the same matrix group, compact subgroup, diagonal parameters, smooth action and matrix-unit derivatives. It exchanges the two sign blocks, preserving the opposite-sign gaps. The dual tensor form and its scalar on each summand both change sign, so the same maps and projections give the decomposition for the original form.

Take the spectral variable w = −μj + (n−1)/2. At w the smaller quantum determinant is zero. Its comatrix CH(w) acts on smooth columns by djpj, where dj = ∏b≠j(μb−μj) is nonzero by regularity. In the ambient determinant at w+1, put the distinguished coordinate last and expand the last row, then the remaining last column. The diagonal term contains the smaller determinant at w on the left. Applying P brings the smaller-block derivatives through P, so this diagonal term vanishes. Each other term has the signed smaller cofactor followed by EazEzc, in that order. The two expansion signs give a common minus. On every smooth η the resulting identity is

cG Pη = −∑c [CH(w) Φ(Ezcη)]c,   cG = ∏s(λs−μj+½).

The half-unit is the difference between the two ranks’ central-character shifts after increasing the spectral variable by one. The midpoint assumption makes cG nonzero. If pjΦ vanished on every smooth vector, every summand on the right would vanish since Ezcη is smooth. Then P would vanish on a dense subspace, contradicting ‖P‖ = 1. We have obtained some smooth η₀ such that pjΦ(η₀) ≠ 0.

A smaller step in U(2,1). Put T = 6,000. Take λ = (4T,2T,0) of signs (+,+,−) and μ = (3T+½,−T+½) of signs (+,−). The merged sequence is G+, H+, G+, G−, H−, so the starting pair satisfies the discrete branching criterion. Lower the last μ to −T−½. The ambient opposite-sign gap is at least 2T and the smaller gap increases from 4T to 4T+1, all above 5,400. The midpoint is −T. Here w = T, the smaller projector denominator is 4T, and the ambient scalar is (5T)(3T)(T) = 15T³. Division by 4T normalizes the projector. The nonzero scalar 15T³ forces a transverse vector into its image. He, Definition 1 and Theorem 0.1 on discrete branching[33].

Why can the projected vector still be tested inside the ambient representation?

The formula for pjΦ uses operators in the smaller group. Every smaller-block derivative commutes past the intertwiner in the sense E′abP = P Eab on smooth vectors. Pull each cofactor back to the ambient generators in that block. Denote the resulting operator in row l, column a by Cblockla(w). Then

(pjΦ(η))l = P Rlη,   Rl = dj−1∑a Cblockla(w) Eaz.

Each cofactor is an ordered minor of size n−1. A factor is a single derivative plus a scalar, and one further derivative stands on the right. Consequently each Rl is a linear combination of words of length at most n. We use this bound when integrating an ambient coefficient with Rl applied to its moving vector.

Write ρ(h) = ‖h‖F² and let φ(h) be the complex conjugate of the σ′-coefficient of a unit vector v in its lowest compact type. The lowest-type decay estimate at the shifted parameter gives |φ(h)| ≤ Cρ(h)−(n²+1+n). For fixed smooth η, conjugating an ambient generator across the translate π(h) produces products of an entry of the embedded h and one of its inverse. Both matrices have squared Frobenius norm ρ(h)+1. Each pair costs at most ρ(h)+1 ≤ 2ρ(h). Repeating for at most n factors gives ‖Rlπ(h)η‖ ≤ Cη,lρ(h)n. Thus for any ambient test vector b,

|φ(h) ⟨b, Rlπ(h)η⟩| ≤ C′ ‖b‖ ρ(h)−(n²+1).

The last power is Haar integrable. Indeed the Haar volume of ‖h‖F ≤ B is at most a constant times B2n² for B ≥ 1. To see this, choose a small closed ball O about the identity in the real vector space of complex n by n matrices, lying entirely among invertible matrices. Each hO has the same positive Lebesgue volume since |det h| = 1. Their union for ‖h‖F ≤ B lies in an ambient ball of radius C B. For any matrix in that union, choose one h₀ whose translate contains it. All other such h lie in h₀(OO−1 ∩ H), a translate of a compact set of bounded Haar measure. Integrating this overlap bound proves the volume estimate. On the shell 2k ≤ ‖h‖F < 2k+1, the integral of the displayed power is therefore bounded by a constant times 2−2k.

Suppose all ordinary ambient coefficients integrate to zero against φ. For smooth b, move the formal adjoint of Rl onto b. The adjoint reverses each word and replaces Eab by its signed transpose generator, so it preserves smoothness. The resulting integral is one of those ordinary coefficients. For general b, approximate by smooth vectors. The integrated majorant above bounds the change by a constant times the norm of the difference. This proves that the word-inserted integral also vanishes for every b.

How does the surviving coordinate give a copy of the lowered representation?

Write x = Φ(η₀) and choose a coordinate l with (pjx)l ≠ 0. Put that coordinate in a column y supported only at l. The invariant form on a tensor summand gives a scalar cj satisfying

cj ⟨rjy, rjx⟩ = [y, pjx] = ε′l ‖(pjx)l‖² ≠ 0.

Testing one coordinate prevents cancellation between the positive and negative coordinates of the tensor form. In particular rjx and rjy are both nonzero. The translates of either span a dense subspace because σ′ is irreducible. Translate x and y independently so that their images a and b in the σ′ model satisfy ⟨v,a⟩ ≠ 0 and ⟨b,v⟩ ≠ 0 for the same lowest-type unit vector v. Denote the translated column of y by y₂. Equivariance of Φ writes the translated x as Φ(η₁) for a smooth ambient vector η₁.

Integrate the signed tensor coefficient [y₂, pjΦ(π(h)η₁)] against φ for a fixed Haar measure. In the shifted Hilbert model this becomes the integral on the left below. Schur orthogonality, with κ′ the positive reciprocal formal degree for this measure and the inner product linear in its second argument, evaluates it exactly. Duflo and Moore, orthogonality of square-integrable representations[12].

cj ∫H φ(h) ⟨b, σ′(h)a⟩ dν = cj κ′ ⟨v,a⟩ ⟨b,v⟩ ≠ 0.

If σ′ were absent from the restriction, the integral construction of an intertwiner would force every ordinary ambient coefficient against φ to integrate to zero. Expanding the very same signed tensor coefficient by coordinates gives a finite signed sum of the word-inserted integrals above, now with tests P* (y₂)l. Each would vanish. This contradicts the displayed Schur value and proves occurrence for μ − ej. Unitary equivalence carries the resulting intertwiner to every model of the prescribed signed parameters, as required in the descent.

How do we find a smooth vector that sees the occurrence?

At the start of a single lowering, an occurrence gives a bounded nonzero H-intertwiner j from the smaller discrete series σ into the ambient representation π. The distant occurrence provides such a map for the first pair of parameters. At a later move the preceding lowering provides one for the current pair. In each case the only datum carried into this argument is an intertwiner. We now choose a fresh smooth ambient vector whose coefficient average detects a copy of σ.

Write ρ for π restricted to H, and use inner products linear in the second argument. Fix Haar measure ν on H and let κ = 1/dσ for this measure. For a unit vector w in the lowest compact type of σ put φ(h) = ⟨w,σ(h)w⟩. Let n be the dimension of the smaller Hermitian space and put N = n+1. The gap for this step is 200N³. Here is why this suffices for absolute integrability.

For a noncompact group let q₀ be the smaller signature index, t the Euclidean norm of the logarithms of the singular values of h, and F its Frobenius norm. For t ≥ 1 the lowest-type coefficient estimate gives |φ(h)| ≤ exp(−25N³t/√(2q₀)). The coefficient of t in this exponent has magnitude at least 12N². For t ≤ 1, unitarity gives |φ| ≤ 1. Since F ≤ √n exp(t), both bounds imply |φ| ≤ C F−12N² for a fixed C. The shell count on the smaller group bounds the volume up to radius F by a constant times F4n² for F ≥ 1. The dyadic sum converges since 12N² > 4n². For a compact group the unit bound and finite Haar measure suffice.

Define the bounded averaging operator Ra = ∫Hφ(h)ρ(h)a dν. Since ρ is unitary, ‖R‖ ≤ ∫|φ| dν.

Put b₀ = jw. The kernel of j is closed and invariant. Irreducibility and j ≠ 0 give b₀ ≠ 0. The functional L(a) = ⟨b₀,Ra⟩ already detects this vector. To evaluate it, use ρ(h)jw = jσ(h)w, move j* to the first slot, and apply mixed Schur orthogonality for the unit vector w. This gives

L(b₀) = ∫ φ(h) ⟨j*b₀,σ(h)w⟩ dν = κ ‖b₀‖² > 0.

Choose any unit vector v₀ in the lowest compact type of π. Such vectors are smooth. The closed span of their translates, even starting with this one vector, is the whole ambient Hilbert space by irreducibility of π on G. If L vanished on every π(g)v₀, continuity would force L to vanish on b₀. Hence some ambient translate η is a smooth unit vector with L(η) ≠ 0, and therefore Rη ≠ 0. This step uses translates by the full group G. M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, Schur orthogonality for square-integrable representations[12].

Which normalization identifies the projected coefficient?

Fix this η. Since φ(h−1) is the complex conjugate of φ(h), inversion invariance of ν gives R* = R. Orthogonality of the unit-vector coefficient also gives φ ∗ φ = κφ. Integrating twice is justified by ∫|φ| < ∞, so R² = κR. Put ξ₀ = Rη and r = ‖ξ₀‖ > 0. We obtain ‖ξ₀‖² = ⟨η,R²η⟩ = κ⟨η,ξ₀⟩. In particular the last pairing is real and positive.

The integrated intertwiner construction applied to η gives a bounded H-map J from σ into ρ, with Jw = ξ₀. It begins on the dense subspace on which h ↦ ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ is integrable and sends y to its integral against ρ(h)η. Boundedness permits extension to the Hilbert space. Since the actions are unitary, J*J commutes with σ. Schur’s lemma makes it scalar, and evaluating it on the unit vector w gives that scalar as r². Thus i = J/r is an isometry. Now iw = ξ₀/r and ⟨η,iw⟩ = r/κ. For every ambient vector a, self-adjointness gives the required identity

∫H φ(h) ⟨η,ρ(h)a⟩ dν = ⟨ξ₀,a⟩ = κ ⟨η,iw⟩ ⟨iw,a⟩.

A test in a representation with two copies. Let H be the three cube roots of unity, with counting measure of total mass 3. Let σ(h) = h on ℂ and ρ(h) = diag(h,h,h) on ℂ³. Here w = 1, κ = 3, and R acts as diag(3,3,0), since the sum of a nontrivial character vanishes. Take η = (1,2,2)/3. Then ξ₀ = (1,2,0), r = √5 and the chosen copy sends 1 to (1,2,0)/√5. Both sides of the displayed identity equal a₁ + 2a₂. For instance the original map j can send 1 to (1,0,0). The test then chooses a different copy in the same two-dimensional character space. Taking (0,0,1) as the test would give zero for every a, even though the original copy still exists. This is why the construction chooses η by testing its translates. The same distinction matters when the ambient weight is lowered.

How is the size of the identity term used as the unit of comparison?

Diagonal normalization. The bounded-translate argument supplies an isometric embedding of the σ-model into the π-model, its adjoint P, and a choice of the bounded translate above with ℬ(100)‖Pv‖ ≥ 1. The branching eigenvector theorem, for the formal degree d′ > 0 of σ with respect to μ₀, supplies a smooth unit vector w and a scalar c₁ ≥ ‖Pv‖²/(2d′). For every vector a in σ the diagonal integral has the value

∫H conj(Φ(ι(h))) ⟨a,σ(h)w⟩ dμ₀(h) = c₁ ⟨a,w⟩.

In particular, setting a = w measures the positive diagonal scalar c₁ itself. The subgroup formal-degree estimate gives V₀ ≤ ℬ(11)/d′. Now 1 ≤ ℬ(100)²‖Pv‖² and 2 ≤ ℬ(1), so V₀ ≤ c₁ℬ(212). Multiplying by ℬ(1000) from the local integral gives c₁ℬ(1212). The bound for derivatives of the translated vector enters the integral estimate. The simultaneous estimates allow ℬ(600) for the derivative integral relative to V₀. A single exponent chosen for the full collection is C = 1000 + 600 + 11 + 201 = 1812. At scale b the construction takes B = b² and assumes log(8mb²) ≤ 6 log b. Thus ℬ(C) ≤ exp(q) with q = 6Cm⁴ log b.

Return to an arithmetic frame. At a real place τ choose an adapted frame Dτ that changes the arithmetic Gram matrix to signed coordinates, with Dτz equal to the distinguished coordinate vector. Then the distinguished column of DτgDτ−1 is exactly Dτgz. On the stabilizer the conjugate model reverses the coordinate order in both rows and columns. This is a continuous group isomorphism ρ with continuous inverse. The image of the arithmetic-coordinate Haar measure μτ is another Haar measure on the model group. Haar uniqueness gives ρ∗μτ = λτμ₀ for a finite λτ > 0. Consequently absolute integrability transfers in both directions. The integral of the norm gains λτ, as does the diagonal scalar after conjugating the smaller model's coefficient. Write cτ = λτc₁. If Iτ(g) is the absolute integral in these coordinates, then

Iτ(g) ‖Dτgz‖₂2m+5 ≤ exp(q) |cτ|,   2m + 5 = 2n + 7.

For example, multiplying μτ by 3 triples both Iτ and cτ. Their ratio still obeys the same bound. A. Sutherland, Number Theory I, Lecture 13, Theorem 13.3 (Haar uniqueness)[34].

What measure and weight does a single rational class contribute?

Write f for the number of real places, and fix a Haar measure on the product of their stabilizers. In the chosen frames this measure is κ times the product of the local Haar measures, for one κ > 0. The translated coefficient is a product of local functions, each absolutely integrable by the preceding result. Fubini gives an absolute integral of κ∏τIτ. Applied to the diagonal pairing it gives c∞ = κ∏τcτ. The product of the bounds therefore has exponent Q = fq and diagonal factor |c∞|. Haar uniqueness, Theorem 13.3[34] · T. Tao, An Epsilon of Room, I, Theorem 1.1.23 (Fubini–Tonelli)[18].

At finite places take a self-dual lattice Λ containing z and a nonzero level ideal 𝔪. Let K be the subgroup preserving Λ and acting trivially modulo 𝔪, and K′ its preimage in the finite stabilizer. Its finite-place Haar measure μf(K′) is positive and finite. The subgroup is open and contains the identity, and is compact because the stabilizer is closed and K is compact. For a translate g, the finite coefficient is the indicator of Sg = {hf : gfι(hf) ∈ K}. If h₀ belongs to this set, cancel gfι(h₀) inside K. Membership then says exactly h₀−1hf ∈ K′. Thus its measure is zero when it is empty and μf(K′) otherwise. For the identity term it equals μf(K′).

Given the adelic Haar measure, choose real and finite Haar factors whose product pushes forward to it. Indeed, multiplication identifies the two factors with the adelic group. Push forward any product of Haar measures and absorb the positive scalar from Haar uniqueness into the real factor. Let x be the chosen point in the stabilizer and γ a rational representative, set g = ι(x−1)γ, and write zγ = γz. The integral of the absolute coefficient factors as μf(Sg) times its real absolute integral. Denoting this adelic integral by Iγ(x), the estimate actually used in the sum is

Iγ(x) · (∏τ ‖Dτι(xτ−1)zγ,τ‖₂)2m+5 ≤ exp(Q) |c|,   c = μf(K′) c∞.

This c multiplies the value of the cusp form in the identity contribution. For every other class, multiplying the absolute coefficient integral by the supremum bound for the cusp form gives an upper bound on its weighted contribution. The congruence test and the lattice estimate for the sum then decide whether the identity term dominates. A simultaneous rescaling of the integrals and of the identity contribution preserves the comparison.

Fix the row input and pass through the grid

Suppose the reader prescribes a different smooth vector w ≠ 0. If the initial pairing vanished on every real translate of t(w), the real-translate vanishing theorem would make it vanish on t(w′) as well. Choose a successful translate h. Right invariance of the quotient integral moves h to ι(h⁻¹) in the core factor, where equivariance expresses it as a change of vector. Testing on vectors whose maximal-compact translates span finite-dimensional spaces suffices by the compact-finite vanishing theorem. This gives a vector v of that kind with P₀(y(v),t(w)) ≠ 0. Core surjectivity puts y(v) in the span of the bottom values Ψ₀ of allowed descending column chains. Rapid decrease makes the period linear on this span. At least one such Ψ₀ still pairs nontrivially. From now on keep that column chain and u = t(w) fixed.

At each stage the column function Ψi is a downward theta integral of Ψi+1. On the row side, apply the first i upward lifts to u, using real polynomials and finite test data chosen for those steps. At an odd stage the resulting period is a Fourier–Jacobi period, which also uses an auxiliary theta function on a line. At an even positive stage it is a Bessel period, tested along a unipotent subgroup against its character and paired on the smaller group. The grid comparison uses the conjugates of both the column and row functions. At the first stage, conjugating the initial period keeps it nonzero. A seesaw identity, which interchanges the two theta integrations, then produces a nonzero Fourier–Jacobi test.

Why can one insist on the prescribed tests at the next lift? Suppose all candidate Bessel periods vanish. Unfolding gives a Fourier–Jacobi functional vanishing on the images of all the allowed data under the transform taking test functions to the smaller pair of spaces. These images contain a nonzero lattice vacuum vector (fixed by the specified lattice translations) and its allowed Heisenberg translates. The vacuum irreducibility theorem for this functional forces vanishing on the whole vacuum space. Evaluating on the product datum from the preceding nonzero Fourier–Jacobi period contradicts this. Thus some Bessel test works. The Fock spanning theorem for the same class of functionals then gives a polynomial and a finite coset label at this step. Updating only these two entries leaves the earlier partial row lift fixed. The reverse transition similarly gives a Fourier–Jacobi test at the next odd stage.

Trace four steps. For m = 4 the sequence of nonzero tests is P₀ → Fourier–Jacobi at 1 → Bessel at 2 → Fourier–Jacobi at 3 → Bessel at 4. Each arrow asserts that a choice succeeds. The four complex values can differ. For any allowed even m ≥ 2, induction ends with a Bessel period at m, because the last index of the form 2k + 2 is attained at k = m/2 − 1. The partial row lift there is the full row lift.

Why one archimedean pair can serve every row

The preceding choices can depend on the row. At the final vertex the smaller Hermitian space is positive definite and the distinguished middle vector has negative norm. With the prescribed Harish–Chandra parameter and weight gap at least 120 times the cube of the terminal row rank, the space of compatible local Bessel bilinear forms at each real place τ has dimension at most one. Fix a generator bτ there, taking zero for a zero space. On pure tensors, fixing all coordinates except τ makes the terminal period a scalar multiple of bτ in that pair of local variables.

Here is the small algebraic step that joins the places. Write β(p) for this period on tuples, grouping the two inputs at each place as pτ. If any bτ vanishes identically, so does β. Otherwise choose p⁰ with every bτ(p⁰τ) ≠ 0. Replace the coordinates of p⁰ by those of p one at a time. At each replacement, cross multiplication cancels the unknown scalar for that slice. This gives

β(p) ∏τ bτ(p⁰τ) = β(p⁰) ∏τ bτ(pτ).

Only the product at the reference tuple needs to be inverted. Pure tensors span both spaces, so bilinearity extends proportionality to every pair of inputs. Composing the resulting common bilinear form with the real row-vector map for w gives Aw(ρ,ξ). Every tested period now equals Aw(ρ,ξ) times a scalar depending on the row, column and finite datum. A successful first test fixes a pair with Aw ≠ 0. Each further nonzero row has its own successful column and finite datum and hence a nonzero scalar. The fixed pair detects that row. The argument uses the real branching and decay estimates, core surjectivity, the two unfolding identities, Fock spanning and local Bessel uniqueness with its weight-gap hypothesis.

The base-coordinate contradiction

Let Pq be the base quotient map and iℂ its injective realization on the quotient coordinates. The coefficient identity says that a root of unity times a nonzero product of local constants times ψb(iℂ(emb(Pqy))) equals κ times a matrix coefficient for every input y and every reading b. If κ = 0, separation gives iℂ(emb(Pqy)) = 0 for all y. Positive rank supplies a coordinate vector e₀, and surjectivity supplies y with Pqy = e₀. Injectivity would give e₀ = 0, whose zeroth coordinate reads 1 = 0. Thus κ ≠ 0, and the common matrix can be normalized with base phase one. The quantitative estimate for discarded types, the theta adjoint input, and the bottom period, ascent and top weight-gap theorems enter as suppliers in this argument.

Why the jets at 2 and 3 stay integral

A theta entry is obtained by differentiating the normalized series at zero. A Taylor coefficient can have a denominator at a small prime even when its derivative is integral. For a series F(z) and a tuple m of nonnegative orders, its jet is ∂mF(0) = (∏j mj!)[zm]F. The estimate says these derivatives have p-adic norm at most 1 in every integral frame admitted by the construction. This gives valuation at least zero for the entries formed from them.

Fix a word u, its auxiliary tuple μ and a finite place w of residue characteristic p. The place is level-free when p differs from the word’s level prime T and the two auxiliary primes g₀, g₁, and lies outside the tuple’s excluded set Qp(μ). For each such place with p ≠ d, the entry bound covers every step i < m with even product of adjacent ranks NiNi+1 and every pair of lattice classes at that step. Level freeness supplies the admissible combination of translates. A separate test classifies primes of the host. The first class consists of the primes dividing the host modulus QS, including 2. The construction assumes a splitting bound of at least 3. It gives (−d/3) = 1, so d ≡ 2 mod 3. Also q ≠ 3. Thus 3 belongs to the first class if it divides QS, and to the split class otherwise. The integrality proof uses the congruence in both cases. The global proof obtains its inert Frobenius estimate separately.

The factor that cancels the denominator at 3

Work over the completed algebraic closure of the 3-adic numbers. A discriminant-normalized period lattice has invariants g₂³ − 27g₃² = 1. Complex multiplication gives an algebraic integer j = 1728g₂³. The proof chooses a curve W with equation y² = x(x − A)(x − B) matching these invariants. Its discriminant is 16[AB(A − B)]² = 1. The bound on j gives |A² − AB + B²|₃ ≤ 1. These two conditions imply |A|₃, |B|₃ ≤ 1, so the curve has integral coefficients.

Write b₂ = a₁² + 4a₂ for the standard invariant of this integral Weierstrass equation. The formal theta calculation contains b₂/12. To see how the factor 3 disappears, take the CM endomorphism β = −1 + 2ω, where ω = (1 + √(−d))/2. Its conjugate is −β, so β² = −d and ββ̄ = d. The kernel has order d prime to 3 and its nonzero points have integral curve coordinates. Both β and β − β̄ = 2β are 3-adic units. The endomorphism identity uses the following combination.

(β² − 1)b₂/12 = −((d + 1)/3) · b₂/4.

The integer (d + 1)/3 and the 3-adic unit 4 give an integral right side. For the example with CM discriminant −23 this reads (−23 − 1)b₂/12 = −2b₂. It works for every integral b₂. The formal curve theorem combines this bound, the integral kernel coordinates and the unit β − β̄ to bound every positive derivative of the correction series φ in the additive coordinate.

Here φ is the zero-constant correction that appears on passing from the local curve parameter to the theta expansion. The scalar theta theorem starts with a lattice period whose half-period images under ω and ω̄ lie outside the lattice. Each shift is killed modulo the lattice by a positive integer N prime to 3. The half-period and the shifted half-period have orders dividing 2 and 2N. The torsion translation formula then gives integral coefficients for each translate multiplied by exp(+φ) in the curve parameter. The formal change to additive variables supplies the inverse correction exp(−φ), using the positive-derivative bounds just proved. Multiplying the two exponentials cancels the correction. The argument passes to finite sums with integral weights and to the permitted integral frames.

The ordinary model and the fourth tensor power at 2

Here the CM condition d ≡ 7 mod 8 supplies an ordinary model W′ for a scaled period lattice, with integral coefficients, unit discriminant and |a₁′|₂ = 1. Let u be the 2-adic image of the scale factor. The invariants g₂, g₃ scale with weights −4 and −6, so the normalized discriminant gives Δ(W′) = u−12. Its norm is 1, hence |u|₂ = 1. Undoing the scale multiplies each coefficient aj by uj. The resulting equation matches the original periods and retains the unit a₁. On that model the 2-adic theta theorem gives integral series for the odd-order translates of the chosen half-period theta function in the curve parameter. The derivative of the formal logarithm is an integral unit series, and the proof converts the product of those series to integral additive jets.

To return to the given frame, the proof writes the fourth tensor power of each translate in four independent blocks of variables. After the integral linear substitutions, evaluate the derivative having the same multi-index m in each block. If J is the requested jet of one translate, this derivative is J⁴. Thus |J|₂⁴ ≤ 1 gives |J|₂ ≤ 1, even though 4 is divisible by 2. For example, with m = 2 and one variable per block, differentiation gives (2![z²]F)⁴. Integral linear combinations now give the required entries. The remaining geometric inputs here are the good ordinary CM model, the scalar half-period translation theorem at 2, and the normalized lattice and tensor identities used to express the original theta section.

How many factors of √p can a determinant lose?

At the discriminant prime p = d, a derivative can pick up one factor of a scalar S with |S|p ≤ √p each time it differentiates a matched pair from the exponential. Alternation in the determinant limits the number of such pairs. Fix a step of the lift with input and output ranks N₀ and N₁. For each label t there are two sets of coordinates, denoted by − and +. Write y±tab for the theta variables, where a indexes an input coordinate and b an output coordinate. The kernel already constructed has the form Θ = exp(−S∑t,a,buty−taby+tab)H. Here |ut|p ≤ 1, and every derivative of H at zero has norm at most 1.

Encode the differential operator by a polynomial G in two kinds of variables. The entries X±tra specify a frame row r. The symbol Z±tab stands for ∂/∂y±tab. A Young diagram is a left-aligned array of boxes with weakly decreasing row lengths. For each column of height h in a diagram, choose h distinct output coordinates in increasing order. Take the determinant of the matrix XZ on the first h frame rows and those output columns. Multiply these determinants over all diagram columns, signs and labels to obtain G. Substituting the derivatives for Z and evaluating the result at y = 0 leaves a polynomial in X. The entry theorem bounds every coefficient of that polynomial for every permitted column choice.

For a fixed label let α and β be the − and + diagrams. Write |α| for the number of boxes and α₀, β₀ for their top-row lengths, hence also their numbers of columns. One paired contraction on the symbols is the operator Δt = ∑a,b ∂Z−tab∂Z+tab. The contraction bound is

ΔtnG = 0   if   n > Ct = |α| − α₀ + min(α₀, β₀).

Expand each − determinant by permutations. Every term contains one factor from the top row per diagram column and |α| − α₀ factors from other rows. Differentiating a − factor from row r and output coordinate b leaves the operator ∑aX−tra∂Z+tab on the + side. For r = 0 it replaces column b of a + minor, when present, by the same vector with entries ∑aX−t0aX+tia in row i. A second top-row replacement in that minor differentiates a constant column or produces two identical columns. Both determinants vanish. Thus a surviving term uses at most β₀ top-row replacements on the + side and at most α₀ on the − side. Ordinary derivatives commute, so the other row operations can be moved past the top-row operations. Each contraction consumes either one of the |α| − α₀ other factors or one of those common top-row slots. This proves the cap.

Compute both contractions in a two-by-two example

Take one label, two input and two output coordinates. Let α have one row of two boxes and β two rows of one box each. Choose separate output coordinates for the two height-one − minors and both coordinates for the height-two + minor. Specialize the − frame’s top row to (1,1) and the + frame to the identity. In this paragraph number the matrix coordinates from 1 to 2 and omit the label. Write U = Z−₁₁ + Z−₂₁ and V = Z−₁₂ + Z−₂₂. Write the + matrix in row order as (a,b), (c,e), so its minor is B = ae − bc. The operator is G = UVB. Differentiation gives ΔG = V(e − b) + U(a − c). Applying Δ to either summand gives 1 − 1 = 0. The four derivative slots therefore accommodate just one contraction. To isolate it, choose H(y) = y−₁₂y+₂₂ and u = 1. In ΔG the coefficient of Z−₁₂Z+₂₂ is +1. Only the term of degree two in the exponential can complete the degree-four derivative, giving G(∂)Θ(0) = −S. If vp(S) = −½, this specialized value attains the one-contraction bound. These frames and this residual series illustrate the local algebra.

From formal contractions to a valuation of the lift

Why does Δ control an actual Taylor coefficient? For a fixed frame monomial Xm, assign a multi-index κ of derivatives to H in the product rule. The rest must differentiate matching − and + coordinates, with h derivatives of each sign at a coordinate that occurs h times in the exponential. Its coefficient has a denominator h!, while the two derivative factorials give (h!)². One h! remains in the numerator. Let nt count the matched pairs at label t. After extracting the derivative of H and the factor ∏t(−Sut)nt, the remaining coefficient A is an integer, a signed sum of binomial choices and the surviving factorials. In the symbol polynomial its exact identity is

(∏t nt!) A = [XmZκ] (∏t Δtnt) G.

The brackets extract a monomial coefficient. The factorial on the left counts the possible orders of the paired differentiations at each label. If one nt exceeds its cap, commuting the operators brings that power next to G. The right side vanishes, so A is zero in ℤ. For every surviving term |A|p ≤ 1, the derivative of H is integral, and the absolute value of the remaining scalar is at most p(∑t Ct)/2. The ultrametric triangle inequality gives the same bound on the finite sum. With vp(p) = 1, every nonzero coefficient has valuation at least −½∑t Ct.

The family uses a common bound for prescribed diagram rows. At step j = i + 1, write cj,t for this count at the chosen word. At an unmarked label it equals |α|. At a marked label it is |α| − α₀ + α₁ + β₀, where α₁ is the second-row length, or zero if that row is empty. Both values majorize Ct. In the example they are respectively 2 and 1. Thus all pairs of source and target lattice classes satisfy the entry bound −½∑t cj,t. The selected theorem uses it at each place above the distinguished discriminant prime that is free of the word’s level prime, the two auxiliary type primes and the primes excluded by the tuple.

For the bound on the whole map, let Mj be the maximum of ∑t cj,t over the finite set of words. At p = d the prescribed main term is Fram(j) and the error allowance is Fram(j) + Mj/2. Their difference is −Mj/2. There is a separate denominator valuation δ = vp(DΓ) for the chosen word’s integer DΓ. The entry-to-lattice comparison subtracts δ at each lift, with a credit ηδ at the first lift, where η denotes the comparison parameter. For a tuple used by the chain and a ramified source vector in the specified lattice, composition gives the column bound ∑j(−Mj/2 − δ) + ηδ. The comparison of jet entries with lattice maps and the kernel shape at d are the two arithmetic inputs to this transfer.

From the ramified entry to an integral pairing

At p = d the contraction estimate allows denominators. Fix a place w above p, a word, a used tuple μ, and a lift from stage i to i + 1. Assume p differs from the word’s level prime and its two type primes and lies outside the twist set for μ. Write vw for the integer-valued order at w and e = vw(p) for its ramification index. The local calculation measures an entry in units where p has valuation one. The lattice uses the integer order. This distinction determines what scalar we can divide out.

From polynomial coefficients to a lattice test

For each source class c, target class c′ and target column choice I, the differentiated theta kernel gives a polynomial QI in frame variables. Suppose its monomial coefficients all have norm at most p−B. The source lattice tests a different set of polynomials: products ∇J of the prescribed column minors in the source frame. To transfer the same bound, the proof writes QI = ∑J bJ∇J with every |bJ| ≤ p−B. The integral projection onto the span of the minor products fixes those products. Combined with membership in that span, this gives a bounded expansion without dividing by a change-of-basis determinant. The coefficients need only exist.

An input from the source lattice has, at each c, a rational representative whose functional takes values of norm ≤ 1 on every ∇J. Applied to QI, the ultrametric inequality therefore gives norm ≤ p−B. The kernel identity identifies the target reading with this value times a scalar of norm one. Two rationality facts now matter. Each class map sends the evaluated vector to the evaluation of a rational target vector. Also, the norm of each target reading is realized by an element of the coefficient field. Its nonzero order is an integer ≥ eB and hence ≥ ⌈eB⌉. Choose a in that field with vw(a) = ⌈eB⌉. Dividing the target vectors by a makes all their readings integral.

Where the stabilizer denominator goes

The lift sums the class maps with weights 1/|Γc|, where Γc is the stabilizer of the source class. Let n be a common positive multiple of their orders and write n = pkn′ with p ∤ n′. Then 1/|Γc| = p−krc, where rc = (n/|Γc|)/n′ is integral at w. Sum the divided vectors with these integral coefficients. Their readings remain integral, and preservation of the specified space of forms puts the sum in the localized target lattice. Thus the original output belongs to a p−k times that lattice. Its scalar has integer order ⌈eB⌉ − ek. The selected family has trivial stabilizers at i = 0 and uses n = 1 there. Later stages use the common stabilizer multiple DΓ.

Check one ramified denominator at 23

Take the local ring of ℚ(√−23) at 23. With π = √−23 we have vw(π) = 1 and vw(23) = 2. Model two class outputs by π−1 with weights 1/2 and 1/23. Each output meets B = −½ exactly. With n = 46 and k = 1 their sum is y = 25/(46π), of order −3 = ⌈2B⌉ − 2k. Indeed π³y = −25/2 is a unit at 23. This example checks the scalar and weights of a single lift. As a separate one-dimensional pairing, multiplication by y takes π³ times the local ring into that ring.

Why shifting the input makes the pairing integral

The column theorem adds the stage bounds on the prescribed ramified input submodule. Write δ = vp(DΓ). At d, each stage j has a uniform contraction allowance Mj/2, where Mj is the maximum over words of the sum of the local contraction counts. The main term cancels its copy in the error. The lower bound for the column is −∑jMj/2 − (m−1)δ for m stages. A further pairing with an integral terminal test can cost δ: if the column is a scalar times a localized integral vector, multiply the scalar by its rational period. The unrounded period estimate incorporates this cost. Other places supply their own bounds.

Let sw denote the resulting family allowance for the period on the input lattice N, in units with vp(p) = 1. The selected record keeps τw = ⌊ewsw⌋. The source lattice for the bilinear map becomes N′ = (∏w 𝔭w−τw)N. Locally this introduces a scalar of order −τw, so a reading of order at least τw becomes integral. A negative allowance shrinks the input lattice. The ceiling above normalizes an individual rational output. This floor specifies how far the global input lattice is shifted.

For each w, the selected tuple presents the localized row lattice Rw as the image of its test-column lattice under the projection followed by its frame map. On these columns the period equals the desired bilinear pairing times a phase of order zero at w. Local integrality therefore holds on all of Rw. A coefficient-field value integral at every finite place belongs to its ring of integers: the prime factorization of its principal fractional ideal has only nonnegative exponents. This proves the inclusion Bword(N′) ⊆ R∨, where R∨ consists of linear functionals integral on R. The conclusion also applies to a map with zero image. The proof of nonvanishing at the base tuple uses the separate positive-rank and separation argument.
